reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Giving Roland Emmerich an excuse to assemble sequences full of rampaging wooly mammoths, the director's "10,000 BC" has little going for it save its scenes of said prehistoric pachyderms. The tale of ancient humans battling their ways through the stone age amounts to nothing more than a typical hero quest with bursts of character-based intrigue. The production is solid, and Emmerich stages epic stretches featuring CGI beasties and scrambling tribesfolk. This vast cinematic canvas rings empty without a truly compelling narrative, but the film rates, at least, as a watchable diversion.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Takeshi Kitano’s first Outrage film plays like a reaction to all the complains among western cinephiles/critics/programmers about his recent work. As meta films goes this could not be a simpler case of beware of what you want: Kitano returns to his gangster film roots but empty it out of all the poetic tics that made films like Sonatine or Hana Bi popular in the festival circuit in the first place. There is no meaning here, just mayhem. Essentially a remake of Mario Bava’s Bay of Blood with a bunch of greedy Yakuzas dispatching each other in more and more creative bloody ways. The only way Kitano could drive the point home more is if he had called it “Yakuza Slasher”. Kitano ingenuity never falters, but the film also never complete leaves its straight jacketed conception.

This movie is goes through the politics inside the yakuza gangs in Japan. As a first part of trilogy, the movie discusses the story of several Yakuza groups in Japan, the politics and rivalry and mob wars between them in a raw and extremely harsh way. Movie had a detailed and slow narration in order to portray the brutality and unpredictability between them. Both as a director and an actor, Takeshi Kitano gave his best as a raw and rough character throughout the movie, extremely unpredictable along with other characters as the story goes on. reviews.text: "1922" is a slow, methodical look at guilt and the consequences of moral compromise. Adapted from Stephen King’s novella "1922," it's a film that will divide certain audiences. After a summer of successful, suspenseful King adaptations (IT, Gerald’s Game), this acts almost as an anti-king film. It’s a film that basks in its atmosphere; it's also a film that's solely focused on its characters rather than plot. Thomas Jane stars as Wilfred James, a dedicated ranch owner who conspires with his son Henry (Dylan Schmid) to murder his wife Arlette (Molly Parker) when she starts the process of selling the family ranch.

reviews.author: Evelyn Rose
reviews.text: Audie Murphy's penultimate film and the last American western directed by William Witney. The result is an interesting example of the studio system western at twilight. Though bookended by moments that pass this off as tribute to American military heroism, it's hard to know how anyone could come away convinced that joining the American military is a noble or rational enterprise. All that's expressed with conviction is Murphy's consumption by violence (he needs to be restrained from beating his own soldiers to death), Kenneth Tobey's bruised face scheming for desertion, the teeny-bopper soldier killed by his own bloodlust delirium ("Let's go get us an Apache!"), and his terrified baby brother who keeps saying he never should have joined the army. Its closing image of an American flag registers as a sick joke in a movie where the biggest threat to the lives of U.S. cavalrymen is clearly other U.S. cavalrymen.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Hunting for weird underground movies you tend to come across a lot of bizarre porn, stuff you just didn't realize would be someone's fetish at all (like girls stuck in quicksand or crushing snails in stiletto heels, or cosplayers doing CPR). I've occasionally seen some downright disturbing shit, but the worst nightmares this seems to be able to come up with (outside of snuff of course) are like latex and enemas and Peter Stormare. But despite its absurdly prudish grasping for some outré kink hell, this does manage to manufacture some moments of genuine dread and real empathy for its victims, especially in the scenes involving the dead girl's mother. You also get a taste of some early Mega Cage. There might've been a truly, exquisitely ugly version of this material, but Joel Schumacher probably wasn't the guy to handle it. A bad movie I like.

reviews.text: In Germany, this was marketed as a sequel to Rush. It was given the title Rush II but there are no similarities other than the name of the lead character being "Rush". At least he's called that in the german dub. The DVD from CMV's "Trash-Collection" offers a very scratchy print with skipping frames and bits of sound missing - pure grindhouse flair.The movie mixes genres like there's no tomorrow. There're elements of post-apocalyptic movies, westerns, Indiana Jones-type adventure, sci-fi, action, comedy, and zombie-films. It's great fun and definitely better than its predecessor. reviews.author: Ira Brooker
reviews.text: I try to start every new year watching something post-apocalyptic, and A Man Called Rage seemed like an appropriate title to bid farewell to the abyss of 2016. It's pretty average stuff on the whole - a steroid-powered antihero leads a ragtag team of commandos across a nuked-out Italian wasteland in search of a stash of uranium while fending off indifferent radioactive mutants and a vicious crimelord in a Volvo sedan - but it has a few good action sequences and there's a dorky likability to the thing. I gotta give it up for Rage's high-necked spandex tank top, the workout video soundtrack, and a plot twist straight out of "One Tin Soldier."

reviews.text: On the whole, this isn't really anything special: just another Italian post-apocalyptic film with some perfectly serviceable action and characters, but I really like how optimistic this film is. The heroes come out on top because they took the time to be kind and generous to a band of nomads, they acknowledge the importance of knowledge as much as physical resources, and it ends on a triumphant note of everyone coming together and resolving to build a new world, even as they acknowledge that it won't be easy.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: The decision to make all of the fantasy sequences black and white while the "real life" sequences are technicolor speaks so much to the unorthodox philosophy of this movie. The afterlife may not be such a bad place, but there's something more appealing, more romantic about the fleeting, the evanescent, the malleable. Eternity is static (everyone dead is wearing the uniform in which they died, clinging to the beliefs with which they died), while on earth there is love, sadness, hope, grief, learning, growing, drama, etc. The afterlife isn't necessarily heaven. Heaven is love, so choose life.

reviews.text: The fresh pain and grief of the war transmuted into a passionate, metaphysical argument for the idea of love conquering all, where the realm of the hallowed dead for all its splendor cannot hold a candle to a single rosebush pulsing with color in the land of the living. Its sentimentality is so exposed and confident that it becomes an act of defiance, a refusal to give in to the night. And just when you think it will not, cannot, get any better, the Archers bring the climactic trial to a brief halt to absolutely fucking dunk on the British for being history's greatest monsters even as the country was still celebrating beating back the damn Nazis.

The courtroom scenes were a marvel for a lot of reasons, including how diverse they were for a film made in the 1940s. That diversity seemed part of the point was also heartening, even if it doesn't exactly delve deeply into the concept.

The airmen in a modernist other world, with their new wings under their arms, carefully wrapped in dry cleaners' bags. The long, empty beach, interrupted only by a line of clothes. The joyous, impossible reunion.

Less concerned with being an epic melodrama but instead presenting a somber account of how these events played out from moment to moment, all on that night. The model work is especially impressive for the time but I can’t lie, there’s something about the technical mastery of the 97 version I missed here. This understands enough that the story speaks for itself but there’s just not that extra ingredient to really hook you in. This most definitely nostalgia speaking. So even if it doesn’t have a special place in my heart like the Cameron movie, it’s still very impressive and worth checking out.

reviews.text: It's such a shame when you have an incredibly complex and interest subject, but end up with a film as dull and insipid as this one. reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The idea isn't terrible - merging her poetry with her life, showing the harshness of isolation, which is a potent force in the story of a closeted queer person. But it doesn't come through properly. We get no real glimpse of her queerness; the most we get is a conversation between her and Susan Gilbert that touches the edges of it, mostly on Susan's side. And the terrible performances, especially from Cynthia Nixon (she can't even convincingly flail about), bog down the film. If the idea was to make their dialogue sound like rote poetry recitation, it worked, but it did not make the film better. Davies is better than this; so much better than this. I chalk this up to a failed experiment and bad casting. Let's stick with the humor and joyous exploration of a hidden queer life that is Wild Nights With Emily and leave this dreary mistake be.

reviews.author: Sam Van Hallgren
reviews.text: Extraordinary. A sustained aesthetic miracle of a movie. All the awards for Cynthia Nixon. It's a master class. Most stars of biopics get credit for pulling off uncanny impersonations; Nixon here makes you believe that you are actually witnessing one of the most brilliant, singular and eccentric minds of the 19th century. Advantage Nixon.

reviews.author: Brian 🐒
reviews.text: We are told, by the effervescent Vryling Buffam, that America cherishes hypocrisy. What would it mean to pursue the opposite—integrity? To live a life without hypocrisy, an honest life? An ethical life? Buffam, despite her outspokenness, declines to commit to that question. Its potential answer is too lonely for her to contemplate. She keeps her rebellion private, and urges Emily, her best friend, to follow the same course. “But I can tell you will not,” she sighs, “and I envy you your courage.”

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: I tend not to cotton as much to Linklater's occasional digressions into pessimism (I still need to revisit BEFORE MIDNIGHT but as of now I find its oversimplification of once-rich characters into petty, hyper-gender-specific squabblers to be a great disappointment). But from A SCANNER DARKLY's grim opening, which tacitly updates Rory Cochrane's good-natured stoner from DAZED & CONFUSED as a total burnout hallucinating bugs forever crawling over his skin, the deep cynicism and dejection is balanced by Linklater's natural sense of humor. Indeed, what I loved most about the film, apart from how beautifully the rotoscoped animation captures the fluidity of Dick's prose, is how it reorients Linklater's penchant for run-on philosophical chat as addict-speak.

The lens flares, the wide shots, the blue suit and red dress.It took me a while to calibrate my brain for this movie. The rhythm of any of Godard’s films is the equivalent to the song “gecgecgec” by 100 gecs. This is the only place you’ll find a 100 gecs reference in a Godard review. But my point is once things do start to click and you embrace that rhythm, everything makes a little bit more sense. I’ll probably appreciate this more on a rewatch.

In recent years, however — at least since 2009’s “Air Doll,” a contemporary fairy tale in which Bae Doo-na plays an inflatable sex doll who comes to life — the great Japanese humanist has downshifted towards more openly sentimental slice-of-life stories, churning out low-key masterpieces with such regularity and deceptive effortlessness that it can be easy to take them for granted.

At the end of all of his movies I just want to spend more time with his characters. I want to see what more will happen to them. I want to see how their relationships will develop, grow, fall apart. Koreeda's films are sometimes filled with familiar figures (in After the Storm there's the ne'er-do-well father, the frustrated ex-wife, the hopeful, yet realistic mother, and the also hopeful and realistic child), characters we have seen again and again, but they are so well-crafted and just so damn human that they deserve a longer existence than they are given.

reviews.author: Ken Rudolph
reviews.text: In early 1980s Italy, Marco was a leftist revolutionary who committed a heinous political murder and was granted asylum in France. Twenty years later, in 2002, he has a 16-year old French daughter, is completely disassociated from his Italian family in Bologna, and is an academic suddenly faced with deportation back to Italy to serve a life prison sentence. He goes into hiding, and sets in motion an escape with his reluctant daughter to Nicaragua. That is the set up for a fairly involving drama about the consequences of political terror, not only to the terrorists, but also to the associated, innocent family members. The film is slow to develop its action plot; but ultimately succeeds as an especially illuminating people story.

reviews.author: TheKinoCorner
reviews.text: I can see why Klimov was a bit disappointed in this film. It's beautiful, entertaining, and well-paced, but there is a sort of emotional distance to everything that's happening. This film may get confusing for people who don't know anything about Russia in 1916, but I thought that it made everything pretty clear. I see some people complaining about there being too many characters and they don't know who is who, but I don't see this as much of a problem. The two protagonists are Tsar Nicholai II and Rasputin, both of whom are easily distinguishable from the other characters.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A bit dry for an ostensibly psychological portrait of Rasputin and (to a lesser degree) Nicholas II, but Klimov's juxtapositions of baroque, colorful period detail and repurposed newsreel footage of the '10s and '20s do as much as Aleksei Petrenko's quietly deranged performance to communicate just how terminally stagnant Imperial Russia had become, a mirage of enlightened despotism whose ruling class was every bit as susceptible to mysticism and superstition as their supermajority of illiterate peasants. The sight of Rasputin slinking through lavish palaces looking like a beggar is so jarring as to lapse into farce, let alone when you see him tuck wads of rubles under his filthy tunic or coerce noblewomen into sex. Petrenko's wide-eyed, unblinking performance initially codes Rasputin as a true believer, but his constant manipulations reveal the shrewd plotter beneath the beatific seer.

reviews.author: Sean
reviews.text: Agony, is a story about the rise and fall of Rasputin, how he influenced the royal family of Russia and made a lot of enemies while doing it. Aleksei Petrenko portrays Rasputin as a mad man (he's known as The Mad Monk), getting into fights, sexually coercing women and muddling Russia's army into tactics that lead to heavy casualties in World War 1. While nowhere near as brilliant as Come And See. Klimov directs the film with expertise, it does get a little off the wall strange in some places, one can see he was influenced by Kubrick here a little, but that's just me. Petrenko is great and hard to keep your eyes off of as he has a commanding presence in this film. My only problem with the film was that there were to many characters and I often felt confused as to who was who.

reviews.text: Prior to his masterpiece "Come and See," the only film he is known for in the west, Elem Klimov produced and directed the definitive film on the life of Rasputin, one that does justice to the madness of the man. This is in no part to overlook the acting from Aleksei Petrenko, whose performance alone warrants a viewing from anyone. Yet, the real genius of the film comes with its engagement of Imperial Russia's agony, quite literally its painful, swift decay into historical detritus, at least from the perspective of the Soviets. Tsar Nicholas (or perhaps in the west Anastasia) may be the most well-known figures of this moment, yet Rasputin lags not far behind and perhaps best embodies the…

reviews.author: Jordan Rutherford
reviews.text: Klimov’s pinnacle is most certainly Come and See, but this movie is an interesting blend of documentary, biopic, historical drama and fever dream that should not be missed. It can feel a bit scattershot and a bit over populated by characters that are hard to keep up with as to who is who - and you may want to brush up on our 1916ish Russian history before watching - but this movie manages to be mezmserizing, much like its focal character. The scenes with Rasputin are particularly intoxicating and the acting by Aleksei Petrenko is visceral.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A Better New Hollywood rework of They Live by Night than Altman's remake made around the same time. The doomed romanticism is very close to Ray, but the post-war emotionalism gets filled in by Elton John songs. It has a certain New Hollywood contrivance to it—the poeticized loserdom against the couple's genuine attraction, the way things seem a little pat in their inevitable train wreck logic. Mutrux claims he conceived Bobby as a John Garfield character, and Paul Le Mat, who is quite good, is a little too 70s sensible guy for that, but he does well to avoid the more sentimental aspects. Lovely shot by William Fraker. It is a great couple on the lam car movie shot just around LA.

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: I guess some people think this is exploitative, but it and the people in it are so inspiring to me. I love Mark Borchardt’s obsession with film; how he talks excitedly about shooting on 16mm black-and-white reversal stock and then later spends months stuck at a flatbed, cutting his direct-market thriller together. Watching this at a time when everyone has an HD camera and edit suite in their pocket, it’s amazing to watch a group of people who probably have no formal training actually shooting, tracking, and cutting their own movie together. Using a camcorder to make a cheapo SOV version of Coven or Northwestern would’ve been copping out — they wouldn’t be movies.

It comes across as friendly and understanding rather than sneering, but it acknowledges that not everyone is cut out to make the Great American Movie.

I would sometimes have to drive around our neighborhood and find him: we could take away his car keys, but we couldn’t keep him trapped in our house. Most of the time he seemed blissfully unaware of his circumstances, but at other times I could see in his eyes that he knew he was losing control.

reviews.text: Religion has always been foreign to me. I’ve never had faith in any organised teaching or found virtue in the actions of religious groups. This is perhaps why I find films like Andrei Rublev so enticing. Depictions of people living their lives based on a belief system I reject is always fascinating, partly due perhaps to crass exoticism, but also because it highlights the spectrum of human existence whose irrationality I struggle to comprehend. Andrei Rublev is among the greatest films ever made to tackle religion because it highlights a series of important events in the life of one devout man without being a didactic sermon on faith. We see the importance of Christianity to Russian culture, nationalism and heritage…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: Early 15th-century Rus’ a land caught between the dying embers of Mongol overlordship and the rising aspirations of a Moscow-centered power. Shadows of the past loom, the Mongol-Tatar yoke, once iron-tight since the 13th century, has frayed, giving way to hazy murmurs of liberation and the slow forging of a new political order. This is a world being torn and stitched again, where princely dukes jockey for supremacy, and Moscow slowly emerges from fragmentation into something more potent, more unified.

reviews.author: YI JIAN
reviews.text: Really not much I can say, Andrei Rublev is a film meant to be lived, not watched, let alone read or listened. Tarkovsky was way ahead of his time, even until now in the 21st century we are still barely catching up to his artistry. His omnipotent camera dances around with the grace of a veteran ballerina, capturing the beauty of chaotic harmony with ease using his trademark looong takes. The film is massive, both in terms of theme and length. To this day I still have yet to see a work by Tarkovsky in which his overwhelming ambition doesn't show on screen. In a way, with it's awe-inspiring portrayal of medieval Russia, Rublev is Tarkovsky's Copper Bell.

reviews.author: Lara Pop
reviews.text: It always hits me like a ton of bricks in what degree a film's efficiency can depend on the director's technical expertise. It can be the dividing line between mediocrity and being a masterpiece. Andrei Rublev would be nothing without Tarkovsky. Since I do not aim to write an all-inclusive review detailing each segment of the film, I will cut to the chase and establish the centerpiece of my review, one particular quality in the director's immense skill repertoire which impressed me like nothing else in cinema has. That feature is duality.

reviews.text: Road to annihilation. Most of the drama is primal, but it is presented by Preminger in a less neoexpressionist manner than most post-war thrillers, the emotions are big and violent, but the images are as exhausted as the characters feelings. There are two people tied together until they can push their violent desires to its inevitable conclusion, and the movie is set to follow it in its determinist destructive logic. Preminger made this as a loan to RKO, and it is very instructive about the old studio system and how it relates to major auteurs. In some key eyes it does differ from his Fox thrillers: the images are a bit harsher, Mitchum presence hangs over everything and some of…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Angel Face is an outstanding film noir directed by Otto Preminger, not to mention an absorbing examination of infatuation. It stars Jean Simmons and Robert Mitchum, both of who provide impressively understated performances, with Simmons portraying the nefarious female with frightening believability. The dependable film noir themes of fatalism, fixation and passion associate themselves to the narrative right up to the bitter end, and it certainly owes a level of indebtedness to Tay Garnett’s The Postman Always Rings Twice. This is one of Preminger’s most preeminent movies.

reviews.text: “Angels One Five” (RAF radio lingo for altitude 15,000 feet) was the first British post-war production to deal with the Battle of Britain. And it doesn’t suffer from artificially injected aspects that fill up too much time of the 1969 movie (such as the lifeless romance of Christopher Plummer & Susannah York).

reviews.text: Apache Rifles recalls Delmer Daves westerns in its structure and character building. There is so much narrative whiplash in the final twenty minutes I contemplated giving anywhere between two to four stars, ultimately settling on an average score for a lame time jump and too tidy a bow on the proceedings. Audie Murphy gives another great performance supported by Michael Dante, Linda Lawson, and LQ Jones to name a few. Speaking of a Daves western, the former actor embodies the Jeff Chandler Broken Arrow recipe for his lead Native American performance. Linda Lawson is quite beautiful and LQ plays a solid part. The mystery aspect is the best part of Apache Rifles, unfortunately it gets tangled up in too much melodrama and stifled by an ending the writers seemed to throw their hands in the air for.

Jones!) and the capitalist puppetmasters who use them as muscle to wrest land away from the Chiricahua. A little surprised that Murphy — who, remember, was the guy who only agreed to star in The Quiet American if Graham Greene's anti-American sentiments were turned upside down — went in for something so (for its time) progressive and anti-military, which is to say, you still have to deal with redface, white saviors, and a whole lotta grey area around the intrinsic concepts of Manifest Destiny and the reservation system.

With that as a backdrop, a young woman and her talking cat (the result of a failed scientific experiment) search for a cure to illness and death, and wind up on a big and ridiculous adventure. This reminded me a good bit of Kazu Kibuishi's The Amulet in scale and color, but it also resembles various French comics and films, like The Rabbi's Cat, which also veers from serious to surreal, and manic to melancholy. This one was a lot of fun.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: With Aragami, Ryuhei Kitamura condenses the same low-budget verve of Versus into a 70-minute duel of words and weapons. Gothic folktale mood meets frenetic samurai action: one dark stormy night, a lost soul and his mysterious host in a sinister isolated temple, an otherworldly tale and the ultimate challenge. While the two central fights are fantastic kinetically-choreographed affairs that superbly utilize its limited single-room setting, it’s the before and after that makes Aragami such a fun watch. The dynamic between Takao Osawa and Masaya Kato is as exciting as their confrontations, shifting from cordial and tense to bizarre, funny, mythic as this fateful night progresses. A sleek and gorgeous exercise that ends on a wicked tease.

There are selections from some of the world’s foremost auteurs: Godard does a bit on bodybuilders, Altman stages an opera attended by asylum inmates, etc. Oddly enough, some of the best work is done by the lesser-known local British directors (this was a British production): Julien Temple mounts an amusing farce starring Beverly D’Angelo and Buck Henry (RIP), and Franc Roddam’s especially touching “tragic lovers” tale featuring Bridget Fonda’s first film role. It is not really an opera sampler for people who don’t know much about opera and the disjunction, in most of the selections, between the aria libretto and the images on the screen is likely to puzzle those who know the arias/operas.

reviews.text: People often mocks Tarantino preference of William Witney over John Ford and as absurd at it indeed is, I must say the trio of Witney/Murphy mid 60s westerns are among the richest takes on American official ideology contradictions and not that far behind Ford similar explorations. It helps that they are reflected in one of the more contradictory among Hollywood leading men. This one was the only I haven't seen before and it is as good as the other two. It is technically a remake of Phil Karlson's The Texas Rangers which I saw the other day as is a strong film, but this is far more expansive and troubling in its historical tapestry. Witney slow methodical direction takes it apart from most Murphy vehicles which tend to be more spare ands miniature in feeling. It has an exhausting quality as things simple get pushed and barely solved. A history of violence eating itself.

reviews.text: A nation born by brothers killing brothers. Witney's unadorned, upfront historical recreations have that forceful sense of realism deeply strengthend by the frequent focus on Murphy's eyes, which are probably the most honest thing I have ever seen on screen. Not only his eyes but also his hands putting a brother to sleep, a physical gesture that could only be reproduced by someone who had already lived something like it. Or maybe also when he sighs, which translates a kind of existential desolation I have very few times seen so acurately portrayed. A man who truly put his heart out there, exposed while acting - I've never seen someone so strong and so vulnerable, so imposing but also so pitiful.

reviews.text: Out of the ten movies included on John Carpenter’s ballot for Sight & Sound’s greatest films of all time list, four of them were Howard Hawks films. So it only makes sense that he would start his career in earnest with one of the most handsome and economical B-thrillers of the 1970s that remixes the siege movie dynamics of both the pragmatic hangout western camaraderie of Rio Bravo and the lean, mean, apocalyptically angry horror of Night of the Living Dead, and restages them in a post-Dirty Harry LA cops vs. street gang warzone environment. I think some of the old-fashioned simplicity of this used to make me underrate it a bit, but I’ve really come to appreciate what this manages…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Every time I see this I get more convinced that there's never been anything as cinematic as those pieces of paper getting hit in the first attack. A masterpiece of spare down understatement. A very elaborate thrill machine that is pitched as low key as possible and it is more devasting because of it. The only real mistep is the occasional cut for the patrol cops. Many filmmakers have tried a urban western, but Carpenter not only one of the few to really find ideal analogues, but his sense of stylization matches not only Hawks, but the genre's essential simplicity. It is also the key film on Carpenter career long Hawksian obsession not because it lifts the plot of Rio Bravo and a few other motifs, but because it turns Hawks dedication to the idea of men of work stoic accepting death and pushes it towards pure horror.

reviews.text: You know the iconic poster for this movie, with a giant woman sultrily terrorizing highway traffic? It's maybe a little bit misleading. This is really a James M. Cain-esque desert noir wherein a scumbag gaslights his alcoholic heiress wife. Gradually, sci-fi elements intrude, with special effects so crummy and low-budget they approach the avant-garde. A translucent giant, for example, wears a costume obviously left over from some medieval adventure movie and rides around in a spherical, diamond-powered spaceship. Once the radiation from his touch has enlarged the poor heiress, she's represented through an echoing voice and a manacled, Claes Oldenburg-style papier-mâché hand.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Obsession taken to its most demented plateau; an obsession so deeply rooted in an inherently psychosexual eschewing, eventually resulting in a misogynistic, detestable act of complete objectification, stemming from what began as mere observance, then the need to solely and entirely control—rather than to coexist—which has now spiraled into depths of madness only reached by the most abhorrent and, perhaps even more apropos, the most pathetic. What we see in this film is a culmination of a man’s failures, frailties, insecurities, misconceptions and delusions. It’s mortifying even to watch, but crafted so damn compellingly with such little regard for any and all of your sensibilities that you cannot look away, until suddenly it has escalated so far that looking away becomes all you can do.

reviews.author: getyaasstomars
reviews.text: Powerful and thought provoking cinema. Enigmatic in it's meaning and not likely to be understood by general audiences. Barnyard is a challenging and complex look at homophobia, racism and sexism. Few film's explore the LGBTQ+ community in such an honest and sensitive way. This is the perfect film to watch for Pride Month. The scene where Biggie Cheese sings Mr Bombastic is striking in it's brutal honesty. The animation is gorgeous and bold in it's use of colours. The decision to make the male cows have udders is nothing short of genius. Barnyard is on par with Kubrick's work in how much detail is put into every frame. There's so much symbolism and hidden meanings that it makes films like Andrei Tarkovsky's Stalker look like children's entertainment. Barnyard received negative reviews when it was released but it's really a misunderstood masterpiece that's crying for reappraisal.

reviews.text: I have a story to tell about this film. I lived my entire childhood in a small town without movie theaters. In 2000 I had the opportunity to go to the cinema in a big city with three friends. We didn't have access to the internet nor did we know about the most anticipated films, as we were practically children. Looking at the movies being shown, I thought: "John Travolta as an alien in a space adventure? It must be cool". I convinced one of my friends to watch it with me. My other two friends went to see Gladiator in the other room. They had the time of their lives. That day still haunts me.

On Friday nights, the owner will play 35mm prints from his collection, and there’s no rhyme or reason to the selections, and seemingly no commercial considerations either. Sometimes he’ll play a middling Italian horror movie. A few weeks ago he played The Winslow Boy. And this week he played one of the most reviled films of the 21st century - a movie that has stubbornly resisted any kind of cult following, contrarian critical reappraisal, or millennial nostalgia. Us Kingsway-heads were excitedly DM’ing each other all week about it.

reviews.author: Will Menaker
reviews.text: In the decade following the end of World War II, the Yakuza emerges from the radioactive ashes of Hiroshima and grows like a cancer. They go from fighting rape-crazed American GIs in refugee camps to getting huge contracts with the US army in time for the Korean War, insinuating themselves into virtually every aspect of the Japanese economy and state. This unfolds in a sometimes dizzying blur of shootings, stabbings, assassinations, betrayals and alliances. There is a main character, but he often disappears for long stretches as the individuals involved get eclipsed or snuffed out by the grim and news-like recitation of events.

They are instead made into snapshots of their final moments. Obituaries made stylistic, but these images aren't pretty. They're rough, hewn and caked in dried blood. reviews.text: Life is a bit like poetry, with beautiful stanzas, verses, clusters of events, and periods of progression, as well as regression. Each day in someone’s life, each week, each month, each year, they experiences situations which change the path of their existence. Events which begin to define their spirit and mold their psyche into something magnificent and unique. Some paths are bumpy, some are smooth, some are winding, and some are graceful. Not graceful in the sense of elegance, charm, or admirability. Rather, a path of grace is a way through life determined by a flash of divine wisdom: one specific exposure to the soul, or core, of what it means to be human. There is darkness in every corner…

A WWII drama-comedy, "Before Winter Comes" follows a refugee camp in Austria just after WWII to help displaced civilians. Played straight, the comedy falls into place when it needs to and it is funny. While it didn't feature any of J. Lee's amazing cinematography that I'm use to from him, the Austrian location are gorgeous. There was a love triangle that didn't add to much and I will admit the movie loses steam in the second half, but the incredible cast of David Niven, Topol, John Hurt and Anthony Quayle keep "Before Winter Comes" afloat. I don't have to much to say on it, but it was still a funny and enjoyable movie.

Israeli actor Topol is good as an interpreter who is the cunning type, always running between the raindrops. Director Steven Soderbergh first mentioned the project idea to Michael Douglas during the filming of Traffic in 2000, but the powers of cinemadom judged the story "too gay to be commercial," so it languished in need of backing till HBO finally took a gamble on it as a made-for-TV movie. Two Golden Globes and eleven Primetime Emmy Awards later, Soderbergh's vision is complete, and the tale of the last decade in the life of the world's most extravagant piano-playing showman has been told, masterfully.

Sometimes you just need to scream. A lit candle. Fuckin' curses. Reelz of film. Tickling is fun. The line-up. Ding-dong. Lights, camera, action! Cows like to graze. The letter from Mum. reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: Another in the great tradition of films about filmmaking, this is the rare entry about something other than a screenwriter, director, or actor: in this case, a meek British sound engineer, hired away to a scruffy, disreputable Italian studio to provide quality sound design for a grotesque-sounding giallo full of garish misogynist tortures. The film's genius is in never showing the film that the engineer (played by Toby Jones) is working on—the camera just focuses on his wincing responses, as he stabs cabbages or sizzles water in a pan to make the proper squelching or burning sounds. His descent into the hell of creative participation in something he doesn't believe in strongly recalls the madness of Barton Fink, but the…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: a second viewing makes Strickland's most interesting obsession more apparent: his insistence on pragmatically examining genre tropes. here it manifests with what's still my favorite element of the film, the intense focus on the analog tech. slow zooms on audio pots or tape coursing through a Nagra. but that pragmatism has the side effect of robbing this of some genuine tension; the guy having a mental breakdown trying to get reimbursed for a plane ticket is very funny, but by design it's not particularly exciting. Jones' meek protagonist's sensory unravelling just strikes me as banal, the obvious choice, and (for me anyway) it doesn't disintegrate audiovisually anywhere near abstractly or anxiously enough. i'd be very interested in seeing the original short version of this Strickland apparently made in 2005.

Moreover, sound is the most important element in the film, excessively used to expose tension and discomfort through screams and other random sounds, aiming to provoke sudden scares or create sharper tension in the scenes. Here lies the first flaw of the work: I see a lack of identity and understanding of what the film truly aimed to be. These elements are used so unevenly that both the rhythm and the story itself…

reviews.text: The Hammer we all know and love went belly up in the 80s and their film library was bought by various media distributors. It wasn't until 2008 that the company released its first film in over 30 years, Beyond the Rave, via MySpace in 20 episode uploads. I personally didn't bother with it back then, and not just because my internet was the old kind. Hammer, known for castles and fog, doing a movie involving raves and the Iraq War? reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Not bold enough to use its context with the war to make any meaningful commentary on it, so why bother bringing it up at all? A cheap ploy to make the main character more sympathetic? A lame way to give him a time limit? Regardless, it's an easy way to lose my interest almost immediately, and it never regained it. A few moments suggest this could have been at least visually appealing (a pile of bodies on the dance floor?), but it has that slick modern horror look without any of the gothic flourishes of the original Hammer run. Nods to its predecessors were few and poorly executed (mostly in the casting of side characters), and worst of all, it's edited like a seizure.

reviews.text: utterly devastating. addiction as being trapped inside your own head while everyone else around you has to deal with all the worst aspects of yourself pushed to their limits -- a loving father decides that the only way he can have his perfect family is in death, perverting a biblical scripture when there is no god directing his actions, only the madness that is induced by a chemical imbalance that no one had the courage or care to redress him for. nic ray's weird discontinuities and abrupt tonal shifts are perfect corollaries for an america imploding on itself during the cold war -- the descent of a patriarch into a theocratic fascist feels so real and scary, because i think so many of us have had fathers with two faces, hoping to never see the ugly side but knowing it is there all the same... as much as i hate to admit it, freud was right about some things.

reviews.text: An anthology of very moody, meticulously-stylized horror shorts by Bava which opens with grounded, domestic psychological torment (the first murderous Giallo phone stalker thriller short has to have been an inspiration for the opening scene of Scream as much When A Stranger Calls and Black Christmas) and eventually transitions into full-blown primary color gothic surrealism with monster decapitations and doomed curses. Boris Karloff as a Serbian vampire farmer (with a uniquely romantic element thrown into the bloodthirst lore) has all the Hammer production design, fog, gore, and Poe atmosphere you could want, and the last short in particular is peak Bava. All candles, dolls, and hideously frozen, possibly re-animated corpses in a spooky, decadent artificial dreamscape that feels like the birthing ground of Argento. The crash zoom on the dead elderly seance woman holding the cat in her rocking chair had me losing my mind.

reviews.text: Damnation and the erosion of reality, both will arrive slowly and take you over. Bava most labored film, every image careful thought and cultivated with so much care actors appear to move in slow motion even in face of jump scares. This might be the first movie that was really thought as a star vehicle for its filmmaker, forget host Karloff, Black Sabbath is all about allowing Bava to flex his muscles on different registers of the fear film. No wonder the Italian cut (avoid the AIP one at all costs, the wurdlak will visit you otherwise) ends with the rather abstract The Drop of Water. The variety of the tales are an essential part. The sum of the three stories is larger and more effective than their individual qualities.

reviews.text: Years ago, on a dreary Autumn afternoon, a boy, in his early teens, sat down to watch television. What he found, alone in a shadowy living room, was a horror film. Marked by age, the film was not contemporary, but it was immediately engrossing. Shadows mixed with pastel bursts and blood-red smudges. Sets were imposing and old-world, crammed with hidden nooks and dangerous corners. Characters were drawn bearing sharpened nails and teeth and carved brows. The name of the film was unknown to the boy, or perhaps the images were simply the stuff of his own afternoon nightmare. Regardless, the now-adult who once encountered a horror film on a rainy Saturday afternoon remembers those images every time he comes across…

reviews.text: Of all the things a movie about a witch-haunted woods must do, especially a movie which grounds itself materially in the documentation process, the provenance by which notice of this haunting is delivered or transmitted to the viewer, the recipient of this transmission, to be haunted itself and in turn to haunt the viewer is the most vital, most important task of such a movie. For what are movies but hauntings themselves? A spectral emanating from the past which attaches itself to a viewer, binds itself and becomes part of. If such a movie is constructed as to resist its own propensity to haunt, and instead is actively cast aside, unhexed even during the viewing, it undoes itself, undoes the pact, the covenant, between the viewer and itself.

That stuff is done pretty well and definitely helps to paper over the cracks where writing is concerned, since all that is very basic and familiar material done with little panache here. MJW too, has a nice presence to him and is certainly more than convincing as an ass-kicker, which is why Blood and Bone mostly works as nice dumb DTV fun.

The more Mitchum I have the luxury to see, the more I’m thinking the reason his cool, could-be-icy stoicism works so well is because he filters his own brand of aloofness through an underlying weathered edge and emotional vulnerability at its core. And it’s this rare mix that makes him such an inherently captivating presence on screen, his steely demeanour the guard beyond which a myriad of man's darkest secrets are seemingly hidden down deep. reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: Wise and Musaraca, fresh from Val Lewton’s smithy where they forged iron-dark horror noirs, leave wet city streets for the open range. They don't create an aesthetically noir Western (there are no chiaroscuro flow is his) but a philosophically noir Western. The powerful are abusing the system. The fix is in against the little guy. Bad choices are made that fester until they need to be lanced or they will burst. This is the young Mitchum, a noir hero who "always has a consciences breathing down his neck,” the ancestor of fatalistic Mitchum archetype in The Lusty Men and Eddie Coyle. The reason these characters work is because they are standing on the shoulders of this younger Mitchum.

You can imagine my joy, then, when Bloodsucking Pharaohs in Pittsburgh does this in the first few minutes. "How is the rest of the film?" you ask. "Shite," is my reply. Here, Nancy Allen is the prototypical leading lady, she gets cast in Travolta's movie, and at first he falls for her and wants to love her, but eventually he realizes she's just a dumb whore and goes from cajoling her to barking orders at her to make her hit her marks, remember her lines. Eventually, he gets her killed and moves on to make more movies, taking from her the only useful thing to him: her death rattle. Pretty dark!

reviews.text: I am genuinely depressed about the fact that there was no 1990's Showtime/John Carpenter Horror Anthology Show primarily because it means we only have Body Bags in which to enjoy Carpenter's delightful Horror Host Turn as The Coroner, and only the three stories contained within Body Bags to suggest the television program it could have been. reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: "Tales From the Crypt" by a different title. Essentially a knockoff produced for Showtime but never picked up, and just like that show this has a bunch of cool actors and occasionally burns off some flashy style. The first segment, Carpenter's "The Gas Station", is easily the best one. He self-consciously rips himself off (stealing shots right from HALLOWEEN, for instance) and there are a lot of fun cameos (including Buck Flower). The other two episodes are naturally littered with cheap irony and some nice gore effects, and hey, they're like 25 minutes apiece, no big deal. Best part of the whole thing is the host segments featuring "The Coroner", basically The Cryptkeeper but it's John Carpenter in scary makeup making shitty puns, which is pretty tough to beat.

The last two don't quite have the effectiveness and mood of the first story but they're still weird and fun and the whole thing is connected by John Carpenter himself doing an extended re-animated cadaver standup bit.

It was always nice seeing him in a role, whether it was in Revenge of the Nerds, The Long Riders, or Escape from L.A. Of course, I never watched Lizzie McGuire but I’m glad that Carradine was able to work for decades & more importantly, had a loving family & judging by random Instagram posts that were in my feed two months ago, had many friends.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: The days leading up to a hate crime are recreated via a series of arresting images. Two punks kiss beneath a swirl of exploding bottle rockets. A gaggle of white football players gyrate to trap rap around a gigantic fire in a field. The details of a stomping are recalled in hyper slow-motion. A bloody silhouette clings to the phone as a son tries to explain to his parents that his brother is dead. There's a roughness to the performances that recalls Penelope Spheeris' SUBURBIA, but the power contained in these compositions more than makes up for any amateurish acting or didactic message delivery. The ethereal cinematic talent on display is undeniable, and Jameson Brooks is now totally someone to keep our eye on.

reviews.text: Hal Asbhy's biopic of Woody Guthrie - an acclaimed film in its day, but not much seen or talked about anymore. Its most praised element is Haskell Wexler's cinematography, and the praise is merited. What a gorgeous movie. So many impossibly lovely "magic hour" shots. A lot of period pieces feel overpolished, but this movie's Dust Bowl era looks convincingly real, like a place actual people actually lived. I like that this is a movie about poverty that looks beautiful. I'm still recovering from being immersed in the dreary porridge tones of Women Talking, which communicated that This Is A Very Serious Subject So We're Not Here To Have Fun. Times can be serious and bad but also possess beauty.…

reviews.author: Dirk Diggler
reviews.text: Lockdown ain't that bad when you can spend time watching good movies like this. Perhaps a bit too long and slow-going, but personally didn't care, maybe because I got all the time in the world at the moment. It's a movie as much about a specific period of time, as it is about Woody Guthrie. Great music, of course, and it's absolutely beautiful visually, striking and hazy photography, often reminiscent of Days of Heaven. The movie oozes authenticy in its depiction of the Great Depression, and its texture is tangible, you can almost smell the dust and feel the dirt. It's a wonderful biopic that feels big, but is still so laid-back and understated, both sweet and tough. This hit just the right spot this afternoon. Finishing this Ashby day with Being There!

She thinks she's hit paydirt when she sees a grainy video of an exciting punk band, seemingly singing a song with the refrain of 'Surfin' to Pass the Time'. reviews.text: Broken Embraces feels like a more mature Almodóvar film. For starters, there's no rape or sexual assault. Though that doesn't mean the characters are able to escape Almodóvar's usual melodramatic pain and torment. Broken Embraces has less comedic trimmings than many Almodóvar efforts and takes itself sufficiently seriously. It's a complex, twisty story with multiple timelines and perspectives. It draws on memory, love, and pain to create a ripe melodrama that is very engaging. It has some very cool shots, and Penélope Cruz steals the film (as usual). De una u otra forma, ambos tiempos conviven en el presente. Esto es importante porque todo flashback aparece a raiz de una fijacion y/o narracion de un personaje a otro y no al estilo de El Padrino II.

Taken together, these films – 10 to Midnight, The Evil That Men Do, Messenger of Death, Kinjite and Murphy’s Law – comprise a provocative and under-rated group of inter-related works, toying with the notion of what might be termed “reactionary nihilism”. Indeed, they effectively make the Bronson / Thompson partnership one of the more vibrant teams to work in the disreputable exploitation B-movie field, perhaps second only in the actor’s career to his films with director Michael Winner in the 1970s. Yet the association between Bronson and Thompson also began in the late 1970s when they teamed for several unusual films that…

reviews.text: Fernando Di Leo’s Milano Calibro 9 is a real tour de force. The stage is set in the opening - a botched money handover ends in 300 grand going missing and an extremely mean spirited death and torture montage at the hands of psychopathic gangster Rocco. Cut forward three years and Ugo Piazza is being released from jail - only to be hounded by Rocco, who believes Ugo took the money. The film forsakes the action focus that makes up much of the Poliziotteschi genre in favour of a more drama and character focused approach. It's a film with a story to tell, and doesn't need to keep the interest up with constant action scenes. The characters are well drawn…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: It perhaps shouldn't be surprising how much overlap there is between the politics of spaghetti westerns and those of poliziotteschi. Though the former genre started earlier and was very much on its last legs when the latter came to the fore, they nevertheless share a firm belief in anti-elitism, and the almost inevitable corruption of those in power. Ultimately, the films reveal, even the most idealistic cogs in the state's machine find themselves bowing before the machine's power when push comes to shove.

reviews.text: In 1976, Evelyn Foster started to become concerned with her daughter's ability to transition from kiddie films to more adult fare. She knew that the day would come when her daughter could no longer make it in commercials and Disney movies, and would have to start taking on more mature projects, if her fledgling acting career was ever going to achieve any sort of sustainability. So, after intercedence from the Los Angeles Welfare Board, a prominent UCLA psychiatrist, and governor Jerry Brown, the then 12 year-old Jodie Foster was allowed to appear in Martin Scorsese's history making film "Taxi Driver", altering her future as an actress forever.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Carny is a bizarre little late 70s/early 80s oddity. Jodie Foster and Gary Busey head up an amazing cast who take on tiny roles (Meg Foster, Tim "Dollman" Thomerson, Elisha Cook Jr., Fred Ward, Kenneth McMillan to name a few). Everyone delivers fantastic performances, which is lucky considering how character focused this is. Busey in particular is wild as the sad caged clown, and Robbie Robertson of The Band is quietly affecting as his partner in crime. Foster, of course, steals the show. The plot is mostly subdued, the setting grimy and real, but the film spins into delightfully bonkers territory in its last act. Carny is nothing spectacular, but it has that special brand of gritty yet comforting charm found only in films of this particular vintage. I dug it a lot.

reviews.text: Iranian American film director Tony Zarrindast was known as the "Persian Ed Wood". His 1996 film Werewolf was considered “a gift from God” on Mystery Science Theater 3000. Here at Movieland, this film is also a gift from that same god. The film stars Iranian actor Behrouz Vossoughi alongside Sybil Danning and Colleen Camp (not the only movie they both appeared in). Camp is going for grounded while Danning… she packs her performance into a rocket ship and launches it into a black hole… in a good way. I need to make a pilgrimage to the filming location in Pasadena - it was shot in David Lee Roth’s mansion, but I don’t even care about Van Halen, I just want to be in the presence of the set from this production. Some movies can’t be labeled good or bad, only wholly and uniquely the vision of its insane director, and this is one of those movies. 🐈‍⬛

It's huge Hollywood widescreen but then wonderfully claustrophobic in the cramped bomber planes. The one bomb raid scene from inside the plane has amazing anxiety marbled with dry humor. Nichols is also playing with time and editing in a very progressive for the time way. His first four films were really on the cutting edge of New Hollywood. The cast is also littered with pros across the board and it is a joy to…

reviews.text: Having just spent an entire day watching Walter Matthau movies, I can confirm that he can make a womanizing dentist likeable, a drunken deadbeat little league coach lovable, and an incorrigible shyster ambulance-chasing attorney downright adorable. But he can also pull another trick, which is to suck most of his natural humor and charisma out of his bone marrow but remain intriguing, watchable, and even magnetic. His Charley Varrick isn't the romantic kind of career criminal - he unapologetically works with violent killers, and he's not saving up to get his kid brother an operation. He, like the men in many Siegel films (including this one), is just doing his job. He's smart, though, and that gives him a fighting chance, provided he can stay smart and broke rather than dumb and rich. A lesson for us all!

"People kill for money like this" Charley acknowledges in the one of the few moments the movie betrays looking at a bigger picture. Most of the time everyone is just to focused to get going to think much beyond their resigned beat down desperation. Matthau's Varrick carries himself with the same distance be it dealing with sex or mourning or violent thugs after him. And somehow his atitude rubs off on everyone else in the picture, all parts of the same machinery, except from Robinson's young gun who is too dumb to get it and Baker hitman who probably had never had a soul to get crushed in the first face. The only victory here is to be able to still be going in the next minute.

Save from Stephen Dorff’s young punk/plot catalyst who seems to drop off a separated movie, everyone seems tired and ready to drop dead and outside the Harvey Keitel/Famke Janssen scenes which have some warmth, the gloomy tone never leaves. Some fine blunt action and location work, and very willing to let its old-fashioned fatalism run its course.

reviews.text: Contains the most life-affirming closing shot of any gangster film I've ever seen. After a hundred minutes of cat-and-mouse where undercover cop Ko Chow struggles at every opportunity to not get sniffed out as a traitor nor get shot at by his own unconcerned superior officers, the film ends with a deadly Mexican standoff both between the gangsters and the police. Caught between sides, Chow realizes he doesn't belong to either and has only gotten so far out of sheer loyalty; however, at this point he's no longer sure whether that loyalty is to his force, his girlfriend, or his partner in crime. Perhaps it's simply to see things through. We celebrate him regardless.

A saxophone breaks through the bustle of Hong Kong's dense streets, a keening mating call searching for a partner that never responds.

reviews.text: A British Mercenary (Sean Connery) arrives in Cuba in the employ of Batista's forces to put down Castro's revolt, only to have a chance encounter with a former flame (Brooke Adams), who operates a cigar factory. The mercenary's attempts at rekindling their romance are complicated by the fact that she is married, along with the danger that the revolution presents their affluent class. The fact that the husband (Chris Sarandon) is a contemptible lout does not make the choice between the men less difficult, though having a stake in the ruling class does complicate the mercenary's growing disillusionment with his employers.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Much like Richard Lester’s earlier Connery vehicle Robin & Marian, an uneasy marriage between 70s cynical revisionism and romantic sincerity. Not quite the triumph of that earlier film, but Lester clear images carries a punch. Lester by this point has most leaved behind his satirist tendencies, but he still very able with the occasional absurdist image which the disaster movie inspired script offers him plenty of opportunity for. It has predictable little to say about Cuban revolution beyond the occasional blunt commentary (Batista getting introduced watching Dracula will always be funny), but the film longing for idealism be it romantic or political remains rather moving.

reviews.author: Mark Mooney
reviews.text: Richard Lester’s Cuba is set against the backdrop of the 1959 Cuban Revolution. The plot follows British mercenary Robert Dapes (Sean Connery), hired to aid Batista’s regime, who becomes entangled in a rekindled romance with Alexandra Pulido (Brooke Adams), a factory manager’s wife. Their personal drama unfolds amid political upheaval, weaving themes of love, loyalty, and inevitable change. The ensemble cast, including Jack Weston, Hector Elizondo, Chris Sarandon and Denholm Elliott, delivers solid performances, with Connery’s commanding presence anchoring the film.

reviews.text: The introduction of this one kind of rambles through shots of mid 19th-century Cuba, go figure. It portrays the events leading to the 1958 Cuban Revolution and the rise of power of Fidel Castro. It hosts a few diegetic Christmas songs catering to a December 21st release date in '79. While portraying a few historical events, the film focuses much more on Connery's romance, and the historical events focused on are more political than military in nature, which for me are turn-offs all around. Also this film portrays a variety of factions all seemingly with different motives, some of which may or may not have been hidden, and all of which were fairly confusing to me. Even as such there are several entertaining scenes with good action and fairly entertaining dialogue. It's not a terrible film all things considered.

reviews.author: Burrows
reviews.text: Ultimately, I think I come out of this film on the PLUS side of the ledger. However, the romance woven into slice of life story about the latter days of Cuba's Bautista government tends to ruin things. Sean Connery is charming, sure, and Brooke Adams is a fascinating presence--plus her character has agency. However, the whole thing is at odds with what Lester really wants us to look at. He wants to show us the management at the factory, the class structure of the society, the corruption of the political and military leaders pre-revolution. And that's the material which is interesting.

We've got the rods, the royalty-free rock, Bruno Vesota (seriously, this motherfucker is everywhere), 30-somethings playing teens, and we've got the debut score of film music icon John Williams, who seems to be showing his affection for Elmer Bernstein's jazz scores with a main theme that is to The Man with the Golden Arm what Richard Band's Reanimator is to Bernard Herrmann's Psycho. What we don't have is the direction. Even the lower end of AIP's teen films of the 50s knew…

reviews.text: A surprisingly solid bit of Irish-centered fantasy from Disney, Robert Stevenson's "Darby O'Gill and the Little People" combines leprechauns, banshees, and a young Sean Connery for an endearing and enduring piece of work. Revolving around an Irishman whose greed lures him to run afoul of the indigenous and titular leprechauns of the film's village setting, the narrative is a refreshingly layered combination of wish-fulfillment, adventure, romance, and effective chills. The robust story is supported by a production featuring textured designs, evocative faces, and energetic pacing. The film offers a pleasing and satisfyingly engaging experience.

Russell is great here, he elevates this from being an average run-of-the-mill cop drama, as well as the supporting cast which includes Scott Speedman, Brendan Gleeson, Ving Rhames and Jonathan Banks. As a David Ayer written film, you definitely know that this thing is gonna have it's fair share of brutal moments, most notably the opening robbery that shows the murder of FOUR INNOCENT BYSTANDERS, JESUS FUCKING CHRIST DAVID. Overall, Dark Blue is a solid yet forgotten cop drama, which is also one of Ayer's better works, especially comparing to the shit he's been churning out nowadays.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: A white man makes a film with a bunch of African-American actors that portrays a white man who pretends to help African-Americans but is actually using them and working with the Klan. Is it self-awareness? Is it oblivious? Is it something in between? These questions are unanswerable, because the film that is made is beyond reason, beyond convention, and beyond ridiculous. It is farce, certainly, and probably laced with satire, though who can say. Certainly the filmmakers were aware of the stereotypes they were clowning on, but if they intended it as satire or just thought they could get away with it, I don't know. I suspect a bit of both.

reviews.author: Patrick Pryor
reviews.text: Darktown Strutters hits its stride (get it?) when it shuts up and lets the magnificent costumes and production design and wild music do the talking. I loved the down'n'dirty accentuated L.A. locations, like the comic strip rib joint and police station featuring an oversized racist map. And the plumage and spangles and hand painted art on some of those motorcycle outfits and pig costumes and pot-sickle(!!!) vendors really made the movie stand out from other Earth bound gritty blaxploitation fare. I felt like I had died and gone to absurdist hog heaven whenever the search for Cinderella cooled off and Darktown Strutters treated us to a Stax artist serenade or fast motion klansmen chase or Colonel Sanders adult baby surrogate. With style for miles and some biting humor to boot, I'm glad my eyeballs absorbed Darktown Strutters on a theater screen and saw every Jack Fisk designed caricature loom large!

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A rather dissonant Blaxploitation farce that moves freely between anger and low comedy. Written by George Armitage under what I can only assume was influence of some very heavy shit and directed with straight forward care by William Witney of all people. It is the sort of film whose last act includes a madcap motorcycle chase in which the heroine is chased down by KKK bikers in full attire. While most directors under Corman stable would likely underline all the offbeat humor, Witney just let the material and its many radical tone shifts register by itself which just makes things even more absurd.

reviews.text: I love finding little gems like this. Dead End is packed with great performances, fantastic cinematography, and a few Depression-era social messages as well. It’s set in the tenement slums near the East River (roughly East 53rd Street), an area that the opening scroll informs us was just beginning to become gentrified. There is melodrama in the story but also real grit, and Wyler’s pacing is such that even when it hits a weaker moment, it doesn’t stay too long there.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Dead End premiered on Broadway in 1935, in the heart of the Great Depression. According to legend, Eleanore Roosevelt saw it three times, prompting a command performance at the White House which, in turn, resulted in FDR commissioning a slum study. The headline of the New York Times review of the film was “... 'Dead End' Presents Anew a Prima Facie Case for Revision of the Social Scheme.” All of which is to say that, when this story was first told, it was a vivid tale of the world in which its viewers lived, and one with a clear social agenda.*

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: One of the best films I've seen this year! During the first hour, it's easy to just see this as a stellar old-school western, with its stunning rural setting, desolate landscapes, memorable characters, and a remarkable soundtrack that is used sparingly to set everything up. But, with its whimsical, surreal visual elements and off-beat wit, it really becomes a genre-blend after that. It's meditative, but also humorous. Whimsical, but conceptually profound. Poetic in every way possible. It's similar to many Lynchian films in that it feels like a dream. It's as if you're quietly floating along with a man who is transitioning from total and absolute innocence to experience and full-fledgedness. Because of its experimental nature, there will definitely be things I missed, but that only adds to my want to rewatch.

His performance is simple, but he is able to do so much with his seen, angry performance. It’s Susan Sarandon as Sister Helen who is carrying the film with meaning and emotion. If you experience any emotion in this film, it’s because of her. She drives the story beautifully with her wonderful character arc. Tim Robbins’ direction includes some very impressive and well planned long takes the help show conversation. The sad feel of the movie feels realistic and dark. If a bit too tedious for me, Dead Man Walking is a harsh, character-driven drama that features two great central performances and some impressive direction.

reviews.text: Dead presidents has one of the best cuts in a film I've seen, the transition from one scene to another is amazing. its So smooth and well done that I had to rewind it a few times because its so good. the film itself is underrated, I haven't heard many people talk about it or seen it on any lists or YouTube videos about it. I loved the directors other film menace 2 society and was just as impressed with this. A coming of age film, domestic drama, war film and crime heist film all in one film focusing on the main characters journey in the story. It's gritty, shocking, poignant and sad. A film that also explores how soldiers were treated after Vietnam and explores the decade that the film is set in. Very well made and a hell of a good story.

reviews.author: RensDad666
reviews.text: Damn this one gut punched the hell out of me. The Hughes Brothers’ 1995 blend of Vietnam war drama and crime thriller tour-de-force Dead Presidents is so much more than I’d anticipated on paper. A Coming of age story. A critique on the horrendous governmental treatment towards military veterans after service, and the horrors of war fundamentally robbing a generation’s potential. A complex character study, and account of an ultimate psychological undoing. Through its central protagonist, played convincingly by Larenz Tate, Dead Presidents snakes its viewer through an optimistic late 60’s NYC, through the misguided Vietnam war, and conflicted return to a struggling city and home resembling nothing our characters’ memories served up before leaving.

reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: Just an overall "feel-bad" kinda film. Expertly directed by the Hughes Brothers along with an ensemble full of talent, Dead Presidents finds a gaping hole within its writing, leaving many vital moments in Anthony's life as vignettes instead of one fluid story. The second half of the film spirals hard out of control in the way that few films are capable of. One film in particular, Very Bad Things, is sort of my "go to" example of this niche, where characters continually make terrible decisions expecting something better to happen and it never does. Also, yet again, the Vietnam War is used as a one-dimensional catalyst. Beyond those marks, if you can focus on the acting, direction, and blazing soundtrack, you may enjoy yourself more than the three stars you see here.

reviews.text: When Seidelman shoots her characters often times it is from the feet up, but it's not about a sexual gaze or the leering of bodies, but instead it's to get a full look at an outfit. Her lens becomes a mirror that moves from heels to hose to dress to necklace to make-up to hair, and it's almost always shot through the eyes of a character who happens to be a woman. There's a lovingness in gesture towards this camera movement that screams "Look at this outfit!", that personifies a covetous feeling that is most present in Desperately Seeking Susan's role model as New Wave Goddess imagery through Madonna, and it's entirely about the ensemble instead of the body which makes Seidelman's lens feel intrinsically linked to clothing. In turn this makes the way she shoots women to feel like both a celebration of women and femininity.

reviews.text: Hitting all the most expected notes of aggressively patriotic propaganda, the WWII service drama Destination Tokyo was the directorial debut of screenwriter Delmer Daves, who dabbled in several genres over his lengthy career (I'm a big fan of his gloriously soapy melodrama A Summer Place). The film offers a who's-who of the Warner Bros. roster on board a US Navy submarine bound for Asia on a bombing mission: Captain Cassidy (Cary Grant) is at the helm, while the crew includes happy-go-lucky horndog Wolf (John Garfield), fussy cook "Cookie" Wainwright (Alan Hale), a proud Greek-American called "Tin Can" (Dane Clark), nervous newbie Tommy Adams (Robert Hutton, a thousand leagues better than his performance in Love and Learn), more seasoned veterans Mike…

reviews.author: John Frankensteiner
reviews.text: Mediocre American propaganda film, and not "propaganda" as an overstatement, literal propaganda. But there is one scene that I will remember for the rest of my life: John Garfield puts on a voice record letter for himself and 10 other sailors, the voice is the wife of one of their recently deceased buddies. As the record plays, the wife talks about her love for him, the children's love for him, and how they pretend he's there for dinner every night, even make him a plate of dinner like he's still there. It's an incredibly beautiful audio letter from someone who truly loves this man. Each sailor's face drops the longer it goes on, and one-by-one they exit the room as it becomes too much to bear.

Even with its limitations, the performances are great, the tension builds steadily, and the film ultimately works as a war movie, submarine movie, and siege movie.

It's all about how the eponymous detective (Ralph Byrd) and his feisty stalwart "Gwen" (Lynne Roberts) get on the trail of the vicious and malevolent "Stark" gang. These guys are involved in just about every criminal activity known to man, but it's their international antics - including espionage and sabotage - that particularly interest our sleuth. Again, as with "Flash Gordon" these worked far better as weekly episodes with jeopardy points at…

reviews.text: This serial begins the same way as Citizen Kane, with a newsreel documenting the life and death of the central villain. This was one element that lead Pauline Kael to declare an uncredited Herman Mankiewicz the true genius behind this, as argued in her article “Resurrecting Zarnoff” in Those Enduring Matinee Idols #17 (July 1972). This in turn has inspired the latest film from Don Glut, Mank vs. Credit Stealers Inc., debuting this November on Tubi TV, with an all star cast including Brinke Stevens, TJ Storm, Marv Wolfman, Bob Burns, Ann Robinson, and Charles Dance as Kogar the Gorilla.

reviews.author: Larry Yoshida
reviews.text: Ralph Byrd is the definitive Dick Tracy, but this has little to do with the comic strip. Instead of being a big city cop, he's a G-Man. Tracy has caught master spy Zarnoff (Irving Pichel). However, Zarnoff escapes by faking his death... in the gas chamber! Zarnoff begins a campaign of industrial espionage and sabotage. Instead of Tess Trueheart, Tracy is aided by Gwen (Phyllis Isley, who would be better known as Jennifer Jones). Typical great Republic serial action. Worth a look despite not being faithful to the source material.

reviews.author: Cheshellen
reviews.text: Dick Tracy's G-Men (1939, John English, William Witney)All 15 episodes of this fast-paced crime-fighting serial are neatly uploaded to YouTube, making it a lengthy 302-minute viewing, especially considering Jennifer Jones’ relatively small role (billed as Phylis Isley) as Gwen, Tracy’s secretary assisting in the pursuit of the villainous Zarnoff. Still, I was delighted to watch my first vintage serial, full of pulp-era flair and classic thrills. A treat for fans of old-school heroes, serial enthusiasts, and Jennifer Jones completists alike. #jenniferjonesjune

reviews.text: If I'm being totally honest here, Digging for Fire came completely out of left field for me. What was supposed to be just a filler to kill time between the bland Z for Zachariah and the epic 80's-gasm of Turbo Kid ended up taking me completely by surprise. This clever mix of Woody Allen and Force Majeure turned out to be an incredible human dramedy that examines two very different stories, and yet one doesn't manage to direct the attention from the other. Both stories flow in their own way, and seem to coincide perfectly with each other. The abundance of comedy, mixed with just the right amount of heartfelt drama, makes it a near perfect blend.

No one can do anything about it because computers. Lloyd Bridges is a Secret Service agent who pulls a gun on a pizza delivery, and William Shatner plays a jittery fugitive dead set on picking up Yvette Mimeaux seated next to him. Predictable at first, but gets weird really quickly, and the last 20 minutes are a blast, with a railroad depot crew defying…

reviews.author: Jake Calta
reviews.text: From the director of Vanishing Point comes a disaster film, like and unlike much else in its field. Disaster on the Coastliner sees an all-star cast dealing with an entire section of a railroad in control of a disturbed technician. Not much else I can say other than sweet baby Jesus, I never thought Amtrak trains could be as scary as they are here. The stunt work and practical effects are hair-raising to say the least. A lot of craft went into this absolute behemoth of a TV disaster flick. The cherry on top of it all: Gerald Fried's thunderous, Moogified score. Good for quite a few thrills and seeing plenty of engaging character actors.

reviews.text: As a film about mental illness made in the 1950s, Don't Bother to Knock is unexpectedly sensitive, not only with regard to its troubled central character (Marilyn Monroe as Nell), but also when it comes to the people around her. Within just 75 short minutes, director Roy Ward Baker and screenwriter Daniel Taradash manage to allow considerable growth in Richard Widmark's cynical pilot character, Jed, and treat characters that would sometimes be mocked or marginalized — middle-aged parents, a strange, awkward elevator man — with tremendous grace, shaping them into full human beings rather than the caricatures they might have been in the hands of others.

reviews.text: There's a mystifying and almost inexplicable appeal to Albert Pyun's low budget cannon. For films that can easily be called unrefined, incomplete, half-baked, and schlocky, Pyun confidently emits a distinct tone with appropriate needle drops. One step further than that, Old Al implements inspired guerrilla filmmaking, with here the aid of cinematographer Walt Lloyd (Sex, Lies and Videotape), unleashing sweaty set piece after sweaty set piece. Unfortunately not all of Al's films are great (or even good for that matter), but it just so happens I can now call one of his movies exactly that.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: Albert Pyun's 1987 thriller gets to the primal appeal of the movies: 'watching good-looking people lead lives that are far more interesting than yours.' The opening ten minutes of "Down Twisted" focus exclusively on a group of mysterious, well-coiffed thieves driving motorcycles and speed boats, meeting in rain-slicked parking lots and warehouses, making duplicitous deals and exchanges, all set to airy synthesizer music. It's Michael Mann or Tony Scott without any kind of underlining ethos or point-of-view on humanity: it's pure surface attraction, MTV images arranged in the loosest of narrative structures.
