reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: One of Albert Pyun's signatures is to inject heavy social or philosophical themes that you would never expect to find in the low-budget genre exercises he specializes in, but this is pure escapism, a globe-spanning adventure with a bunch of thieves (one of whom has a garrote wire wristwatch like John Lithgow in Blow Out!) chasing and bumping each other off in pursuit of a shiny religious relic, basically Pyun's version of a 1940s studio thriller, all about the universal daydream of traveling to an exotic locale, having an adventure, falling in love, and looking cool. This needs to be restored and made available in its proper aspect ratio yesterday. Five, or maybe 50, stars for the closing montage of the movie's greatest hits set to the Fine Young Cannibals, pure cinema, could eventually become a religious artifact of its own!

reviews.text: Gnarly, single location horror picture where a sniper starts plugging bullets into a gaggle of stranded college kids, each shot splattering brains and causing bodies to burst with fountains of gore. Becomes increasingly wet as the picture chugs along, each character not so much a person as they are a moist fleshsuit for this madman to use for target practice. Similarly, Kitamura is utilizing the isolated stretch of country road as a canvas to deploy every camera trick - deep focus, split diopters, extreme composite close-ups - he's got in his pretty deep bag. Becomes completely ludicrous by the end, involving gory car crashes, enflamed parents and a final goofy gag that’s totally unearned, mean spirited, but that’s what this whole thing is, after all.

reviews.author: Jake Calta
reviews.text: The tried and true ARKOFF formula is in action with this low-budget exploit, chock full of hot rods, rock-n-roll, and juvenile delinquents (what else). Stand outs include John Ashley in a bad-boy/discount-Elvis-mode, the hilarious Frank Gorshin with his James Cagney-good looks, and the positively alluring and charming Fay Spain as the indecisive, eponymous speed demon. The film's biggest fault is the cripplingly formulaic writing. You can see every twist, turn, and beat of contrived drama from a mile away. Admittedly, what saves the film from being too generic include: Lou Russoff's sharp dialogue, a cast competent enough to deliver it with conviction, the fun set pieces, that blink-and-you'll-miss-it runtime of 70 minutes, and those sweet drive-in vibes. Dragstrip Girl was a blind buy on my part, and I find myself pleased with this swinging American International deep cut, in spite of its rather noticeable flaws.

reviews.text: The two lead performances and the cinematography are really special. Ali Barkai's endless intense stare and Youssouf Djaoro's looming, unblinking presence causes such incredible tension from the moment they lock eyes all the way through their increasingly complicated relationship. Both men are so wound tight and intense and director Mahamat-Saleh Haroun with cinematographer Abraham Haile Biru are constantly finding new, stark ways to frame their scowling faces against bare environments. Long passages go without dialogue and so much communication is physical and frank but not without depth. It's quite interesting watching this a few days after This Man Must Die and being given everything we felt that film lacked. Meaningful, interesting characterisation and actual tension as the one seeking revenge…

Similarly to 'When Night Falls,' which I recently reviewed and loved so much, Dry Season presents an interesting perspective on post-war narratives as well as revenge flicks. Instead of showing the violence and the horrors, Mahamat Saleh-Haroun takes you on a torturously slow-paced journey full of longing and emptiness, with a phenomenal ending that culminates and comments on revenge as an act and masculinity as a construct. The biggest problem for me is that the idea is bigger and more ambiguous…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: It's interesting how common revenge is as a plot line in films. The most popular plot line is almost certainly the exact opposite--love--just as it is in music. I don't think revenge is the second most popular plot line necessarily, but it has to be up there, possibly in the top ten. It's interesting in the context of popular film plots because of its stark contrast to the love story--a story so popular it gets wedged into films that do not need nor should conceivably have them in them--and because it suggests a universality to the revenge story, which seems absurd on the surface of things. But when you think about it, what a revenge story really is is the…

reviews.text: An exceptionally well made film, hits a sweet spot where content and theme converge with aesthetics to produce a condensed, convincing and coherent whole. The narrative maintains a palpable, if quiet, tension throughout. The dialog veers towards the minimalist (partly for good plot-based reasons, which aren't immediately apparent), colour palettes / costuming are utilised expertly to direct and focus the viewer's attention, and physical action / interaction predominate, visuals left to illustrate rather than leaning on forced dialogs etc.

reviews.author: Julian (Seeking Film)
reviews.text: The Chadian Civil War ended before Amit was even born, but its consequences still echo in the life of the 16-year-old in 2006. Not only did it remove the boy's father from the world before he himself could enter it, but the perpetrator of that atrocity, alongside all other war criminals of his ilk, has been granted amnesty by the state, leaving no room for justice in the court of law. From here, Mahamat-Saleh Haroun paints in Dry Season his own portrait of forged justice—one whose adherence to the established formula of examining reluctant revenge missions gives way to a sparing but effective examination of the relationships driving that conflict.

reviews.text: I think we all have a 'type', and when it comes to films, Daratt fits very well into mine. It was commissioned as part of a series of films commemorating Mozart's 250th anniversary (along with works by Tsai Ming-liang and Apichatpong Weerasethakul, not to mention Garin Nugroho's great Opera Jawa), and so at a plot level it uses some of the simplicity and big themes common to great opera: in this case it's a film about a young man taking revenge on the murderer of his father (killed during a prolonged civil war).

It's a bit episodic and has tons of redneck stereotypes. reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: If the films of Mia Hansen-Løve are haunted by the merciless march of time, they’re less preoccupied with its passage than they are with its ellipses. Whereas Richard Linklater plays the subject like an accordion, collapsing the years together and pulling them apart in order to transform the space between, Hansen-Løve bangs on it like a drum, her staccato stories finding beautiful music in the off-beats. Eden is the 33-year-old’s fourth feature, and while its male lead, historical interest, and occasional American setting might suggest that it’s a departure from her previous work, this riveting but resolutely uncool epic ultimately feels like less of a new direction than it does a new perspective. The beat may have changed, but the song remains the same.

The first thing that you'll probably notice about Eden is its strong visual style, from the colorful cinematography (which does start to dim alongside the lifestyles of the characters as the movie progresses) to the beautifully stylized text used to structure the film into segments. I think that the visuals were probably my favorite aspect of the film... the acting wasn't bad, but it wasn't anything special either. The script is damn good, with some really funny jokes that contrast certain moments of genuine melancholy - just like the tracks used in the film, a balance of elation and sorrow.

reviews.text: Bikercop-Movie, Roadmovie, Neowestern, Sozialstudie. Momentaufnahme, Mordfallermittlung, sind nur einige Schlagwörter zum ehemals geschmähten und kritisierten Kritikerfeind, der aber nichtsdestotrotz zum Kultfilm avancierte und trotzdem noch, zu Unrecht, ein kleines Schattendasein führt.Der radikale Gegenschuß zur HighseinFreisein-EasyRider-Schmonzette, aus der Sicht des überambitionierten Motorradcops Wintergreen, der sogerne Mordermittler sein möchte und auch prompt in einen solchen verwickelt wird. HARLEY DAVIDSON 344 entpuppt sich als eine Art Gegenwurf zum populären Bikerkino, zeigt die Gegenseite mit ihren Höhen, Tiefen, Schwächen und Stärken. Eine Verbeugung an die John Ford-Western, mit ihren starken, standhaften und prinzipientreuen Helden, der hier vom charismatischen Robert Blake so treffend verkörpert wird. Umso mehr knallt einem das Ende um die Ohren und wirkt noch lange nach. (Leider) Einmalundniewieder-Filmer und Musiker/Produzent James William Guercio hat hier nachhaltig seine Spuren in der Filmlandschaft hinterlassen, Spuren die leider von vielen erst mal gefunden werden müssen. Für Fans des anspruchsvollen amerikanischen Kinos und für Männer mit Prinzipien.

reviews.author: Jonathan White
reviews.text: I hadn’t seen Fail Safe in decades, and didn’t remember much of it other than Henry Fonda and the brilliant final scene. It was only in the last year that I came to realize it was Sidney Lumet. Over the years I’ve loved many Lumet films, including Network, Dog Day Afternoon, 12 Angry Men, The Verdict, and Death Trap without realizing they were his. I think this may be because his trademark is subtle. It isn’t stylistic, it’s all about the characters. All of his characters are fully drawn, and completely believable. Even those as out there as Howard Beale. Beyond the script, Lumet seems to have that magic that can draw the best performances out of his actors.

reviews.author: Dirk Diggler
reviews.text: I love stripped-down, dialogue-driven and close-quarter dramas like this, where in the hands of a true master - such as Lumet - the uncinematic becomes cinematic. Telephone exchanges becomes the most tense scenes you'll see. The stark b&w cinematography, claustrophobic close-ups, the use of silence - all magnificent. It stars two of my favorite actors in Fonda and Matthau and my word do they act the shit out of this one. The suspense and emotions builds and builds and the scenario keeps getting more terrifying. Final minutes are haunting beyond words. True shame that the release of Dr. Strangelove completely overshadowed this, they're both magnificent.

reviews.author: Kevflix And Chill
reviews.text: Really loved this. Cold War thriller that imagines a scenario where the fail safe mechanisms of nuclear warfare breakdown and the worst case scenarios play out and no one has any power to stop it. It’s a tense thriller where the tension has been ramped up by its minimalist production and score. Though a product of its time, it’s hard not to see how fail safe could speak into the present, particularly the use of artificial intelligence. The prescient fear of the consequence of relegating world altering decisions and safeguards to artificial mechanisms, while we sit on the sidelines watching our own doom play out on computer monitors, powerless to alter our trajectory. Dark stuff and a fantastically dark ending. Released in the same year as Dr. Strangelove, this is a fantastic companion piece from the brilliant Sidney Lumet. Highly recommend.

reviews.text: Murnau’s most baroque work - an instance of the director working both within maximalism and in examination of maximalism as well. It's opening and closing moments are Murnau at his most melodramatic - but everything in between is him at his most inquisitive. It's constantly stimulating to watch - shards of light blasting in from everywhere possible, constant smog, and some of the most haunting poses and faces in movies. This is what makes this film so interesting - rather than level the usage of these effects for simple sensory response, (ala, say, Walsh's Thief of Bagdad) Murnau appears to use these effects for the purpose of dialectic with the story - in turn becoming a critique of the trickery…

A narrative that defies all boundaries, a masterwork in merely visual storytelling. This is a true testament to the visual power of film and the value it can deliver. The extent to which film has degraded in its ability to deliver a great visual story is astounding. Evidently, 90% of new releases now lack the understanding that film is a visual medium, resulting in so many projects that are completely lifeless and bland.…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: There are not many works of silent cinema that have managed to condense, with such visual virulence and symbolic sophistication, the metaphysical dilemmas that underpin the human condition. From the first frames, of liturgical brilliance, the spectator is immersed in a spiritually and visually dense atmosphere that immediately announces a cosmic confrontation: the eternal struggle between good and evil, between spirit and flesh, between fate and free will. The opening, a true cinematographic hierophany, in my opinion, is one of the most sublime moments of German Expressionism, not only for its technical and compositional precision, but above all for its ability to invoke horror and ecstasy in equal measure.

reviews.text: F.W. Murnau's "Faust" is often labeled one of the greatest horror films of the silent, if not any, era. "Faust," however, is more than a horror film, and categorizing the film in one genre box may sell it short. The film combines primitive horror conventions with those of the fable and fairy tale. Regardless of its true genre, the classic story of a man who trades away his soul for earthly pleasures is brought to life by Murnau with haunting imagery and classic storytelling devices.

reviews.author: Waiching Liu
reviews.text: Finding Forrester is a film that I would describe as a combination of Dead Poets Society, Good Will Hunting and Dangerous Minds, with a hint of basketball thrown in for good measure. The film is directed by Gus Van Sant, who did 1997's Oscar-winning, Good Will Hunting starring Matt Damon, Robin Williams and Ben Affleck. A film in which I personally felt was elevated by the performances, more so than through the screenplay and the script. In contrast to many others, I was a little underwhelmed and thus, there weren't enough moments that made me want to love it, as much as it wanted me too.

reviews.author: Erhard K
reviews.text: Jamal Wallace (played by Rob Brown) is a young black man from the Bronx who loves basketball and poetry. He observes, with some disdain among his friends, a mysterious man nicknamed "the one in the window" who watches them from his apartment. In a bet between friends, he breaks into his apartment, finds his library interesting, and returns another time. A beautiful friendship is born. Forrester (played by Sean Connery, who also produced the movie) is a very famous writer who has only published one successful book! He improves Jamal's writing, which raises doubts in his literature teacher, Robert, who suspects that he is not the boy who is doing better and better in school. The performances of the three…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A deeply unresolved marriage between the narrative rote and lovely observed snapshots. Pretty much everything that has nothing to do with plot is wonderful, with Van Sant’s careful gaze and good ear in good form. But when it has to move things along, Finding Forrest turns uncertain, unsure if it should play up the more maudlin elements of its story or try to tone them down. This is still a lot better than its rep as assembly line oscar hopeful suggests, the good stuff is truly goodand Brown and Coonery have a very nice rapport the allow the film to move along as well as possible under circunstances.

It's a simple enough story with Lo Lei as a student who after he learns everything he can from his current master is sent to train with the superior teacher so he can defeat the local tyrant in a martial arts tournament. It's a nice change of pace with Lo Lei playing the hero as he usually is the villain in these movies but there are plenty of…

reviews.text: The film that is often credited with bringing the martial arts movie to a western audience. Five Fingers of Death makes the most of simple plotline - mixing moments of drama with numerous hard hitting fight sequences. We focus on a promising young apprentice who travels to a new martial arts school to improve his skill, but falls foul of the local gangsters on the way. It's a story of honour and revenge - with the concept of "an eye for an eye" being taken quite literally! The basic story is interesting but the film ups the ante with some side plots featuring various rivalries between the numerous characters. There's an array of memorable villains with their own unique styles.…

"Here in New York City, it created somewhat of a sensation," he writes, "with people paying full admission for standing room only!" He loved it and painted a picture of "sitting on the second-floor balcony steps with an audience that...insisted on screaming throughout the entire picture, and I darn well joined them!" In…

By combining the winter sports shenanigans of On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (this franchise loves skiing) with more suspenseful underwater sequences than Thunderball (this franchise loves sharks), this twelfth entry in the James Bond saga makes up for a lack of plot progression in the first two acts with fun action across the board, and relatively low levels of sexism. Furthermore, it features trad climbing! Let's go!

reviews.author: Blain LaMotta
reviews.text: A stunning examination of masculinity in crisis and how one split second decision under duress can change the whole infrastructure of a family unit. Increasingly tense dialogue exchanges ensue. It's also surprisingly humorous at times. Some bravura sequences in this sucker too, like the epic avalanche long take, and the stressful, thought-provoking bus ride that closes the film. The scene at the bar with the song Reload playing in the background might be my favorite though. It tells a lot by doing very little. Lots to debate in this one. Authentic performances, restrained direction, and gorgeous cinematography round things out. Any film that can make me question myself deserves all the praise I can muster. Superb job, Ruben Östlund!

reviews.text: Tom Holland’s directorial debut is a masterpiece of 80’s horror. Combining just the right amount of comedy and thrills, it checks all the boxes. The practical effects by Richard Edlund and Ken Diaz are phenomenal and still hold up to this very day. One of my favorite portrayals of a vampire is Chris Sarandon‘s Jerry Dandrige. He’s suave, charming, handsome and just below that façade, menacing. You can see why Susan Sarandon married him. Then we have the late, great Roddy McDowall, who has given us so many iconic roles during his career, Peter Vincent was the cherry on top. Halloween is just around the corner, time to start dusting off the oldies but goodies.

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: In a filmography such as Ron Howard's where I feel he has few truly great films and is at his best as a middlebrow gun-for-hire, it's movies like Frost/Nixon where I can see Howard working best as a director. Here, he's working with a sharp script from Peter Morgan and directs it with energy and class, utilizing a top-quality cast to tell a story that is urgent and interesting. It works as well as it does because Howard is such an unfussy filmmaker who's comfortable in so many different genres, with this being a very entertaining drama that manages to make a series of TV interviews exciting and involving. The somewhat odd documentary-style inserts he uses also adds some insight to it, and Howard also gets a pair of great performances from his leads to help make Frost/Nixon one of the best films in a career as varied and diverse as his.

If anyone other than John Carpenter had made this movie, I think it would be far more beloved than it is, and I think it is a film in deep need of re-evaluation. 'Ghosts of Mars' operates at near-'Planet Terror' levels of crazed, what-the-hell cheapness/looseness, but does so with exquisite craft and care. The sets are like any dusty mining town Anywhere saturated in red-filter. The vehicles are pure 60's/'70's scale model-kit.…

reviews.text: This is the American re-edit of Godzilla (1954), which jettisoned huge chunks of Ishiro Honda's original footage and added huge chunks of new, American-shot footage. The new American footage features Raymond Burr as reporter "Steve Martin," who comes to Tokyo to visit his good friend Dr. Serizawa, with whom he never shares the same frame. The first 40-or-so minutes of the original film are seen in quick fragments, like a highlight reel, with Raymond Burr always off to the side asking his translator what's going on. There are a few unconvincing over-the-shoulder shots where he talks to characters from the original film. There's a hilarious scene at the beginning where we see the devastating aftermath of Godzilla's reign of terror,…

reviews.author: johnlease
reviews.text: Ossie Davis was an accomplished actor and a fearless activist. In this picture, Davis perfectly nails the patter and persona of a Black preacher.The cast not only includes Ossie's own beloved, Ruby Dee, but we also get Sorrell Brooke representing the local gentry as the Ol' Cap'n and Alan Alda, with a perfectly ridiculous Southern accent, as his silly liberal son. Davis provides remarkable quotable dialogue which includes pithy observations, biting social commentary, and rapid-fire philosophy. The excellent black and white photography comes to us courtesy of Boris Kaufman who also did the job on the unusual BABY DOLL (1956).

Dee is little more than a prop here there is relentless misogyny to the prop and the mocking of Dee is hardly sufficiently ironized, particularly as the film moves towards a weird rehash of Fordian hokum from the 1930's or 40's. this move is borders on juxtapositional it's so stark, but nothing is really yielded from it that wouldn't be obvious to even a 1960's audience that such minstrelized notions of blackness were racist. though the film's still softened and extensive depiction of the white southerner (who looks like Colonel Sanders) never fully dispenses his stances so despite being made in 1963 it almost feels like the period race drama its maybe trying to parody or antagonize. an intriguing relic for sure.

reviews.author: Stanley Fried
reviews.text: The DVD I watched was released under the name of the stage play Ossie Davis wrote and starred in along with his wife, Ruby Dee. This is a relevant today in 2025 as when it was released in 1963. A joyous comedy the culture of racism, it satirizes white prejudice, white expectations of how African-Americans should conduct themselves in the presence of white folk, and how obvious all of this is to anyone with the ability to see it. The performances are all spot on characatures of what a white audience might expect of black folk and what black folk might expect of white folk. Ossie Davis laid it out quite clearly without holding any punches. A delight to watch.

reviews.text: It took me like, two years to finally **get** this movie - reducing me to a blubbering, sobbing mess midway through. Still, I feel there is still a good deal to be said here than what has been already been done. Film Socialisme was cinema as 'cine-tract'/political tract, this is cinema as philosophy. And while the 3D is integral to viewing the film, it is still a means to an end - JLG finding new ways to express his ideas rather than creating "new" shots and such nonsense. It's worth noting that JLG himself did not see this film in 3D until after its premiere. This movie does not establish new ways of seeing, but rather is about finding new…

reviews.text: being, dwelling, thinking; godard on solid ground after the odyssean journey of film socialisme, setting to the task of creating a new poetics of cinema out of the ashes of the 20th century's narrative hegemony -- every shot here has a double to which it is juxtaposed, images which rhyme like couplets, radioactive colors and bit-crushed contrasts, holderlin's ister as the enigma of space-time which poses the central question for any filmmaker: how do you navigate depth within the flatness of the projected light? godard's answer seems to be a return to a revived impressionism -- break apart the cinema into a thousand pieces, scatter them to the winds like the body of osiris, and see what becomes of them; make the world into montage, a new cinema belonging to every soul.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: There was a period that seems near incomprehensible to me now where I actually thought this was probably the weakest of Godard's post-2000 work - perhaps because it's one of Godard's least explicitly political films, but I underestimated how deeply poetic it was in its place. Beautifully structured and designed (I'd also vastly underrated how sophisticated Godard's montage had become since working digitally with this and Film Socialisme, despite always loving the latter). Needless to say, a masterpiece and obviously formally stunning, but much can be said about Godard's visual and tonal manipulations and modulations, heightening and lowering colour as he sees fit but perfectly encapsulating the emotional tenor of the "refuge" each couple finds in their respective affairs -…

reviews.text: Almost certainly the most confrontational film about the Asian-American experience since “Better Luck Tomorrow,” Justin Chon’s “Gook” is about as subtle as a trash can smashing through a pizzeria window, but this isn’t a story for subtle times. Set on April 29, 1992 — the first night of the Los Angeles Riots — it’s not a story about subtle times, either. On the contrary, this messy but lived-in drama is intended for a climate that’s tilted towards hatred and erasure, an environment in which people are forced to scream their voices hoarse just to remind the world of their basic humanity. You don’t call a movie “Gook” because you feel heard.

reviews.text: Half Leone update, half-delirious excessive 90’s buddy action/comedy from early on Dimension history, before they find a more professional niche. Directed by Deran Sarafian and written by Stephen Sommers, two men who could not do a realistic scene, if they actually believe such a thing exists. Plenty of character actors scene chewing (I will never decide if Patrick Stewart is atrocious or amazing in this one), Lambert and Van Peebles aren’t the most dynamic of duos, but Lambert is doing one of his deranged I can be funny performances and Van Peebles can play him straight fine. Serafian makes every set piece a bit louder and Sommers dialogue is pure non-sense even for this level of filmmaking (when the guys question Sally Kirkland for having a shotgun in a bathtub she answers “I lost my rubble duck”). Good colors, relentless pace, gleefully amoral. Good or bad, American cinema just doesn’t make this kind of disposable cartoon for multiplexes anymore.

reviews.text: Hell Drivers looks incredible. The black and white is crisp and clean, and the restoration work that got it there is absolutely impeccable. The sound design, too, is striking, because of the carefully inserted, background presence of the sounds of nature, underneath and around the constant roaring of the trucks. The care with which the audio so thoughtfully reminds us of the outside, larger world is quite admirable. In addition, some of the actors — particularly Stanley Baker and Herbert Lom — do really impressive work with characters that are very, very (VERY) thinly written (Good Guy Atoning for Mistakes! Good, Loyal Immigrant!).

Fortunately for us, Hell Drivers director Cyril Endfield rarely cared enough about hegemonic “common sense” to stop at one or two; he often moved to three, veered into four, would've barreled past five if he hadn't enjoyed an untapped phoneline so much. reviews.author: Richard
reviews.text: A slamming indictment of modern employment practices made in, erm, 1957. Tom Yately—played by Stanley Baker with his usual rugged intensity—is fresh out of prison and finds a seemingly well-paid job driving a ballast truck, which his employer requires him to drive at startling speeds, doing the maintenance and upkeep himself on his own time. There are definite parallels with The Wages of Fear. Unsurprisingly, his employer has hired far fewer drivers than required for its contract and is dangerously cutting corners, quite literally, to pocket the difference. The satire is absolutely spot on and shows that such abuses are nothing new but have just been made easier by the gig economy.

reviews.author: Daniel Shillito
reviews.text: Hired to Kill is like if Andy Sidaris made The Expendables but with none of his usual energy. It boasts performances bad enough to make even Arnie wince, forgettable action and comedy that is completely unintentional. Yet, it's a pitch-perfect encapsulation of 90s direct-to-video shlock with a fairly meaty budget given all the explosions and globe-trotting location work, with fan favourite Brian Thompson getting to play the hero for once and bolstered by relatively memorable supporting roles by frigging Oliver Reed and George Kennedy. There's no real style to the direction but it's all done with competency and earnestness which shine through the film's otherwise weaker aspects while Jerry Grant's score feels like it was constructed from the outtakes he had left over from his work on Magnum P.I. and The A-Team. While it's a little dull at points, Hired to Kill is still an entertaining and pacey little B-movie, if a bit bloodless.

reviews.text: 100-word review: A hidden gem, delightfully blending espionage and comedy, which stands out for its charm. Matthau’s dry humor is brilliantly matched by Jackson’s sharpness, making for a thoroughly entertaining, surprisingly sexy duo. The clever humour relies more on witty dialogue and situations than slapstick or over-the-top action, setting it apart from other spy movies. Kendig’s rogue actions reveal the frustrations of those bound by rigid systems, making his journey feel liberating. However, Kendig's near-perfect elusiveness does detract slightly from the suspense. His ability to effortlessly outsmart everyone sometimes feels too easy, lessening the tension. Still, Hopscotch remains a highly entertaining romp.

Glenda doesn’t really have that much to do, but she and Walter have considerable chemistry in their second film together, after the much-lesser House Calls. reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Nearly without context for its plot, this film simply leaps into a very basic premise and keeps going, throwing kill after kill at you while ramping up its creepiness by emphasizing the ways in which men treat Susan. It strips away so much of the pretense of other slashers in favor of depicting the simple and all-too-real motivation of misogynistic possessiveness. The medical setting makes the disbelief Susan is faced with even more resonant, mirroring the experiences of millions of women (though maybe not necessarily with the whole witnessing a brutal murder part). Somehow this low-budget slice of slasher manages to be more interesting and insightful than many more popular or slickly produced titles. There's a touch of unfortunate ableism mixed in, however, that muddles the (unintended?) message.

reviews.text: 100-word review: An amusing spoof of the aviation classic, which I personally already consider self-parody. Its humor can feel hit-or-miss. Charlie Sheen takes on the role of Lt. Topper Harley, a comically over-the-top version of Tom Cruise’s Maverick. Sheen nails the look and swagger of a budget Tom Cruise, and his performance often leans into the absurd, which works for the gags. There are exaggerated aerial stunts, ridiculous locker room drama, and a volley of visual gags that parody iconic scenes like the volleyball game. However, the humor is uneven, sometimes clever but other times too reliant on slapstick and low-hanging fruit.

reviews.text: A direct sequel to the Sherman Brothers' 1973 musical adaptation of TOM SAWYER, HUCKLEBERRY FINN sees Jeff East reprise his role as the titular character, setting off on the Mississippi with runaway slave, Jim (Paul Winfield). By nature a darker story than TOM SAWYER, so its musical numbers seem even more shoe-horned into the narrative. Glosses over many of the book's racial themes in its quest to be a cheery musical, but the leads are strong (especially Winfield), and Harvey Korman and David Wayne inject some much needed energy in the film's second act as a pair of wily con men.

reviews.text: Part of the legend of Martin Scorsese is the story of him screening his Roger Corman produced movie Boxcar Bertha (his first commercially produced theatrical feature) for his mentor John Cassavetes. However, despite the fact he acted in many of them (Devil’s Angels, Machine Gun McCain, The Incubus), Cassavetes had contempt for exploitation pictures. After seeing the film, John said to Scorsese, as nice as he could, “Kid you just spent a year of your life making a piece of shit.” Then John clarified, “Look, don’t get me wrong, it’s fine for what it is. But you don’t want to get caught up doing these sleazy exploitation flicks. Leave those for the other guys, you’re better than that.”

reviews.text: Every year, on the evening of August 6th, the people of Hiroshima gather along the banks of the Ota River and light more than 10,000 paper lanterns as the final part of a deeply moving peace ceremony. The memorial event caps off a day of reflection that includes film screenings, musical performances, and a wide variety of different speeches. Hibakusha — survivors of the nuclear blasts — gather around the Atomic Bomb Dome, many of them joined by their children and grandchildren. One particularly animated man performs a parable about the horrors visited upon his hometown, while a British ex-pat translates his story into English for the foreigners in attendance. The atmosphere is solemn, but not somber. There’s good food.…

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: The obvious point of comparison for In This Corner of the World, an anime set on the home front during World War II, is with Isao Takahata’s 1988 Ghibli film Grave of the Fireflies. But in spirit it’s more akin to Takahata’s later work: the world-dissolving subjective images of memory in Only Yesterday and the episodic focus on the family of My Neighbors the Yamadas. Fireflies is about devastation, about the terrible consequences of war and, more specifically, of the cruel pride that makes for such wars, but Corner is about resilience, about a people to whom war is happening, with or without their complicity: it’s more Mrs. Miniver than anything else.

It’s even shot so differently from everything they’ve done. The character of Herb Myerson feels like the sole fantastical element they included here as a hint of a much weirder, much Coen-er movie, but nothing else comes close! Can absolutely see why someone (past me included) would not like this, but there’s something so distinctly crazy about it that I can’t help but dig it. reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: The film as recrimination of reality because reality itself could not reconcile itself. It is paradoxical that those in power stay in power even, or perhaps most, when they are most indicted, because who's going to believe the word of a nobody citizen against that of one above suspicion? It can't be happening, even when it is happening, already happening, because it can't possibly be happening. Mass cognitive dissonance; the powerful warp how reality is experienced. These abuses are absurd because absurdity is a tool, unbelievable, so they are no longer believed. It is only in retrospect that the paradox is unpacked, abuses confessed to because they are relegated to the past. These things used to happen but not anymore. Now? That's absurd. There is no abuse. Something like that could not possibly happen now.

The film directed by Elio Petri, and written by him together with Ugo Pirro, is the product of the new climate of liberalism propitiated by the protests of the late sixties, which brings political passions to flare up also on the screen, for the benefit of a cinema that is finally able to perform important civil tasks.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: 1962, this film echoes a period in which the Soviet Union, still under the weight of the memory of World War II, sought ways to deal with collective trauma. While many Soviet films of the time exalted military heroism and patriotic glory, a small portion of directors, included Tarkovsky, focus their vision on the darkest and most existential aspects of war. Instead of glorifying the battle, Tarkovsky portrays its futility. The war is not here a stage of bravery, but a theater of irreparable losses, of destruction of the psychological and the soul.

One problem most of these films have is the casting of Jane Eyre. She is supposed to be plain, yet they cast people like Joan Fontaine, or in this one, Susannah York. It is a straight-forward, quickly-told version. So quick sometimes that you wonder how they fell in love. And St. John Rivers is played by Ian Bannen as almost a madman. No wonder she scorned him. Overall, the Timothy Dalton version is still my wife's favorite.

Plot makes no sense, every joke dies painfully, like The Loved One turned inside out, or a backwards issue of Mad Magazine where all the humor goes in reverse. Didn’t think J. Lee Thompson could get more racist than Kinjite: Forbidden Subjects but he pulled that off like 25 years earlier. Notre Dame tried to get this movie pulled from release for depicting their football team in an unflattering light, but the Fighting Irish get off the easiest here.

What could have been a sly satirical goof, à la Dr. Strangelove, on US foreign policy during the Cold War is rendered completely idiotic by all of the actors playing the comedy to the back of the room for maximum wackiness. I know this was the era of "camp" but even the Batman show knew that it's so much funnier to deadpan absurdities than to shout your punchlines and roll your eyes…

reviews.author: Dante
reviews.text: "So bad it's good" culture is truly a plague on online cinema discourse, people will watch a movie, enjoy the movie, but because it's deemed "cheesy" or "cringe" or whatever there absolutely has to be a pretence about their enjoyment only being tongue-in-cheek. It's one thing to genuinely not enjoy a movie, but it doesn't make sense to act like a movie that you get a great deal of entertainment from is "bad". Sure, there's a degree of technical competence in which a work can be judged on, but Johnny Mnemonic isn't exactly an art film with no budget. It's not any less technically competent then any other Hollywood sci-fi action movie of the time period.

reviews.text: I saw this movie once before, in the year 2012, when I was 23. I watched it in 20-minute nightly increments on my laptop before falling asleep in my cheap hotel room in Paris. So I will always associate Greydon Clark’s Joysticks with visiting Paris, but now I will also associate it with Toronto’s legendary Kingsway Theatre, where tonight I saw a faded 35mm print. It was a rare thrill to see Joe Don Baker’s beautiful mug fill up a 40-foot cinema screen.

reviews.text: A great musical panorama about upward mobility and class anxiety that is probably still Lee's most radical gambit of let its many disparate part just go as far as they can while still enlighten each other. Lee likes playing with ideas and the main relationship here is entire theoretical by design which can make the main narrative feel hollow until one accepts its just a strong throughline for Lee's anxieties about his own position. Often embarrassing, pretty frank, full of swings, unexpected notes (McKee's big speech) and good small observations (Snipes taking all his frustration at his brother’s junkie girlfriend instead of him). It is hold together by Lee's use of music and the best group of performances he ever got (Turturro and Jackson in particular do career best work),

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: It is always great when Spike Lee is unleashed and just moves around whatever is on his mind, and few of his movies do it quite like this one. Barely interest in narrative and the Jackson thread is allowed to completely overwhelm Sciorra’s plot because in a movie about upward mobility, the anxiety of going down remains the most haunting one. Also, probably the most honest Lee has ever been about his own mixed feelings about his Hollywood career. Ernest Dickerson’s finest hour and Spike’s best cast.

reviews.text: I wouldn’t have minded the shoddy anachronism and confusing pacing so much, with flammable-looking wigs and Michael Caine’s tartan suit, if the movie didn’t take itself so seriously; 100 minutes isn’t nearly enough time to cram a love story, a buddy adventure, mid-18th century scottish politics, AND a commentary on whether, after a major defeat, ‘tis better to continue fighting or move on. It's a too many cooks in the kitchen situation; too many undercooked ideas and storylines to make for a satisfying whole. Even its attempts to convey the bloodshed during and after the Battle of Colloden pales in comparison to Peter Watkins's 1966 recreation for TV, which put you through a wringer on a shoestring. At least Donald Pleasance, Freddie Jones, and Trevor Howard remained reliable presences.

It’s also the directorial debut of Ron Ormond, the crackpot exploitation filmmaker behind such later masterpieces as If Footmen Tire You, What Will Horses Do? and Mesa of Lost Women.

reviews.text: As a classic movie fan, you spend a lot of time with the Western, enough that it's easy to have kind of a skewed view of how the genre exists in the public consciousness. Even before you get to the post-60s subgenre that's entirely about The Hard Truth Behind The Myth, when I throw on a Cowboy Classic, it's very likely to be a complex portrait of an emerging community, or an unsparing and bleak hostage thriller, or a tragedy about the commodification of human life. So it's instructive for a fan of the genre to sometimes take in a random B-list picture and relearn to enjoy the simple pleasures: stagecoach robberies, big meaty punches that all make the same…

reviews.author: A Merrit
reviews.text: Lash LaRue is a very clean cut western star with a great gimmick and there are no surprises here, but it is a fun B Western from Ron Ormond himself. A bullwhip wielding bandit leads a gang on bank heists and LaRue is brought in to get him. He does it by infiltrating the gang and eventually unmaking the bandit. There’s no romance here, but there is some comedic relief, and a big bullwhip fight at the end. It’s actually better constructed than Ormond’s Mesa of Lost Women, and LaRue has lots of charisma to carry things, although this is still a very low budget production to the point it feels made for TV at times.

Bronson does pretty much phone in his performance but that's fine as he can really do all this stuff in his sleep. The action surrounding the central plot is generally pretty good (aside from a subplot involving Bronson's daughter getting felt up on a bus, which doesn't go anywhere, aside from providing a bit of irony). There's a few laugh out loud moments and the film really is just corrupt and sleazy to its core. The final action scene involving a crane in a harbour is well put together and a lot of fun. reviews.text: In Kuroneko the samurai isn't portrayed as the honorable warrior we more than often see them as in movies. No, they are opportunistic low-life men, pillaging and raping when they're not in combat. And two of their victims are a poor mother and daughter-in-law. As they lay in the ashes of their burnt down house, they make a pact with the evil God. A pact that allows them to take human form, but only if they vow to suck the blood - and life out of every samurai in their path.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Though its atmosphere haunts us all, the horror of Kuroneko is nevertheless an unusually specific one, applicable only to one class of people. No one else is threatened by the violent, bloodthirsty beings who rip out the throats of samurai — indeed, many of the others benefit from the actions of the unseen creatures, stripping the bodies of dead men for clothing, coins, and valuables. For those forced to live near them, the samurai are the danger, not the unseen teeth and hunger. If anything, a being that stalks samurai is (whisper it) an ally.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Bloody vengeance has never been so beautiful. Kuroneko is folk horror done right, with a misty mise-en-scène reminiscent of a dark Kabuki tale and some of the most exquisitely arresting and aesthetically stunning cinematography I have seen in quite some time. From the first glimpse of the opening credits to the final frame, there is an emanation of dread and macabre wonder, as we venture through bamboo forests outside the gate of Rajōmon, where various samurai are disappearing into thin air and found bloodied, bitten on the neck amidst the burnt ruins of a peasant home by what the authorities can only describe as a ghastly figure roaming the pitch black woods; plucking out weary ronin and disposing of them…

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Some of the readings on this film by certain critics are so wildly misguided and prone to misinterpretation it's absurd - this is not a dialectical work, Godard was never any good at Brechtianisms. Rather, we see the beginnings here of his late style: total didactic turned into moving poetry. This brings on a remarkable contradiction - this super-didacticism gives us Godard at his coldest, yet finds in this record of collective responses, Godard the dreamer. La Chinoise is about one thing, yet it is expressed entirely through the exchange of ideas. This is the moment Godard stops making films about cinephila and becomes a radical political artist.

reviews.text: Like some absurd inversion of a Faustian bargain, a bet is placed that esoteric knowledge in labyrinthine architecture will work to conquer the afterlife; entombment as a hermetic seal upon the Pharaoh’s exorbitant riches derived from a life of infinite cruelty and sadistic exploitation of the group collective. The pyramid must remain as obscure and impenetrable of a symbol to the masses as possible, so as to ensure that the living do not become wise to their dead rulers. A regime of silence is enforced at all costs: blindfolds are common attire, tongues are preemptively removed, a group of priests agree to a collective live burial alongside their Pharaoh.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: The story of Land of the Pharaohs isn’t the most gripping one, but it is told well enough by director Howard Hawks. What makes the movie worth watching is the spectacle including fantastic sets, fabulous costumes and thousands of (real life) extras. The movie is shot very well and a joy to look at. I also like the actors here. The script tends to be a bit melodramatic and Joan Collins as the feisty, scheming and power-hungry princess gives off some pulpy vibes, but I actually quite like that. It’s a colorful and entertaining performance fitting to the mood of the film and Collins is always very easy on the eye.

reviews.text: Originally a XXX film shot by the director of DEEP THROAT that starred Sandra “LAST HOUSE ON THE LEFT” Peabody, LEGACY OF SATAN was shorn of its sex scenes by rogue distributor Bryanston and released as a traditional horror movie. But it’s much more than that. Blessed with a soul-shaking Moog synthesizer soundtrack (“Electronic Rhythms Created by Arlon Ober and Mel Zelniker”), this is beautiful lo-fi hypnosis and the greatest horror soap opera that you’ve never seen. There’s no glue to hold the 68-minute movie together and it tends to drag towards the end. But that’s okay. The mishmash of awkward eroticism, over-the-top emoting, and inadvertent art-horror techniques yields a transcendent experience. And those SYNTHS! The Ober-Zelniker hit machine knew its way around a Moog Rogue, but not really. I wouldn’t have it any other way. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: Relentlessly chilly, although echoing with a restrained heartbeat, Leviathan is a grandiose and heart-wrenching take on Orthodox religion and the corruption that weaves within its system and those who attend. Andrey Zvyagintsev (I'm laughing at myself trying to pronounce his name) paints an epic picture of genuine characters, incidents of fate, and masterful sequences of delicate restraint and wispy visual interactions.

reviews.author: Bruno Youn
reviews.text: Leviathan is a fascinating tale of corruption and betrayal, relying on some intriguing visual allegories and symbolisms as a way to propel the story. I was surprised by the great amount of witty humor in the first portion of the film, which proved to be very entertaining, also serving as a display of helplessness towards the abuse of power and corruption that surround the town. Then, we follow the destructive paths some of the characters end up taking and the film becomes truly somber. The performances are all top notch and we are rewarded with some of the most breathtaking cinematography ever shown on screen. Director Andrey Zvyagintsev’s geniality consists in leaving it up to the viewer to decide what to make of the fate of these people, ending the picture with a very clever and tragically ironic turn of events. Leviathan is one of the year’s finest films and an absolute must-see!

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: Leviathan ultimately feels underwhelming despite being Andrey Zvyagintsev's most ambitious work. It touches on many recurrent themes in Zvyagintsev's filmography, from adolescence to infidelity, this time with heavy input of political and religious undercurrents, yet it fails to leave an impression regardless.

But at its core, you're still dealing with a story about a grown man using puppets to trick a naive teenage girl into falling in love with him. I get that he's really a wounded soul who uses his puppets to communicate feelings he can't bare to express on his own. That's all well and good. All I'm saying is he's still pursuing a relationship with a sixteen year old kid who admits she's never even kissed a man before. Like I said: creepy. Charming. Sincere. Enchanting at times. reviews.text: This represents an important loophole in bad filmmaking strategy. While it's generally the case that you can't make an intentionally humorous bad movie and have it turn out funny in the right way, what you can do instead is make an intentionally weird bad movie, one that isn't necessarily funny in terms of jokes but is rather amusing in terms of sheer dedication to screwiness (as is the case here). For example, this film not only delivers on its promise of featuring a Lobster Man from Mars, but also goes one step further and introduces Bunny Men from Neptune for little reason. reviews.text: I suppose I should read the book before really digging into this, but I want to say that the one aspect of this that really stood out is how Humbert's obsessive, controlling behavior is so easily confused for protective parenting to those who don't realize he's lusting after Lolita and acting out of jealousy. The implication is one of those searing, vicious jabs that Kubrick is good at making, that peels back the layers and reveals ugliness; it's Freud (who gets name checked) at his most fucked up. It's a bold but somehow not surprising accusation from Kubrick in 1962 (whether he intended it, whether Nabokov intended it, I cannot say): protectiveness is just another facet of sexual domination, of patriarchy, of the view of women as property. It's a bleak outlook he (whoever) has for Lolita's prospects as a free being, but better than encased in paternalistic pedophilic "love."

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Languid, sweaty, brutal redneck melodrama that confirms - along with VANISHING POINT - that Richard C. Sarafian was possibly the most overlooked/undervalued talent to come out of New Hollywood, mixing anti-war and feminist notions with uncomfortable, exploitative sex and violence. We’re all just pawns in somebody else’s meaningless conflict, and even daring to dream is a punishable sin unto itself. Every time I revisit this, I wonder if it’s one of the best films I’ve ever seen. If anything, it owns one of the finest casts of character actors ever assembled, and reminds you that young Jeff Bridges was possibly the coolest looking dude to ever grace the big screen.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Languid, hazy, almost oppressively sad neo Western about the women left behind during decades of war waged by sweaty, psychotic, prejudice-blinded men who can barely recall why their conflict began in the first place. Like MS. 45, finds the perfect balance between hard (redneck) 'sploitation and ambitious art movie, elevated by stagey, robust performances that are tough to look away from, even when they get really ugly (this movie will change the way you see Scott Wilson forever). There's a scene on a porch where a mother comforts her daughter following the most heinous of violations by basically saying "it's best to just blank these atrocities from memory" that essentially sums the entire film up in one bleak, melancholy, unusually touching instance of hot house melodrama. My pick (along with director Richard C. Sarafian) for the most undervalued New Hollywood product.

reviews.text: Season Hubley is in the wrong place at the wrong time. She’s at a rural bus stop, waiting to make her connection to Nashville, when she suddenly finds herself kidnapped and caught in the middle of a feud between neighboring patriarchs Rod Steiger and Robert Ryan. Ryan broke with local protocol and bought a portion of Steiger’s land after it was seized for unpaid back taxes. So far, Steiger’s and Ryan’s respective adult sons have been content to steal each other’s livestock and destroy each other’s stills, but Hubley’s presence serves as a catalyst for intensifying violence, especially after Steiger’s youngest son (Jeff Bridges) falls in love with her.

reviews.text: “you grew up on me — i just changed.”Oh man, I loved this – broke my heart just right. Jack Burns, a misfit cowboy wandering through a world that’s outgrown him, moves with stubborn dignity and a rugged warmth – in what Kirk Douglas later called his favorite role. Lonely Are the Brave (David Miller, 1962) plays like a farewell to the mythic cowboy – a western spirit dropped into a contemporary world that has no place for him. reviews.author: Film at Lincoln Center
reviews.text: In her debut feature, Jessica Hausner probes the uncanny banality of suburban malaise through the eyes of Rita, a teen girl riding sinister currents of adolescent anger and disillusionment. Consigned to the margins by both her family and her classmates, Rita broods and drifts from one rebellion to the next as the tension of her interpersonal alienation builds inexorably to a brazenly violent conclusion. Eliciting performances of casually deadpan menace from a cast of nonprofessional actors, Hausner stages an indelible parable of unflinching existential horror.

reviews.author: Jack🧠
reviews.text: Settling into a live-action anime adaptation can be difficult, especially when I'm so accustomed to the playful animation of Lupin the Third's many adventures. Yet this 2014 reimagining crackles with jazzy energy, capturing the playful, globetrotting spirit of Monkey Punch's groundbreaking series. It brings to life the chaos of Lupin's heists, the sharp wit of Fujiko, the stoic precision of Jigen, and Goemon's lethal grace. Ryuhei Kitamura's direction preserves their animated exuberance. At the same time, Tadanobu Asano's portrayal of Inspector Zenigata provides a grounded, almost tragicomic foil to Lupin's antics, balancing the madness with a sense of weary determination.

Gladly Kitamura gets to showcase some of his more stylish direction. Still not brilliant levels of his early career but not as bad as his first two American pictures (had no style whatsoever). Pretty good direction, it seems like Kitamura had a lot of fun making this. Great sets. Around half of it was English and the rest in Japanese without subs so I probably missed out on some stuff. Who cares, the stylized action is what really matters. It’s pretty fun.

The tough gangster flick you'd expect is really more of a film about Kelly's fear of anything that symbolizes death and how the people in his gang, including his girlfriend, tease him about it. Susan Cabot plays Kelly's gun moll Flo Becker in some surprisingly cold and calculating displays that really grab your attention. reviews.author: Jon Peters
reviews.text: Roger Corman’s MACHINE-GUN KELLY (1959) might not be the most exciting of gangster films, as the film was shot in 10 days, mostly focusing its action in hideouts as characters debate their next action. But the image of a young Charles Bronson sitting in a rocking chair pointing his machine gun at a disagreeing partner, is a cool image. In fact, George Kelly Barnes aka Machine Gun Kelly is an image of the idealized gangster; a criminal possibly born more out of myth than actuality, and his alarmingly calm arrest piqued Corman’s interest in a film about him. “I hired Robert Wright Campbell as the screenwriter and he wrote a very good script with strong, well-sketched characters,” Corman would say…

reviews.text: The wordless opening sequence is Roger Corman at his best. Exciting music scores the execution of a bank robbery and the getaway. Our glimpse inside the bank is captured in a single shot, the violence happening right on the edge of the frame. As with many of Corman’s directorial choices, it’s likely driven by frugality, but it gives that moment an elegance that jars with the frantic lead-up and getaway, and with the grimness of the material in general. Corman also tries to cut corners by setting much of the later sections in a single location, a hideout used by the characters after a kidnapping, but he doesn’t commit, cutting away to outside action too frequently. The pressure cooker quality…

reviews.text: Dang this was actually really good. It’s a gritty WW2 mainly aerial battle that Malta had to deal with and was fundamentally a finger in the damn of the Mediterranean Sea for which there job was to stop the oil transport to Africa during war time. Alec Guinness is excellent as always and there is a narrative of life trying to continue on this tiny island while constantly being bombed without appearing schmaltzy. Actually there is a lot of smart little stories that go on and only add to the complexity of what is being endured by these people and surprisingly water down the main theme. All in all I have to say I really enjoyed this B&W film but recognize that it might really only a gem for those who enjoy lesser known stories and movies of this genre. reviews.text: "Man in the Wilderness" is a 1971 adventure western directed by Richard C. Sarafian. Focused on the grandiose applications of the daunting frontier, actor Richard Harris plays the character of Zachary Bass. Bass is an experienced hunter and tracker, traveling along with a grouping of beaver pelt fur traders in the Pacific Northwest. Tracking a set of deer with another, Bass makes his shot and kill but the other tracker, who is less experienced, only wounds his target. Bass, acknowledging that he needs to finish the job for the other deer, tracks the wounded animals trail leading him face to face with an angry bear. In a pretty visceral graphic display, Bass is mauled almost to the extent of death,…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Hard not to view this through the prism of THE REVENANT (which I enjoyed, by the way). But by admittedly unfair comparison this is far more economical, just as brutal in its violence, and generally unburdened of ostensible profundity. A clean genre picture. Interesting that this has a single, lumbering visual metaphor, that of the fur trappers hauling their boat overland to what turns out to be a dry river, that single-handedly musters all of the handwringing over revenge and manifest destiny and survival and the soul, you know? that Iñárritu's film made such a show of.

reviews.text: The first twenty minutes or so of Man in the Wilderness are pretty compelling – set in the early 1800s in America's Northwest, Zach Bass (Richard Harris) is mauled by a bear and left to die in the wilderness by his fur trapping partners. The remainder of the film consists of alternating scenes of the fur trappers dragging a large boat over a seemingly hostile terrain and Zach struggling to make his way back to civilization. The performances are good, as would be expected by Harris and John Huston, and the cinematography nicely shows off the spectacular scenery, but the film is marred by annoying flashbacks, some odd POV shots early on, a cloying music score, a laughably absurd scene…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: This art western in which left for dead Richard Harris tracks John Huston through wilderness might be a bit too dramatic inert for its own good, but it packs a lot of raw power. A film whose ugliness produces a certain form of beauty.

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Man In The Wilderness is the largely forgotten precursor to The Revenant, telling the classic frontier tale of Hugh Glass (here “Zachary Bass” played by Richard Harris). While Inarritu’s survival thriller was driven by revenge and dreamy symbolism, Richard Sarafian’s film is a survival adventure told with ‘70s sturdiness and in earthy tones. Harris barely speaks in this, but his character is established by his actions and in flashbacks (that thematically matter in the end).

The home movies of her loved ones. These are possibly the only things she'll have left since her husband could die any day in the wake of nuclear annihilation. reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: "Castle’s theatrical exploitation methods—most famously employed with The Tingler—blurred where cinema ended and reality began. Dante makes this explicitly political, with Woolsey both exploiting and revealing the terrors of the atomic age. By the time a bomb explodes on screen, Dante’s framing asks whether the cinema is meant to scare us in there or out here. That the film closes on a truly ominous image—a Vietnam-era helicopter flying along the shore—makes this often silly affair into a sharp attack on the military industrial complex that only subversive fiction can counter."

reviews.text: Joe Dante is just about the only satirist worth a damn whose work is ultimately chooses optimism and affection over cynicism. reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Movies will always be extremely important to me, but in a time of straight-up national crisis I suppose it is inevitable that they will feel less important. I'm a nervous, anxious person by nature, and it's bad voodoo when the national mood is able to match, and surpass, my own floor-pacing tension, and over the last several days it has made it nearly impossible for me to focus on or think about movies (or books, or music, or TV, or anything requiring more than a few minutes of undivided attention) in the way that I used to. The question, then, becomes what role do movies serve in a world that seems seconds from disaster, and this is as intelligent and smart an answer as any. Dante doesn't lose the palpable nuclear paranoia of the Cuban Missile Crisis in a haze of nostalgia, and the non-conformist heart of this can pump blood into any era - the scarier the better.

reviews.text: For all practical purposes, 'Meek’s Cutoff' is a Western. But for many viewers, here lies the problem, for at its heart 'Meek’s Cutoff' doesn’t function like a genre film. It certainly revises and challenges traditional elements of the Western genre — accentuating the females’ perspective, avoiding an action-centric narrative for something more explorative — but 'Meek’s Cutoff' is the type of film that shows a weakness in words like “subversive." Reichardt isn’t just toying with conventions, she is leading us into more uncharted territory. With this, the film encourages a loosening of our understanding as viewers and a willingness to get a little lost.

Patient and liberating, with its strengths not rooted in the typical Western action sequences you’re used to but in gradual exploration. Even one of the simple cuts up to the clouds with the fucking incredible score playing nearly reduced me to tears, for reasons I don’t even know. Seriously great stuff. Nichols has admitted himself that he may have cut too much from this film to keep the story as cohesive as it should have been. reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: A Roaring Twenties gangster saga that only the Coen brothers could concoct, Miller’s Crossing marries the hard-boiled sensibility of classic noir fiction with the filmmakers’ trademark savory dialogue, colorful characters, and finely calibrated set pieces. Gabriel Byrne brings a wry gravitas to the role of Tom Reagan, the quick-thinking right-hand man to a powerful crime boss (Albert Finney), whose unflappable cool is tested when he begins offering his services to a rival outfit—setting off a cascade of betrayals, reprisals, and increasingly berserk violence. The Hopperesque visuals of cinematographer Barry Sonnenfeld, majestically elegiac score by Carter Burwell, and vivid supporting performances from John Turturro and Marcia Gay Harden come together in an intricately constructed slice of pulp perfection that crackles with sardonic wit while plumbing existential questions about free will and our own terrifying capacity for evil.

reviews.text: Spike Lee's WWII men-on-a-mission film follows a group of stranded Buffalo Soldiers taking shelter in an Italian village while protecting a possible magical little boy. Not sure why this is rated so low, except that it's too long; then again so are most war movies. Author James MacBride adapted his own novel, and I like that the film preserves the literary spirit. I never found it boring, but the love triangle is a bit out of place and could have easily been cut. Definitely did not expect the mystery framing plot with its stacked cast and Inside Man vibes. Too bad the schmaltzy payoff is almost as groan-inducing as Saving Private Ryan's.

reviews.author: Tanner
reviews.text: 'Miracle at St. Anna' begins with an elderly black war veteran watching 'The Longest Day', staring The Duke square in the face and stating: "We fought that war too." That's essentially the film's thesis statement and trying to find any black-centric war film is a tough ask. Spike Lee made something approaching that later as well with 'Da 5 Bloods' and while both films are wildly different, they're connected by central conceit. Black soldiers reckoning with fighting a war for a country that seems to hate them. Both groups of soldiers are reminded of their status by overwhelming radio messages. Whether from Axis Sally or Hanoi Hannah, they're made hyperaware that their race trumps any benefit service might have provided…

reviews.text: A messy, convoluted, spiritual, classical Hollywood-style workprint for DA 5 BLOODS. Different war, same America. The pacing is jarringly strange, laborious at times, but incredibly ambitious in the scope of the human interactions it examines in such a condensed narrative timeframe. Combat scenes are particularly cut to shreds by the editing, much like the bodies of the soldiers themselves, who are hit with machine gunfire with unflinching force. Spike and Libatique's images are grand, the equal of anything Ford or Wellman put on screen, just without the coherence.

reviews.text: A força do velho Monkey Business de Hawks - é até mesmo a do cinema como mostrado, por exemplo, no admirável filme de Rohmer sobre Louis Lumière - vem do fato de que o macaco é um macaco de verdade. Um verdadeiro macaco exige de um cineasta uma qualidade cada vez menos aceita hoje: a paciência. A paciência necessária para dirigir um animal produz uma figura retórica que também é uma qualidade moral desvalorizada: o eufemismo. O efeito que um macaco real pode produzir em uma tomada de filme escapa à ordem mecânica do espetacular. - Jean-Claude Biette, "Le cinéma descend du singe", Cahiers du cinéma n° 391, janeiro de 1987

reviews.text: If you've got Carl "Alfalfa" Switzer and Beta from Ozzie and Harriet in your motorcycle gang, it's a safe bet they aren't the Straight Satans or Hell's Angels. Who's your sergeant-at-arms? Satch from the Bowery Boys? Anne Neyland stars as Terry, a thrill-seeking blonde bombshell in a bullet bra who's been playing Randy (Steven Terrell) against Nick (John Ashley) for kicks. Nick's just returned home from prison after treating a pedestrian like a speedbump, and he blames his road rival Randy for the incarceration. Meanwhile the old gang has gotten chummy with a police lieutenant (Russ Bender), who's been supervising them, making sure the kids obey the rules of the road and turned the lot of them into malted-drinking drapes…

That alone feels quietly progressive for 1957.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Thoroughly satisfying film noir based on a novel by the great Raymond Chandler. The film is a trimmed down version of the book (if memory serves) but it's still plenty complicated enough - luckily there's a hard boiled voice-over that kicks in every now and again to keep you abreast of the latest developments. The plot focuses on gumshoe Philip Marlowe, who finds himself on the trail of a broad and a stolen necklace. The plot moves quickly and is plenty of fun - always just slightly the right side of weird and thoroughly charming with it. Dick Powell might not be exactly what you would imagine wisecracking detective Marlowe to be after reading the books, but he certainly makes…

People will know this story as Farewell, My Lovely (and the famed Robert Mitchum movie from the 70’s), which I haven’t seen so a compare & contrast can’t be done. The name was changed-at least in the United States-as… RKO thought people would think of this as another Dick Powell musical like the Busby Berkeley musicals from the 30’s I know him best from. It really creates a jarring tonal disconnect between her scenes and the rest of the film, which is shockingly grim and sleazy at times.

reviews.text: The amount of talent gathered here, to make something so utterly lacking in clarity or intention, boggles the mind. I've seen plenty of worse movies, but I've seen few that are quite so confused about what they're trying to be. The result is an almost impressively expansive dead zone, forgotten even by the annals of late-night cable. Every now and then, Belushi will scream something, Aykroyd will partake in some insane mugging, Moriarty will slip into seduction mode, bits of small-scale destruction will flash past. These moments are oases in a desert of nonsense.

Then the relationship ends and after reality settles in again, you think back and it seems different, you realize you were kind of a dick and that the reason everything seemed beautiful was because you were too wrapped up in your own feelings to see what was really going on, how selfish and manipulative and cruel you were being even in the glow of new love. reviews.text: The idea of mournfully placing two lead characters/performances from a bleak New Hollywood abusive romance drama into a glitzy, artificial Old Hollywood musical melodrama environment is an interesting one and was clearly attractive to Scorsese as a chance to flex his cinematic knowledge and vocabulary in the energetic, colorful club musical sequences + studio backlot NY production design. It's stunning to look at, especially those last like 30-40 minutes that Minelli just dominates. But idk, the actual romance writing was just not particularly convincing at this length and is not helped by the fact that De Niro's never-ending, improvised unpleasant levels are cranked a little too high too quickly for you to understand how they got together in the first…

reviews.text: From its ferocious nihilism to its stylistic adoption by the likes of Joe Strummer, Taxi Driver has always had tendrils connecting it to the punk era, but I'd argue for including, of all things, this opulent tribute to, and travesty of, the MGM musical as one of Scorsese's unintended punk films. Punk's explosive return to zero balanced radical revision with reactionary aesthetic values, and Scorsese's simultaneously intricate recreation of the most opulent traits of the classic movie musical and vicious critique of its thematic implications might truly encapsulate the punk explosion and implosion even better than the director's preceding film.

This is what happens when you worship the god of capital above all else. Grim flick, this one.

reviews.text: There are many film that attempt to capture dreams. However, most of them are rather like observations of a dream— like staring into a glass case box. Night on the Galactic Railroad may be the first time where I truly felt below the conscience with my eyes open. This nocturnal film swallowed me into a dark, silent, and wonderful place. Nothing really makes sense, yet it strangely does— in an intangible sense. The recur of train-tracks, heavy childish breathes, plodding footsteps— isolated sounds. Added, the patient moving frames are entrancing. This was a dream... this was a dream...

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: More madness from the crazy Greek maestro Nico Mastorakis. This time he's shamelessly ripping off the Police Academy series, with the imaginatively titled Ninja Academy. The clunky plot set up begins with two rival ninja academies, before we are introduced to a ragtag group of caricatures that go to train at one of them. We've got a kid whose father insists he joins before he can get his allowance, a James Bond rip off, a mime, a clumsy cook, a Rambo rip off and two girls trying to impress a dude at the beach. You know....the usual bunch. The rest of the film is mostly made up of pointless training montages set to annoying pop music while the various caricatures…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"

Sometimes things are served better when the plot is dumb because the film is self-aware that it is dumb in the first place.

I have seen enough of Mastorakis' films to know exactly what I was getting into. This could have been called "Montage Academy" because there is a new one every couple of minutes with increasingly banal songs (two of them based on the Hokey Pokey) by the Greaseband who sound 100% percent like the song that is now going through your head based on a Greek director's remake of "Police Academy" with a mime, random nudity, slapstick "comedy", and a final ninja battle that does it's best to warrant the first 75 minutes. reviews.text: When the mime is the best part you have to take inventory. This movie is so confused, nothing lands. No jokes, no tension, no charisma. The concept being Police Academy but, ninjas…(and there wasn’t much ninjitsu) really could’ve delivered a campy 80’s smorgasbord of laughs, and with a nudist camp playing volleyball, ninjas singing The Hoky Poky around a campfire, and a cast of bumbling idiots ripe for a martial arts boot camp, it almost does. But deep down it was pretty tone deaf and mean spirited even for the era, and likely not made by people who were having fun. Hard pass.

reviews.author: Christian Di Leo
reviews.text: Sometimes people just mess with the wrong motherfucker. A sturdy, trashy, rip-roaring splatterfest about a group of highway robbers who unfortunately set their sights on a Jason Bourne-esque psychopath/serial killer and ultimately pay the price. Littered with junky dialogue, good to not-so-good performances, buckets of blood and gore accompanied by great practical effects, and plenty of twists and turns, NO ONE LIVES is pure throwback genre fare that definitely ranks up with WWE Films & director Ryuhei Kitamura's best. Luke Evans steals the show as the lead and I very much enjoyed seeing character actors Lee Tergesen and Gary Grubbs pop-up in supporting roles. Was also fun to remember that Mose from Ned's Declassified School Survival Guide, and professional wrestler Tyrus (a.k.a. Brodus Clay) are in this as well. NO ONE LIVES totally hits the target and dishes out a whole lot of bloodshed in the process! Savage stuff!!!!

reviews.text: What makes this, besides the inspired cast (Ritter and Reeves are particular riots), is how it plays the scalating chaos of three act variations on the same act structure against Bogdanovich laidback style, most very controlled long takes. The world is increasing taken by chaos, but the images keep an integrity that gives such chaos a different meaning. A movie about finding pleasure at work no matter the madness involved. The interplay of repetition and how it relates to the craft of putting a play is put to great use as well. The one mistake is Caine's offscreen narration which I assume was add to the movie, it brings an extra showbizz sentimentality that is better expressed in the choreography of performances. Otherwise, this is a formal triumph and a very funny movie.

reviews.text: Such a tight, suspenseful adventure yarn - and a terrific train movie! J. Lee Thompson really knew how to keep you on the edge of your seat. Not in the sense of "Oh isn't that action-y" but "This whole film is a fluid, non-stop flow of pulsating energy". If that makes any sense.

reviews.text: Past always screams for our return, because she is the mother that gave us an identity and a life perception. Life perception is all about coherence, and coherence demands a logic to exist. A logic, not THE logic. There is no such thing. What if that logic is gone? What if 1+1=1 despite our beliefs and inner struggle to conform to norms? A journey then begins, which main purpose is to shed some visible light over the tangible and intangible factors that puts the pieces back in their place.

reviews.text: one of the great benefits about watching slow cinema is that as you watch slower and slower films, your tolerance for said pacing extends more and more, and this warps your experience of watching anything else -- i remember as a teenager that i found tarkovsky's cinema to be interminably boring and long, but watching nostalgia this time felt very quick and concise by comparison to films by bela tarr or lav diaz -- when put up against them, tarkovsky is eminently accessible and exciting! i feel like i can finally appreciate him now that i've seen his style taken in more extreme directions -- it's clear to me now how much of a keystone he is for so many other artists that i love.

reviews.author: CJ Probst
reviews.text: Every time I watch an Andrei Tarkovskiy film I am left completely and utterly drained. His films require an intense concentration and are often times trialing, if you do not fall onto his wavelength it is incredibly easy to get sidetracked and have your mind begin to wander during long takes in which very little appears to be happening. Taskovskiy’s films can be extremely abstract without any recognizable or traditional plotlines anywhere to be found. This is particularly true in the case of the existentially contemplative Nostalghia, his penultimate achievement.
