reviews.author: Josh Gillam
reviews.text: For his first film as a director, Richard Attenborough transferred Joan Littlewood’s acclaimed avant-garde take on the First World War to the screen, in the process creating a kind of satirical anti-war film not quite like any other. Attenborough decided to keep the theatrical structure of Littlewood’s original show, and the film is all the better for it, a deliberately heightened style that gets across that mix of farce and tragedy in so many creatively unique ways.

reviews.author: Will Steele
reviews.text: Rarely do you find a British classic so avant-garde in its presentation and critical in its retelling of as fiercely patriotic a theme as war. Attenborough’s choice to stage World War One as a seaside spectacle in my beloved Brighton just adds to how special this beautifully mournful portrait of war plays today, and certainly did whilst the Vietnam war waged on.

reviews.text: A rather astonishing and stunning directorial debut by Richard Attenborough, Oh! What a Lovely War takes a bit of time making clear just what point it is going for, but by the time Maggie Smith takes the stage in a music-hall number cum recruiting drive, it is evident that a major and potentially powerful anti-war film is under way. Based on a stage musical, Attenborough's adaptation scripted by Len Deighton uses reworded songs of the World War One era to comment musically on the absurdity and tragedy of war, building slowly but inexorably to a foreseeable but nonetheless devastating conclusion. reviews.text: Deep in the windswept marshes of war-torn medieval Japan, an impoverished older woman and her daughter-in-law murder lost samurai and sell their belongings for the most meager of sustenance. When a bedraggled neighbor returns from battle, lust, jealousy, and rage threaten to destroy the trio’s tenuous existence, before an ominous, ill-gotten demon mask seals their horrifying fate. Driven by primal emotions, dark eroticism, a frenzied score by Hikaru Hayashi, and stunning images both lyrical and macabre, the chilling folktale Onibaba by Kaneto Shindo conjures a nightmarish vision of humankind’s deepest desires and impulses.

reviews.text: I´ve rarely seen a movie switch between so many different genres during its runtime. Romance, tragedy, psychological drama, mystery thriller, and science fiction, “Abre los ojos” has it all and all the parts fit well together. The film never lost my interest. It has an original and imaginative plot and whenever I thought I figured it out, it took a sharp turn and kept me guessing again. I also enjoyed the interesting philosophical and psychological themes (reality, dreams, perception, identity, trauma, immortality), experimental structure, stylish direction, and trippy, nightmarish atmosphere. Not to mention a drop-dead gorgeous Penélope Cruz who would make me question my reality, too. If you´re in the mood for a mindfuck film with a Spanish flair, check it out.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Blends the dirty, industrial blue collar sci-fi detail of Alien and a conspiracy noir/morality play western with Sean Connery essentially acting as the lonely space sheriff investigating the brutal exploitation of mining workers at the hands of a corrupt corporation that drugs and kills them (via vivid exploding heads) for profit efficiency. Showing that despite all our astonishing technological advancements, the same capitalist greed of the Old West is still very much our guiding force and even in space sometimes the solution is still a principled, shotgun-wielding cowboy. A fun idea that Hyams stages with incredible genre-bending craft; filthy sets, goopy squibs, and gorgeous miniature/analog FX worthy of Kubrick (that presumably got him the 2010 gig) as the dexterous camera moves through the cramped, tensely pressurized space rig replicating the thrilling chases and brawls/gunfights you'd expect to see tracked on horseback or in a grimy city street.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Pings two of my biggest fetishes in that A) it's not just HIGH NOON in space but one that replaces the fear of rabid anti-communism with its own anti-capitalist streak; and B) it's loaded with analog effects tech (specifically Introvision, an in-camera front-projection compositing process). I know it's weird but I get a genuine kick out of Connery storming through a set of burnished fiberglass saloon-style swinging doors.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Apparently the jury is still out on whether you can make a horror movie in outer space, but you can definitely make a western and here is a superb example. It was produced a few years after Alien and bears its obvious stylistic influence in every frame; they could easily be set in the same fictional universe of faceless, despotic corporations bent on maximizing profits no matter the human cost. While Hyams plays with western tropes, like the new marshal who arrives at a corrupt frontier outpost, he also considers modern themes as well. (Modern for 1981 anyway.) There a heavy emphasis on surveillance cameras, communications intercepts, and the pervasive — or maybe invasive — computer screens, giving the whole film an atmosphere of paranoia and technological overreach. Plus, Frances Sternhagen plays a doctor so cantankerous she makes Bones McCoy look like Patch Adams. What’s not to love?

reviews.text: Paratroop Command is a ultra cheap AIP war movie from the late 50s that has no business being as watchable as it is. His own experience as a WWII combat cameraman shows up in the way he handles violence here. Men die and the movie just keeps moving. There's a Tarantino quote floating around calling…

Un cuarto de la película es material de archivo que sitúa los distintos episodios de la acción en momentos precisos del desarrollo de la segunda guerra. El resto está resuelto en exteriores del muy reconocible Iverson Movie Ranch con cinco o seis actores, cinco o seis dobles de acción, dos chicas, una moto con sidecar y un jeep. Es decir, se podría filmar en la Argentina de hoy y sin el INCAA. El asunto es saber hacer hacerla. Una clave es la concentración dramática. El tema central es el drama del soldado…

The Witney collection continues to deliver the goods.

reviews.author: Ruth Scouller
reviews.text: After viewing Kleiman's shorts, he clearly has a few persistent themes and stylistic influences running through his work. His film worlds are spliced together from a handful of sources to the point where they are familiar to experience and organic in an off-kilter way yet cannot be located on a map, let alone the planet. They exist in another realm entirely, that of film, that altogether alternate yet recognisably reflective universe. He particularly demonstrates a fondness for Russian cinema, which is always felt in the bloodstream of his films and some of the directorial choices, if not always the characters.

reviews.author: Dave Crewe
reviews.text: The community at the centre of Ariel Kleiman’s Partisan is introduced with rare restraint and precision. After a short prologue, we are deposited into a secluded society, buried within sheltering slabs of through which thin rays of sunlight shine. The society (described in most reviews as a ‘cult’, though I’d argue that’s an overly simplistic categorisation) is composed of a dozen or so children, their mothers and patriarch Gregori (Vincent Cassel).

reviews.text: The ideal anti-war film. An endeavour that has been reduced down to its simplest fundamentals. Kubrick managed to depict the process of war dehumanising people, using the protagonist as his puppet, demonstrating the power of communication, and representing humanity as a collective. During a time when many films were pro-war, Kubrick, in his late 20s, posed crucial concerns about the purpose of war and the estrangement caused by it. At his most attentive and compassionate as a filmmaker. Every character represents something, and each war-torn sequence is extremely powerful. This is easily one of the best anti-war films ever made, in my eyes.

reviews.text: Sammo revolts against the means of production one fist at a time. There's a scene here in which Sammo shares a moment in his room with his lady love and it is all the more touching because he is covered in bruises. that makes sense in a movie that contains a little of everything: romance, chases, laughs, tragedy, extended brawls, an anger at exploitation (particularly of women) and awe for the feats the human body can pull. The main questioncreated by Pedicab Driver is how something that includes so much joy is also so masochistic? The mood shifts are Asian cinema at its most extreme and not for the cartesian cinephile. Also contains a fight scene between Sammo and Lau Kar-leung, that fitting for a scene involving the two greatest fight choreographers in movies, ishould be the standard-bearer for a closed quarter fight scenes since then.

reviews.text: It would be inaccurate to say that Sammo Hung smoothly transitions between the vast gulf of tones he uses in this film; the lurches from pure comedy to dazzling kung fu to tender sentiment to brutal tragedy come as fast and crazy as his speed-ramped shots. But this is Hong Kong's gleeful traversal of genres and moods taken to one of its wildest ever extremes, backed up by choreography that isn't just technically spellbinding but backed with real emotional purpose. If Jackie was Hong Kong's Keaton, Sammo was its Chaplin, maybe a smidge less daring on a sequence-to-sequence basis but able to make it mean more.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: PELLE THE CONQUEROR is the epitome of the well-made film. A period piece, faithfully adapted from a beloved novel, with all of the production elements working in perfect unison: the cast, the lensing, the costuming, the locations. But one is constantly nagged by a strange lack of passion and I'm afraid it's difficult to get too involved with Aryan on Aryan prejudice. The project itself feels bland, like some of those Miramax epics from the same period. The faults, I think, lay with the screenplay, which attempts to cram too much novelistic detail into 157 minutes, forcing the film to take too many narrative shortcuts, such as the clumsy overuse of coincidence.

reviews.text: all about the process of grief and the way thoughts manifest in frightening and uncontrollable ways in the face of tragedy, as well as how Stewart's character learns to cope with her brother’s passing as she descends further and further into a faux reality that’s displayed as a legitimate reality on screen. the whole film is exhibited as a double -- almost presenting, simultaneously, multiple and in a sense subjectively parallel existences (think Kiarostami's Certified Copy). Assayas' peculiar presentation method of a potentially "alternate" narrative makes all of the fantastical elements seem like part of the actuality of the protagonist's situation, rendering her story and character arc immensely ambiguous, and also making it impossible for viewers to know, with certainty, whether what they're seeing is part of the film’s true universe or just the internal mechanics of the way in which the protagonist's mind deals with the loss of her brother and the fear of her own demise.

It's formally romantic, treated as a supple craft, an artform like any other that requires skill and practice and the orchestration of simple, beautiful motions of hands and objects. reviews.text: My first experience with Robert Bresson’s cinema, a filmmaker-poet who redefines cinema as an art form, and I completely loved it. The film is certainly inspired (even though vaguely) by Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment, and in its essence conveys a philosophical message, a vision of guilt, redemption and man’s yearning for transcendence. It’s a work that not only communicates but also imposes itself almost like an ideology.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Pickpocket is a film of a lost soul, of a man detached and cold to the world. He exists almost just for the thrill of his crimes, but the film leaves us as just observers to his excitement. This is a sincere and austere film, with no overt narrative tricks. Instead we contemplate and witness a lonely life, a life of someone who sits in a room and practices pickpocketing techniques. He is a man who stands in the middle of the world, but cares only for himself. He lives without fear of God, and the woman he loves cannot save him. This is a film about the pointlessness of the pickpocket and how they add nothing to society. To be nothing is quite an existence. Pickpocket is a small and intriguing film, one of great influence, notably on Paul Schrader, but even today it holds up as a classic.

reviews.text: The dirty New York reflects a nation’s paranoia. A feverish portrait of post-war America, where anti-communism flowed from headlines into fiction. At the height of McCarthyism, when any minimal and distinct change outside the “normal” could be read as a threat to the homeland, the director plunges us into an underworld of pickpockets and informants, where the foundations of patriotism are negotiable and ideology is a currency. The film in a way does not align with the rigid moralism of the time; it punches hypocrisy, revealing that the struggle between capitalism and communism, these two ideologies that in a way in small details, know how to read what happens in reality, but ultimately dissolves into the law of the smartest.…

reviews.text: The grace and delicacy with which Samuel Fuller portrays marginalized people is one of his greatest strengths as a director, and it's something which has never been more apparent than it is in Pickup on South Street, a film he also wrote. Never either condemning or simplistically celebrating his people on the margins — usually criminals, but also sometimes those pushed aside by society; often both — Fuller invariably shows us their souls, including both the darkness and light therein.

reviews.text: Skip McCoy (Richard Widmark) is a professional pickpocket, a man whose survival, whose worth, is contingent on the sly gestures of an eloquent hand. When he touches a woman in this film, first to rob her, then, thinking she's a thief or worse, to hit her, and again (and again) to caress the wound, he isn't just working her over. He's going to work. "I play everything smart," he says, and by the time he says it we're hip enough to know it's a line uttered in the spirit of his maker.

It can be alienating at times, but in Pierrot Le Fou I think the perfect balance is struck between Godard the ponderous semiotician, Godard the strident leftist, and Godard the movie dude.…

reviews.author: Alternate Feed
reviews.text: Gene Roddenberry pitched a terrific premise for a network series (Planet Earth is his second stab, after Genesis II): on a post-nuclear war Earth, the surviving population has balkanized into small settlements of primitive and very distinct cultures. One group, having retained both the technological and advanced moral standards of pre-war society, sends its members from community to community to help rebuild civilization. Alas, this pilot movie suffers from a rinky-dink production and very poor scripting, as a team travels through the surviving underground tube system to a women-controlled town where the men are enslaved, in order to rescue a kidnapped doctor whose surgical skills are needed. Beloved performers Diana Muldaur and Janet Margolin are reduced to cat-fighting in the streets as they vie for the ownership of team leader John Saxon, who has emerged from a deep freeze to help restore human order. So silly.

reviews.text: Trash der unterhaltsamen Sorte. Ein Film, gedreht von einem Mann, mit dem Feminismusverständnis der 70er. Da werden erst Machos von einer schlagfertigen Polizistin vermöbelt, ehe sie dann ein Techtelmechtel mit dem Oberproll eingeht. Story, Inszenierung und Dialoge sind eine Katastrophe, aber immer wieder sorgen abstruse Szenen für saftige Lacher. Well, I will say right here and now that I was absolutely puzzled by that remark. Was this just a mere matter of fact statement, or was something more sinister at play here? It didn't exactly sound like a threat, but then again, we all know Canadians have this extremely gentle way of saying things. Put a "sorry" and an "eh" in a threat and it sounds positively charming. reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: ANOTHER tongue-in-cheek 80s slasher throwback, yay. Credit: some half decent kills, especially the hammer uppercut, and an opening credit sequence that references the golden age of Sierra games, complete with pixelated dissolve. Debit: everything else. Any time the killer isn't on screen, we're treated to long stretches of flatly shot third-rate soap opera, boring bitching and a metatastic discussion about Ferris fucking Bueller (who else) that seems go on forever. The obnoxiousness of all the characters is completely intentional of course. Strangely though, that doesn't make their deaths any more cathartic. Margaux Némé, the one girl who is vaguely likable, or at least not completely detestable, is hot but zoinks - couldn't act her way out of a Louis Vuitton bag. Biggest laugh - the dog eating pizza out of the box resting on a dead man's chest. That's the level we're at here folks.

reviews.text: A god damn masterpiece of how privilege and trauma feeds into a psychosis of deadly narcissism, and more importantly how it poisons external places once thought to be a safe haven. I was in love with Alex Ross Perry's Listen Up Phillip, whose close ups sought intimacy with characters it begged you to hate. Here the close ups are even more nauseating as we spend time with two to three characters who insist on social interaction even as it becomes more and more clear everyone would be best off in total isolation. Even more intriguing is how Perry is able to maintain the film's fever dream point of view, and yet contain a sobriety that is all the more frightening.

reviews.text: Revolving around a reverse eternal sunshine method where memories are recorded for objective view as opposed to being vanquished, "Rememory" finds its premise built on heady science fiction. That genre starting point, however, gives way to a muddled murder mystery that, despite its best intentions, is far less gripping that it should be. Starring a capable Peter Dinklage as the human motor for the plot's dramatics, the production alternates between sleekness and grit in accordance with the story's demands. All of it is solid-enough, but the film rarely succeeds in hooking its audience.

reviews.author: Devon Seltzer
reviews.text: There have been many films that attempt to tackle racism from the perspective of the targeted minority groups, a few (very few) have even dealt with Native Americans, though I think Rhymes for Young Ghouls might be the first to do so from a (relatively) modern perspective. The plot is honestly nothing special, following a young Mi'kmaq girl named Aila who deals drugs to bribe her way out of the local Catholic school, she finds herself in a mess when the cops steal her money. The rather ho-hum material is elevated greatly by the setting of a Canadian reservation, weaving into the crime narrative tidbits of traditional lore and legend, giving the story a grand, timeless feel. Additionally, the film's…

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Before going full genre film with Blood Quantum, director Jeff Barnaby made this energetic and stylish Mi'kmaq-centered drama. Threaded with pulpy elements - crime, caper, gore, ghosts - yet at its core, Rhymes For Young Ghouls is a grim story set against the backdrop of cultural genocide and generational trauma wrought by Canada’s residential schools and Indian agents. The various tonal/genre shifts don’t all comfortably fit together, the pace often feels too abrupt for the many narrative beats Barnaby is exploring, but the drama’s bleak anger is always incredibly raw and potent. The indigenous cast is uniformly strong, with fierce young lead Kawennáhere Devery Jacobs as the show-stealing star. She’s a riveting screen presence who I’m glad to see getting more work (most recently in Reservation Dogs).

reviews.text: Deeply weird, awkwardly dated (blame Crichton's reactionary wannabe cutting edge paranoia). Not only does this mystery hinge on a million-dollar rush Photoshop job but it futilely spends a lot of energy preemptively defending itself from charges of overt racism even while it traffics clulessly in the worst sort of western fantasies of Japanese otherness and decadence. Eating sushi off a naked lady might seem scandalous if it weren't a complete cartoon. Come for the empty stabs at a semi-relevant 90's-style sex thriller (twin ancient buzzterms: "Japan-bashing" and "auto-erotic asphyxiation"), stay for the actually tantalizing buddy pair up of Wesley Snipes and a never-hammier Sean Connery. reviews.author: Richard
reviews.text: I have seen many Robin Hood films, but Richard Lester’s poignant reimagining is sure to be a new favourite. Set many years after the swashbuckling triumphs of Sherwood Forest, Sean Connery’s Robin Hood—made weak by time and fate, but strong in will—finally returns home longing for the romance of his youth. Errol Flynn’s green tights and derring-do are replaced by frailty and introspection. The film’s melancholic ode to ageing heroes and their fading glories reminded me of Tennyson’s “Ulysses”.

reviews.text: Richard Lester's Robin and Marian is a very different take on the legend of Robin Hood. For starters, Robin is old, Marian is a nun, and Sherwood Forest looks very much like Spain. Lester's film may be unconventional in terms of what most people would normally expect from a Medieval yarn about the mystical outlaw, but all the parts are there, from Robin to Marian, Little John to Friar Tuck, King John to The Sheriff of Nottingham, it's simply told in a much more believable way. It shows Robin as human, older, wiser, world-weary, but still a hero, only slower and less formidable than he was as a young man, and that's what gives this film its charm.

This is a film of wartime life, made in the dying flames of wartime. The characters in the film reveal their naivety, as they believed the war would end quickly or a better world would arise. reviews.text: Rust and Bone tells a simple tale of love and of loss. Led by two soul-crushingly vulnerable performances from Matthias Schoenaerts and Marion Cotillard, this film reaches the utmost heights of cinematic naturalism. Combined with Jacques Audiard's intimate close-ups and drifting hand-held camerawork, this film will fully immerse you in a passionate relationship between two damaged souls. Audiard's impeccable song choices further elevate the emotions at play, delivering moving uses of Katy Perry's "Firework" and Bon Iver's "The Wolves (Act I and II)." Rust and Bone can be an emotionally draining film, but the subtle, utterly absorbing depiction of love, poverty, sex and violence will most definitely leave a lasting impression on whoever decides to embark on this soul-stirring journey.

reviews.text: On feeling rootless in a dirty business. It is about an American pimp in Singapore, but really PB aimless Hollywood career. It is very much the start of Bogdanovich's second act, very self-aware but not quite in the ways expected. Saint Jack is sometimes called Cassavetes-lite and while there are similarities (Gazarra, lots of guys boozing together, a hangout atmosphere), the alienation expressed is very different from him. There's actually much more of a certain conspiratorial displacement from some of Welles non American films, but without the more oppressive undercurrents. Gazarra is great and his scenes with Denholm Eliott as a brit expat who searches him for companionship are some of the best either man or Bogdanovich have been involved. Most of the film exists in pure seedy atmosphere and this pull between belonging and unbelonging and Saint Jack manages the hard feat of sustaining it while remaining warm and welcoming.

The new release also splices in some vintage trailers and movie-theatre ephemera at the beginning and the intermission, which might annoy purists but which I got a kick out of. Anyway, a serious cinephile should have multiple editions of Santa Claus Conquers the Martians for different moods.

There’s a discreetly supple shot at the start which alone might make it a worthwhile watch. Payne and Slim Pickens, playing a pair of scouts, enter a watering hole, happy having outsmarted a Kiowa party and looking to get drunk. But if the men in this community feel like they've got limited options, the movie goes out of its way to alert you to the trap women (and minorities) are facing. The guys shirk responsibility with alarming regularity: leaving the priesthood, quitting a job or being unemployed, you can get out of that stuff as long as you don't get "tied down" by an unplanned pregnancy. But for the women "either you're a nice girl, or you're a cunt." Pretty quietly crushing, especially a late, momentary contrast between disco nightclub lights and those on a squad car.

reviews.text: A rare example of an espionage thriller without anything in the way of bombast, Shadow Dancer remarkably can now be considered 'period' given the early 90's setting and focus on the Northern Irish 'Troubles', which if not completely resolved are these days certainly without the sectarian violence that plagued previous decades. James Marsh's film, adapted by Tom Bradby from his own novel of the same name, attempts to reflect that conflict in microcosm through the story of Colette McVeigh, an IRA terrorist cornered and turned by MI5 to carefully expose her paymasters back in Belfast. Shadow Dancer wants to be a quiet, taut exercise in reflective danger but ultimately doesn't quite come together, despite moments of genuine power and a…

reviews.author: ciaran_vallely
reviews.text: The thing that makes Shadow Dancer interesting, is probably the thing that makes it also unsuccessful. The story is really small stakes set against the larger conflict, which is a good approach when dealing with something like The Troubles. And Marsh and Bradby do know how to raise the tension, as many scenes go on and on, incrementally tightening further and further. However, this approach does mean Shadow Dancer is notably light on thrills, or anything to really raise the heart rate, which for a thriller does make it a bit sluggish. It's a very subdued movie, and every performance feeds into that pace. Riseborough does elevate her role where she can, but Gillan, Anderson, and even Owen are given so little to work with that they may as well not be there.

reviews.author: cuckoochanel
reviews.text: Pulpsmith Sam Fuller tackles socially divisive subjects like ingrained and institutional racism and xenophobia, the arms race, sexuality and psychology with hallucinatory surrealism and razor-sharp dialogue in the sensational B-picture Shock Corridor. The film follows Pulitzer Prize aspirant Johnny Barrett (Peter Breck), a journalist hellbent on solving the case of a mysterious asylum murder—from the inside! He has himself committed, much to the vocal disapprobation of his reluctant accessory and girlfriend, Cathy (the inimitable Constance Towers as a burlesque stripper with a heart of gold). Once established in the hospital, Johnny must play a series of bizarre and psychologically-altering cat-and-mouse games to lure out the truth from his fellow patients, each episode a setpiece of melodrama and spectacle.

reviews.author: Michael Casey
reviews.text: It starts with a man running down the street. There is an awful lot of running in Truffaut films, maybe a marathon’s worth, I never counted, but I would be willing to bet that no other director made his actors run as much as Truffaut did. Why? Because it looks good on camera, adds urgency to a scene, provides kinetic energy, and makes the characters active instead of passive, in essence, running is cinematic. The 400 Blows concludes with Antoine Doinel’s long run to the shore, a mere seventeen months later, Albert Rémy (the actor who played Doinel’s father) came running into Shoot The Piano Player and writer/director François Truffaut was back.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: A near-perfect synthesis of style and narrative. Charles Aznavour's Charlie is too real for me; the levels on which I connect with him are scary. A ripping investigation on the filmic representation of females: along with Varda's Le Bonheur, it reveals and subverts cinema's latent bias for "masculine" pictures and male-oriented, machoistic storylines. A sensitive romantic male in tune with his shyness and who respects women: how is this just barely a novel concept in 1960? (Sometimes, you get the feeling some guys think it's a novel concept today.) The final shot is as heartbreaking and memorable as the comedown from a first love.

reviews.text: Has a different feel from many of François Truffaut’s other early works, but especially the more grounded, autobiographical naturalism of The 400 Blows. Yet after watching his playful deconstruction of the American noir, I think that it becomes rather easy to see why Truffaut would be so drawn to David Goodis' pulp scenario. In translating this tale of a disgraced virtuoso to the screen, you sense that there's a great love present for the genre’s tropes, but also for the inherent melancholy of the protagonist’s internal struggle.At a certain point, I couldn't help but feel as if the narrative pacing reads as being somewhat iffy, especially given how the film oscillates between slapstick comedy and somber tragedy.

reviews.text: It says so much about the ultimate destination of Kevin Smith's career that it began when he watched Slacker and felt like it was so thin that it proved he could do the same. Granted, Smith's conception of slacker culture, of people stagnating when they reach their 20s and realize they have no idea what to do and ultimately just bullshitting about Star Wars and sex talk is, on the whole, perhaps more accurate a portrait of youthful wheel-spinning. Linklater's film, on the other hand, is less about a specific generational angst than the collective drain of people of all ages who are just a bit off, who never really got with the program.

Slacker has sort of the same structure of Waking Life (which self-consciously echoes it in ways I was oblivious of when I saw that one), but there's much more to chew on in each scene besides the content of the monologues. The interlocutors are as worth watching as the speakers, their varying degrees of engagement, their relationship with who's talking to them. reviews.text: For centuries, humankind has been vexed by one question above all others: Do Smurfs have sex? Some, such as noted scholar Donald Darko, say that Peyo’s iconic blue gnomes are asexual beings who lack reproductive organs altogether. Others contend that Smurfette — the only Smurf who identifies as female — is solely responsible for breeding future generations, although that argument obviously fails to account for the Smurfs that predated her. Canonically, it’s understood that a fleet of storks deliver baby Smurfs to Smurf Village whenever there’s a blue moon; that sounds a bit suspect, so far as these theories go, but it has the added benefit of being easily explained to young children.

reviews.author: sipovic
reviews.text: Экранизация японской фантастики про сбрасывание бомбы на солнце ради спасения человечества с приличным бюджетом и пожилыми звездами, которая, провалившись на востоке, была срочно перемонтирована для западного релиза, из-за чего режиссер от неё отказался. Сложно сказать, сделало это фильм лучше или хуже, но веселья точно не добавило. Представьте себе фильм "Армагеддон", в котором полёт в космос занимал бы финальных пятнадцать минут, стрельба по астероиду состояла бы в нажатии кнопки на пульте клавиатуры, а основную часть времени Лив Тайлер ходила бы по пустыне в поисках дороги домой, пока зловещий Уильям Фихтнер бесконечно проводил совещания в злой корпорации, пытаясь сорвать космический полёт. Тут вышел очень скучный мэшап историй, в котором не могут толком сконцентрироваться ни на космосе, ни на постапокале, при этом несмотря на заявленные серьезные деньги, фильм выглядит как стандартная кассетная бэшка середины девяностых, в которой к тому же нет ни одной нормальной экшен сцены, это на два то часа хронометража.

reviews.author: Gregory Joseph
reviews.text: Confounding. Resists easy explication, despite its palindromic structure and single-minded characters. Profoundly, achingly lonely, concerned with couplings that are meaningful but always ad-hoc, and always doomed. Pryor passes through shtick--all that the page requires--and finds a truly affecting, desperate performance. Zalman King as jazz saxophonist Robert Troy is totally unmodulated emotionally, the sheer accumulating weight of his ossified depression denying any suggestion of Hollywood romantic self-destruction. DP Mario Tosi--who went on to shoot Carrie and The Stunt Man--photographs the hell out of the film; Troy's world is ornate and classicist, but chilled, and somehow stark despite the persistent natural lighting and burned interior color palette.

reviews.text: Hypnogogic Americana, the kind that so many laud Lynch with, though Harris pulls what’s possibly the more impressive coup, eschewing pure slippage for blurry boundaries. When characters descend from the erotic, palatial and oneiric hilltop boudoir, they participate in the cheap earthiness of carnivals and bars—even the Sleeping Beauty sideshow pauses for a cheeseburger and caesar salad. There’s not a ton going on here amidst the icy opulence, but Harris brings all available poignancy to bear on a rather personable conundrum: what happens when you’ve played the game for so long that you don’t know how not to play the game, even though you really wish you could break from it? Zalman King plays a jazz musician who attends a carnival where he discovers a sideshow featuring a "Sleeping Beauty," a girl who has been asleep for eight years (Tisa Farrow) and is exploited by being offered up to any man who pays a buck for a kiss. Otherwise this is a pretty rote thriller, which is still less of a stumble than its presentation as his crisis rather than that of a betrayed spouse, but also goes out of its way to pin the blame on multiple variants of a macho culture that values women as property, signifiers of status rather than participants.

There's clear noir influence in this - the socialite character plays off the femme fatale angle, luring the working class man away from his wife and son, and into the upper echelons of society. Just shows what film can do. There are some things that don't quite work. The whole French exchange students just seem out of place, it is very distracting, it takes the viewer away from what makes this movie work. reviews.text: Sure, this movie might seem melodramatic and over-the-top, but not when you realize that star Susan Cabot died at age 59 after attacking her son with a weight bar and a scalpel in hysterical fit induced by her life-long bout with PTSD. He wrestled the bar away from her, and beat her repeatedly on the head, later claiming that it had been done by someone "in a ninja mask" because he thought no one would believe his story. He was later found guilty of involuntary manslaughter, after his lawyers proved that the ferocity of his attack was brought on by the drugs he was taking to combat his dwarfism.

Not unlike ‘Rock’ this one also has a great Dick Miller performance, but of course Susan Cabot as the cruel sorority girl with a grudge against the world is the MVP here. It's always nice to see the constant progression with those early Corman movies and how you can tell he's always adapting something he may have learned on the last film. Seeing this in good quality definitely helped to appreciate that it was pretty well shot, and I also dug the opening credits.

reviews.author: Jesse
reviews.text: For those unfamiliar with film serials, they were the cliffhanger adventures that inspired the likes of everything from Star Wars to Indiana Jones. Coming in the form of chapter segments, ending with our hero in dire straits, only to be resolved in the next episode. They often feature the eras pinnacle of stunt performance with everything from fisticuffs to car chases. Republic Pictures was one of the iconic studio putting these films out.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: SOS Coast Guard! A chemical that melts everything in its path! A big brawling bald man who can seemingly breathe underwater! Bela Lugosi with a beard! Bela Lugosi without a beard! Bela Lugosi threatening to disintegrate a Labrador! Fisticuffs! Brother murder! Trucks being rolled off hills! This is relentless action, endless cliffhangers. It's total trash in the best possible way. Lugosi is in fine form as the villain. He falls somewhere between mad scientist and vicious gangster. An excellent combo. The productions values of this serial are surprisingly decent. The effects are creative. I particularly dug the disintegration effect where the footage begins to melt. Like most serials, there's stretches of boredom and full episodes where I struggled to pay attention to what was going on. But for the most part, this is solid pulp.

A serial that was carried by the action, both over and under water with gas in boxes being the most dangerous ingredient, then a orderly well thought-out plot. Would have been difficult to get into had it not been for Bela Lugosi being there to fulfill his contract.

reviews.author: Anthony Nield
reviews.text: Semi-bingeing a serial – watching twelve 'chapters' over the space of a week rather than weekly over the space of a few months – exposes how little breathing room there is, even with a total three- or four-hour runtime. Each instalment after the first is locked into the same formula: quickly resolve the previous cliffhanger before a little talk and action leading to the next cliffhanger. You're never more than three minutes from the next bit of "da-dun da-dun da-dun" scoring and kidnap/chase/explosion/peril. In small doses, as little bursts of excitement, it's effective enough, but in sum, the lack of substance is obvious.

These guys are hurling themselves at each other, no doubt many bones were broken. Definitely influenced by Keaton. I want to say this has the earliest instance of a high speed boat chase in movies, I’m not sure but I haven’t seen one earlier than this.

reviews.text: Spy Smasher was probably the most popular non-Marvel Family superhero for Fawcett Comics. Like Captain America, he was fighting Nazis before the U.S. had entered World War II. He gets the Republic serial treatment here. The big difference between this and the comics is Spy Smasher (Kane Richmond) has a twin brother who aids him against Nazi villain the Mask (one of the rare cases of a serial using a villain from the source material). The Nazis have a cool hoverplane. Top notch action that you'd expect from Republic. Richmond later did three Shadow films for Monogram. Worth seeking out.

reviews.text: What begins as John Carpenter’s quirky, feel-good take on E.T. slowly builds and evolves into what can only be described as an unstoppable freight train of grief and longing made beautiful and uplifting by the sheer heart of Karen Allen and Jeff Bridges, a train riding headlong toward an ending that hits like a brick wall of transcendental emotion. One of those rare experiences where I just sitting there motionless, letting the entire credits roll through with that unfuckingbelievably gorgeous, ominous, haunting score echoing through my mind, thinking of those whom I love and cherish, having spiritual conversations with those I’ve lost, and pondering my place in this universe and the next.

Bridges is obviously doing some spectacular proto-Dougie Jones physical acting and mugging as the alien wearing the widow's hot dead husband as a skinsuit (all the way to an Oscar nomination, no less) but Allen has the more challenging and rewarding task of watching this absurd premise with wide-eyed terror and a gentle, broken heart that slowly warms…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The capitalist idea of a family is a unit of control and profit rather than a loving interconnected and related community designed to nourish and protect, so anything that takes the stereotypical role of the father and presents it as menacing is tapping into the sense that I imagine most of us have that the family unit as we know it is unnatural, violent, and oppressive. The potential violence under the surface of the stepfather, the explosion-in-waiting infuses every scene with the promise of the fist, the knife, the shout, the grab, the hammer. The deconstruction of the 1950s illusion of the nuclear family is hit over the head in the "make room for daddy" scene, but they manage to make their point plain just in the way he looks at women. They are nothing but props for him in his twisted fantasy of the provider.

reviews.text: Jeff Burr is the Brian De Palma of horror sequels. Nobody shoots this junk with as much creativity or enthusiasm as him, as evidenced by roving cameras for his chase sequences, pop soundtracking that would be perfectly ironic if he didn’t totally mean it, and splashes of color and light that sail past “unmotivated” and straight into “Brechtian.” Unsurprisingly, he makes a full meal out of Stepfather 2’s setpieces, adorning them with any and every stylistic flourish the budget allows. It makes for an interesting contrast with Psycho II, both films concerned with their central figure moving on from his past deeds, but where Norman Bates makes genuine attempts at recovery, “Jerry Blake” believes he can double down with no…

reviews.text: Yeah, I dunno. I mean, Terry O'Quinn is creepy and all, but did we really need a sequel to Stepfather? This dude ain't exactly Jason Voorhees, you know? I liked how the first one opened, but it mostly felt like an afterschool special crossed with some Psycho vibes. This one, despite actually feeling like more of a slasher flick, initially, still mostly comes off as some daytime soap opera romantic drama nonsense. I'm easy to please but you gotta give me something to work with. A little more horror atmosphere. A little more blood. Something. I'm just not feeling it. All the fun here pretty much comes solely from O'Quinn's performance, which is the only real reason to watch these.

reviews.text: Dustin Hoffman, Harry Dean Stanton and Gary Busey get into a car to go rob a jewelry store. Right there, you owe it to yourself to see Straight Time. But it's also a gripping genre piece and gut-punching character study both at the same time, smack dab in the 70s golden age of paranoid crime pictures. If you consider yourself an avid fan of heist movies about volatile criminals, if Reservoir Dogs is your cup of tea, if you've seen and liked The Driver or Dog Day Afternoon, and you haven't seen or heard of Straight Time, then you're in for one of the more under-appreciated highlights in the genre and you should familiarize yourself with it, pronto.

reviews.text: A very tragic and considered crime drama that as others have mentioned feels in some respects like the blueprint for the intelligent, fatalistic ex-con humanity and existentialism of Michael Mann. (Was not surprised to learn he did an uncredited draft, the romantic scenes especially are dripping with his sensitive detail about prison life and the kinds of attitudes necessary to adopt to survive it.) However there's an interesting quality to this that could've only come out of this period of the 70s, where Mann would eventually drench this material in impressionistic style this has a hard and blunt sense of almost resignation that's served well by French Connection and Taking of Pelham One Two Three cinematographer Owen Roizman's blunt, grimy…

reviews.text: Straight Time is probably the grottiest, seediest and low-rent-est Southern California has ever looked on film. Like there are bedbugs and/or lice on the print itself, everything covered in a dusty patina of nicotine, sweat and air pollution. The post-prison-release efforts at having a normal job, complying with a parole officer, keeping regular hours are some of the most oppressive time I have ever spent watching a movie, so when those efforts start to not work out so well, the promise of a life of crime seems self-evident, if still way grotty and seedy. This movie is adapted in part by Edward Bunker from his autobiographically-informed novel No Beast So Fierce. He also shares a memorable scene with Dustin Hoffman,…

Pretty ungodly in its harrowing intensity, with Theresa Russell, Harry Dean Stanton and Gary Busey all absolutely bringing it. M Emmett Walsh plays a total prick like nobody's business, and the scene where Dustin Hoffman makes an unbelievable choice that affects the outcome of the rest of the movie is so shocking, I'm not even sure Walsh knew what was going to happen despite having read the script. Fucking phenomenal.

reviews.text: The last and best of the three mid budget western Willian Witney did for later day Republic. Wonderful offbeat very low key starting as something of a home invasion tale turning into a religious parable that also manages to keep so many contradictory balls rolling as a redemption story, a study on hubris and of deviant cracking up a nuclear family. Witney keeps a very good heavy mood and plays with a lot of charged symbolic imagery that is often at odds with each other. Great stunts (that scene with the wild horse is something) and Homeier and Medina do terrific work (Carey usual stiffness rarely put to such good use as well).

That visitor is outlaw Clay Anderson, played by serial asshole Skip Homeier, an actor that always played a dick, regardless of whether he's cast as a villain (which he usually is), or a hero. Anderson's gang has just robbed the town's bank, but his horse has come up lame, and the Jarret farm becomes a hideaway as he awaits his animal's recovery. Carey's Hollis Jarret knows who Anderson is, but believes that given the right amount of positive and spiritual guidance, he can persuade Anderson to turn over a new…

reviews.author: Augie
reviews.text: One of the best films about faith. Faith in your fellow man, faith in the goodness of the universe, in the grace that is all around you. Advice and lectures cannot change a man; give me community and give me gentleness, give me mercy, give me pancakes for breakfast; and maybe I will find my way. There are no coincidences, but there is a flow; I must locate this flow, and trust in it. Law and punishment offer no good to the world; they only increase the violence and suffering and fear. There is something burning in the heart of this film; there is a primal fire; in the quiet shared glances, in the furious kicks of a wild creature, in the struggle of a soul. Before he left us, he saw what he needed to see. He saw the thundering terror in the eyes of a horse; he saw the tenderness in the eyes of a dying child.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: A religious parable of faith and repentance, bewilderment and salvation. A stray horse, an empty church in construction, a woman afraid and an insane preacher with beliefs larger than life. Whitney directs it with a spare dryness that finds many impressive images and some well placed ideas (those long shots towards the end achieve quite an impressive dramatic pungency, and the tempest feels like unhinged lyricism, granting a mythological status to the allegorical fable). On a side note, the horse and the dog are absolutely great stunts.

Furious direction by W. Witney on a limited canvas which plays fast and loose with big honking symbolisms and doesn't hesitate to slip and slide between a placid surface naturalism and tempestuous expressionism with nary a jagged edge, and which breaks at least two golden no-no's of the classical western by gaping at preacher's-wife-cleavage and a small boy being shot in the belly. Rather fascinating.

The cinematography and editing are raw yet masterful, and the acting is naturalistic across the board, with Algenis Perez Soto delivering a phenomenal performance in the leading role.

reviews.text: Sugar Cookies has sort of a weird distribution history. As most major Troma fans will notice, the 1971 release date predates the inception of the company in 1974 which makes it rather obvious that this was an acquisition rather than a production. However, unlike other Troma acquisitions, it was written and produced by Lloyd Kaufman himself so it does have more of the studio’s pedigree than acquired titles that earned more of a reputation on home video than this one did. Luckily, Troma have always released it in its uncut form as it was cut quite heavily to earn an R-rating following its initial X-rated theatrical run. The cut here is the same as the DVD that Troma released years…

reviews.text: T. Gershuny #1 --- Troma's Lloyd Kaufman wrote this. It must've been the fifth or sixth movie he was involved with. It's pretty interesting. Apparently Vertigo was the main inspiration. I didn't think of that when I watched it. But after Lloyd mentioned it in an interview it all makes sense. The director made the Christmas horror-flick Silent Night, Bloody Night right before this one. It also stars Mary Woronov who is amazing in Sugar Cookies. Seriously, she makes the film worthwhile. While the rest of it (style, music, story) isn't bad, her presence is something special. I also liked Lynn Lowry who I've previously seen in The Crazies, Score, and I Drink Your Blood. Besides the cast and some poetic dialogue the movie also has a great shot of some 42nd St. theaters that show See No Evil among others.

reviews.text: "Hey, let's have a teen sex comedy with a focus on Women's Lib!" said nobody, and especially not in the mid-seventies, but that apparently didn't stop this Roger Corman production, written and directed by Barbara Peeters (Humanoids from the Deep, Starhops), from being completed. Three chicks from Iowa (Candice Rialson, of "Eiger Sanction" and "Hollywood Boulevard" fame, and uh, the other two) move to California to teach summer school to high school students pushing thirty, resulting in the usual screwball shenanigans. The girls phys ed class fielded a football team that beat the boys?!!? Haha, no way, what an unforgettable summer. Dick Miller (A Bucket of Blood, The Howling) steals the show (as usual) as the chauvinist pig football coach, and Bill Thornbury (Phantasm, The Lost Empire) scores an early cameo. The boom mic also appears, repeatedly. I had two summer school classes in 1983 that were more engrossing than this.

reviews.author: Jeff Sexton
reviews.text: A jet-lagged sequel, a euro-cool blaxploitation that struggles to recapture the slickness of its predecessor. Ron O'Neal, reprising Priest, is now a semi-retired globe-trotter, but still a get-things-done sort of guy who falls in with an arms smuggling operation. Without the gritty urban setting though, this one falls short. It is I suppose an attempt at social commentary, regarding colonialism and exploitation. It also seems to want to deepen the characters with long dialogue scenes. But the human interests go no place. Indeed entire characters appear and vanish for no apparent reason. The film leaves the viewer unclear what it was going for. It is meandering and includes remarkably little action. Its plot is diluted and confused, and the ending is abrupt and unsatisfying.

No, it's easy to pick apart bad acting, short-sighted directing, and a purely moronic stringing together of words that many of the studios term as ‘prose.’ No, I'm talking about the lack of realism. Realism; not a pervasive element in today's modern American cinematic vision.”

reviews.text: A friend of mine summed up Taffin rather perfectly: if Alan Partridge made an action-thriller, this would be the result. It's so bland. Its premise and conflict so basic and totally undeserving of the grandeur it's given. Everything is bleak. Day time strip clubs (with Father Ted hosting). The holy sports field. A man being bullied and pissed on. Pierce Brosnan is wonderfully unconvincing. Flatly, smugly delivering lines and occasionally screaming uncontrollably. His character, the grimly named Mark Taffin, is so sad and full of contradictions. He claims using your brain is more important than your fists, which essentially just means he frames people for sexual assault. And anyway, he murders people willy nilly so who cares. This might sound like a negative review, but I loved this for its blandness. It's an action film for all the councilman dads out there.

reviews.text: Woody Allen's first film proper is a mock documentary and focuses on the life and times of an incompetent criminal. The comedy ranges from sharp and witty to ridiculous, but either way the jokes come at you pretty fast and many of them work well. Allen takes the lead role himself and the character ends up becoming the same bumbling neurotic that he plays in all of his comedy films. Of course, he's cast opposite the beautiful woman too, another trademark Woody Allen feature! The film is essentially a collection of set pieces, mostly centred around a single gag - the best of which involve two awkward bank robberies and a chain gang escape. It does become a little repetitive in places and the story sags somewhat in the middle - but for the most part this is an amusing comedy, and a interesting precursor of better things to come.

reviews.text: This Freddie Francis directed anthology really suffers from Amicus' absence producing it.Similar to the device used in Asylum, this has a psychiatrist recount four patient cases to his colleague stating he has "solved" them.Despite a stellar cast including the likes of Donald Pleasence, Joan Collins and Kim Novak, none of the stories (or the wraparound) leave much of an impression. An imaginary tiger that might be real, a bike that sends a man into the past, a strange love affair with a tree(!) and a cannibalistic ceremony disguised as a luau are all a bit bland, lacking the macabre, ghoulish edge one expects. It even looks rather plain, opting for a modern (for the time) 70s look rather than the gothic trappings that work so well for these kind of films.I saw this on Sunday (four days ago) and only just now remembered I watched it.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: A very exciting Tarzan film from director John Guillermin, who is more well known for his later 70's disaster epics like "The Towering Inferno" and the De Laurentiis "King Kong." Although this movie was released in 1959, it feels like an early 60's movie to me, with more blunt depictions of sensuality and violence than I'd expect from the Eisenhower era, a precursor to what would come as censorship started to ease up and Hollywood attempted to compete with the small screen. In Guillermin's film, there are a handful of fairly gruesome deaths scattered about the runtime and the 'bad girl' character played by Scilla Gabel is constantly sunbathing along the rivers of Kenya.

reviews.text: Cameron Mitchell plays a creepy video store clerk at the Shoppe of Horrors video store who will help find you the perfect tape for your Halloween fix in this Comet Video release compilation flick. There's something so quaint about the store that will have you longing for the bygone days of VHS and mom and pop storefronts. Happy to have chosen this for International Independent Video Store day! The film clips are liberally and shamelessly spread throughout the film and some titles are repeated multiple times, which means there are spoilers aplenty. It served as an elaborate promo reel for the company, so every clip features the name of its source onscreen. Mitchell hams up his hosting role, but Michelle Bauer sluts it up nicely as a vampy customer who is turned on by gore clips.

reviews.author: Ryan C
reviews.text: Promo for 80s VHS company Continental Video's selection of horror and sleaze classics, including gory bits from films like Blood Feast, Nightmare, The Slayer, Scalps, and Vampire Hookers. Nuff said? No? Okay, well, how about Cameron Mitchell in grey makeup cackling drunkenly while introducing the clips? What more could you possibly want?! Michelle Bauer orgasmically clutching her bosom while demanding that Cameron show her the scariest clips he's got so that she can finally experience fear for the first time? Terror on Tape's got you covered. Of course, in the age of YouTube, this compilation might seem a bit superfluous, but there's still a lot of charm in this thing. A must-see for anyone with a hard-on for vintage VHS tapes.

reviews.text: Doesn't work as a sequel to The Third Man, but this is one hot Dutch -Hoeven. Paulie V excels at over-boiling everything, bringing all of the elements Hitchcock would have had to bury in implication and subtext floating to the surface. He's mixing it in the red with a heavy hand allowing him to layer in subtleties underneath the pop sheen that could easily go unnoticed by someone just looking to watch a pervy thriller. It would seem cacophonous if it wasn't all so slickly deployed (that Jan de Bont photography!). It's unsurprising that he was whisked away to Hollywood shortly after this and equally unsurprising that he was continually misunderstood (Showgirls) and eventually and unceremoniously excused from further mainstream ventures. It's a shame, the world needs more erotic thrillers that are about Catholic guilt and Christ parables that take the form of cyborg policeman action romps.

reviews.text: This is a fascinating movie. It captures the tone and spirit of the original Jay Ward cartoon pretty well, with its frequent puns and fourth wall jokes and you can tell the filmmakers had a genuine love for the material (Robert De Niro had apparently been wanting to make this for several years until he decided to produce the movie himself). Does it all work? No. Many jokes can be obvious and corny, but then you also wonder if that's the whole point. reviews.author: Bilge Ebiri
reviews.text: I first saw this film back in 1995 during a Sidney Lumet retro at the old AFI theater in the Kennedy Center (RIP). I loved it then, but have been perplexed by the various criticisms of it I’ve heard in the years since. So much so that I started to doubt my own response to the film. Finally watched it again, and… It’s a masterpiece? Certainly one of Lumet’s greatest films, and like no other heist movie I’ve seen. That moment early on when Connery, having just gotten out of prison, steps out into the glorious golden light outside, is an all-timer. Also one of my favorite Christopher Walken performances. Lumet knew exactly what to do with a dancer.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A lesser Lumet is still a Lumet, so you can be sure that The Anderson Tapes is competently made, but it is a rather lackluster surveillance state indictment-picture and an even more unremarkable heist movie. Connery stumbles between his American accent and his native thick Scottish intonation, and the supporting cast around him all turn in satisfactory work, but nothing special. It was cool to see a very young Christopher Walken with a skater boy hairdo, and Martin Balsam as a gay burglar is something I never knew I needed to see, but am glad I did. Quincy Jones’ electro-jazz score is the best thing this film has going for it. The combination of funky jazz rips and beep-boop breaks drive home the tension (well, what is there of it) and I can cross this off my list of Jones-scored films that I need to see. Apart from that though, I’ll probably never think about The Anderson Tapes again. Mid

reviews.text: The Big Combo feels like a cold-eyed sequel to The Glass Key, the brutal return of reality to the fantasy with which the earlier film ends. Here, we re-encounter Paul Madvig (the name is different, but the man is the same), a decade-plus removed from his heyday in The Glass Key. After the departure of Ed with which that tale ends, and the loss of the reason and calculation that Ed took with him, Madvig's ego and blind confidence must have instantly made him vulnerable, ripe for the taking by the next Nick Varna, or Ralph Henry, or even Ed Beaumont. reviews.text: Quickie ReviewThe last couple of days, I’ve been on the Watch TCM app and I checked out the package features of director and comedy scholar Robert Youngson while there. His first two anthology films, The Golden Age of Comedy and When Comedy Was King, were a delight in showcasing the early years of comedy on film, particularly of the slapstick variety, and the next day I watched his follow-up for MGM that spotlights the studio’s comedy from 1925 to 1948. This paste-up feature showcases the best of comedy at MGM during that era featuring some wacky moments from the Marx Brothers, Clark Gable, Lucille Ball, Laurel & Hardy, Red Buttons, Robert Benchley, Lupe Velez, Jimmy Durante, Wallace Beery, Cary Grant,…

Almost every soldier I've ever spoken to has mentioned how unrealistic war movies are, but that hardly means the movies don't adequately convey some sense of horror and pain. They present effective characters and we empathize with them, and even if what is shown is both less terrifying than the real thing and more condensed, deeply edited, completely limited as compared to the real thing, even if that is the case, it is none-the-less a depiction of nothing I can fathom wanting to be a part of.

reviews.text: The Big Red One, written and directed by Samuel Fuller, is an epic war movie full of living and breathing characters. Most of them founded on personalities Fuller encountered between 1942 and 1945, and it’s a movie which contains plenty of moments that are comprehensively too distinctive to be entirely fictional. Featuring an ensemble cast including Lee Marvin and Mark Hamill; it's a movie soaked with vignettes that demonstrate how men behave in various horrendous situations that are imposed on them, where all that matters is the state of continual existence.

reviews.text: I wish I could say this movie is better than it is. It boasts promising elements: an interesting idea for a plot, a strong cast, great Technicolor cinematography by Jack Cardiff (the night-for-night shots in the first quarter are remarkable when you consider how much lighting Technicolor typically required), and composer Richard Addinsell’s finest score (the love theme is pretty). The main problem is a dull, talky script. Very little action happens, despite its colorful characters and promising shifts in setting. It’s based on a novel by Thomas B. Costain, whose main claim to fame among movie buffs is that Paul Newman took out an ad begging people not to watch The Silver Chalice (another Costain adaptation) when it aired…

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: Dorothy Provine is a snarling badass in this take on the Bonnie and Clyde story directed with razor-sharp precision by no-budget expert William Witney. He cut his teeth on Poverty Row, but instead of becoming an anonymous journeyman, he used his prolific output to develop a compelling visual syntax. He's a master story compression: A gas station explosion underlines Bonnie's first kill, Bonnie lights up a cigarette and the screen bursts into flames, and a spinning wheel lets us know that its all over. She gets to be mean, the boss, and the most magnetic person on the screen, while all the men are pieces of shit that exist only to be pushed around, as it should be.

reviews.author: hooch_n_arrack
reviews.text: Anachronistic aesthetic choices notwithstanding, this is a tightly constructed character study. It would be eminently watchable just for the fluency and clarity of Witney’s visual grammar and his orchestration of images. However, The Bonnie Parker Story has a good deal more going for it - the razor-sharp dialogue, Jack Marta’s evocative low-contrast black and white cinematography which renders the wintry, desolate backwoods roads and the people who traverse them in various tones of grey, and an absolutely sensational turn by Dorothy Provine as Bonnie Parker. Provine’s performance here is meant to be neither interstitial nor subtle; she is bold and forceful, essentially crafting a performance within a performance, as Bonnie battles to control her own destiny.

reviews.text: Milan Kundera once wrote that “a single metaphor can give birth to love.” But what the great Czech novelist, for all of his genius, failed to foresee, is that a single metaphor can also give birth to a mildly tolerable kids movie in which Alec Baldwin voices a business-minded newborn. For you see, Dreamworks Animation’s “The Boss Baby” isn’t — as the unenlightened masses might understandably assume — just a disposable cartoon about a hyper-intelligent infant who becomes the CEO of a major corporation. I mean, it is definitely that, don’t get me wrong, but it isn’t only that. No, “The Boss Baby” is also, like, one of those movies that’s about something, ya know?

reviews.text: It occurs to me sometimes how insane the central concept of The Boys from Brazil is, cloning Adolf Hitler, the most abhorrent figure of the 20th century, and placing him in the modern world. On paper it sounds nearly pulpy, even absurd, but what makes the film so engrossing is how it integrates this science fiction concept into the texture of a paranoid thriller. It does not develop like a wild science fiction fantasy but it draws you into the uncomfortable danger that humanity's obsession with power and legacy can distort science in monstrous ways.

reviews.text: David Lean directs a proud and accomplished war film that boasts all the qualities as to why he is noteworthy: constantly riveting cinematography, small yet terrifyingly lethal conversations, stern and compelling performances and gripping action. There’s a consistently impressive feat of visuals that are composed of various beiges, greens, and browns and while that may seem undiverse or dull, it proves itself to look shockingly stunning. It’s clear to see why the film went on to snatch so many awards - especially back then as I cannot imagine how audiences perceived this - yet the tension and marvel are released solely from the last thirty minutes. A glacial build-up is, however, required for such a striking final act.

reviews.text: Viewed purely as entertainment, The Bridge on the River Kwai delivers an enthralling, beautifully lensed WW2 yarn. In terms of history accuracy though, it's more suspect. Not only does it downplay the brutality of conditions in Japanese POW camps as well as the privations prisoners conscripted to work on the building of the infamous Burma Railway were forced to endure, but the titular bridge is a fiction. The real bridge (actually two bridges, a steel construction and a temporary wooden one) spanned the then-named Mae Klong river and was destroyed during Allied bombing raids after two years of use. Alec Guiness's portrayal of Colonel Nicholson also appears to deviate from the real-life subject, Lieutent Colonel Toosey. Toosey, by all accounts,…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: The most stark film from Godard early days, devoid even of the mediation that Anna Karina presence offered in Vivre sa Vie. The symbolic charge behind the images creates its own form of movie artifice, one based on an idea of anti film spectacle that Godard wouldn’t touch more regularly until years later, but fits the war movie motif. War becomes a series of oppressive pranks that, instead of diluting increase the danger and waste inherit to it.

Favoring long shots and avoiding the use of music, insert close-ups and the like during scenes of killing, Godard presents war as a place where unseen leaders and rich convince their own miserable, disenfranchised population to vent their frustrations onto a foreign enemy, literally selling people on it via the promise of pillage, rape and the chance to feel the…

reviews.text: In 1960 Jean-Luc Godard had everything going for him. His first feature film, “Breathless”, was released that year to exceedingly positive reviews from critics. The French people loved it as well. When originally released in theaters, the film attracted over 2,000,00 viewers. Godard was hailed as the next big thing in French cinema and as a co-founder of a new and exciting style of cinema, nouvelle vague. This was the perfect time to become a commercial, but Godard refused to go down that route. Instead, he began working on a film about a very non-commercial subject, the Algerian War.

The template is set--naive young woman (future soap star Tracey E. Bregman) is framed (shitbag boyfriend sends her on a flight and stashes cocaine in her skis) and thrown in the slammer. She toughens up after the abuse of the fearsome cell block queen (Barbara Luna) who's working in cahoots with the corrupt warden (a slumming Jill St. John). There's drugs, murder, one tame lesbian makeout scene with two bit players we never see again, and lots of brawls, including a climactic prison yard mudfight.

reviews.author: Diego Tutweiller
reviews.text: I gave a presentation on the science of disaster movies for my geology course this week. Among the inaccuracies cited were 2012's ludicrously slow pyroclastic flow, the incorrect usage of low-silica lava in Dante's Peak, and the entire plot of The Day After Tomorrow. Still, even among this stiff competition, one film managed to stand out. It is a film about American scientists using a pulse weapon to send earthquakes at our enemies, resulting in the magnetic field shutting down. A group of scientists must then use an experimental substance called unobtainium to drill through the magma and detonate nuclear bombs to get the core spinning again. Along the way, they encounter enormous diamonds, geodes, and innumerable other violations of the laws of thermodynamics.

Sarafian (whose LOLLY-MADONNA XXX is an essential example of arty exploitation) as a profane strip club manager tells you all you need to know about this indulgent curiosity of the Miramax era. On the flip side the story also looks at the drunk driver and his journey of acceptance and forgiveness for his actions. While the pacing of this film is very slow and the writing can feel weaker in some parts with a few unnecessary scenes scattered throughout, and far too much slow mo, The Crossing Guard serves as a very introspective look on grief, loss, how we choose to deal with loss and forgiveness. I loved Nicholson’s performance throughout, Nicholson always knows how to dominate the screen no matter the role, and i also really enjoyed seeing him alongside Huston who gives a brilliant performance as well. The writing and directing from Penn is very solid.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A movie so elementally modern that it seems to be both a close for the first great era of filmmaking and a blueprint for what was to come. Its influence is like that of Gilgamesh, such an inherent part of what the medium has become as to be a core part of its DNA. The basic read on this is that it transplants expressionism into realism, and that's not altogether wrong, though it gives the impression that Vidor smooths out the stylistic excesses of that movement. Instead, he refines and arguably expands its scope, taking it from the realm of the symbolic and theatrical and into the richer possibilities for subtle expression endemic to cinema.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: A film that insists on being gentle and crude, moving in unison across an America that believes it has rediscovered its balance: the postwar promise of a “return to normalcy,” the relief after the Spanish flu, the bright (and blinding) thought of a society newly convinced of progress. Even so, the film keeps returning to small interiors, to the grain of skin and to the collapse of a face when hope thins to habit. In John Sims we find a man to whom many promises are made, promises of destiny, of public recognition, of the comfortable domestic triangle that marks success, and we watch those promises settle, like dust, over the furnishings of an ordinary life.

reviews.text: Nathaniel West's novel is so pitiless an observation of life at the very bottom rung of Hollywood that it almost feels cruel to give it an adaptation as lavish as this; the flawless production values, massive set-pieces and iconic '70s stars give it an uncomfortable feeling of very successful people punching down at their inferiors. Taking something crabby and nasty and unwholesome and handing it to a major studio is always going to be a bit of a give-and-take, and sure enough what West's novel loses in grunge and anger it gains in brio and entertainment value.

reviews.text: Overlong and heavy-handed. It's Lynch Lite, but at least it's impossible to be ambivalent about Lynch's work (Lynch is much better at using imagery to his full advantage). This was just one big shoulder shrug. Moral bankrupcy? Meh.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "The Day of the Locust" is a 1975 drama directed by John Schlesinger. Set up within the historical early days of Hollywood, specifically in the 1930s, "The Day of the Locust" goes back to the early dreamer years of the craft where venturing out to Hollywood was often an all-or-nothing bust in prospect formulation. Thus, as the theme of "dreams" is on full display, we see that often the dream turns into a resulted nightmare, especially as "opportunity" passes by, or worse, seemingly destroys everything in its path. The integration of harsh reality to cause dissolution in dreams is actually a noticed trend of Schlesinger, whether it be the daydreaming escapism crushed in his "kitchen sink realism" British New Wave…

reviews.text: Zombie’s ugly, dusty dad-rock western-horror banger that occupies the exact intersection of Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2, The Wild Bunch and Bonnie & Clyde. Repurposing the extremely gruesome Manson family and serial killer paranoia of the 70s (that Hooper and Craven were reacting to) into the dirtiest, most apocalyptic version of mythic, outmoded American outlaw iconography. Somehow a sincere and moving work of exploitation because you get the impression Zombie identifies with being a vulgar punk outsider; “Lord help me, I can't change” feels like it could just as easily be his own mission statement.

reviews.text: Poor Ryan O'Neal was born too late. He could have been the most naturalistic silent performer of all, with a hangdog expression that has only ever been surpassed by James Gandolfini's. Give him more than three lines at a time, though, and the cracks start to form, his flat voice unable to even suggest the same cavernous depths that his eyes can. Naturally, THE DRIVER, which gives him just enough lines that you'll need your fingers and toes to count them all, suits him perfectly. He speaks primarily through motion, his perfectly controlled driving a venting that his cold face never permits. He hardens his countenance for this film, his slackened face drawn up into a frown, but the eyes…

This had to be an influence on "Das Boot" and really captures a dry tension with an affable cast but captures some dry grit without forcing to much of a Hollywood nature with plenty of drama to be had. It gives sympathy for both sides as soldiers doing there jobs even though they might not totally be invested. The two captains in Mitchum(Murell) and Jürgens(Von Stolberg) played excellent antagonists creating a smart chess like apprehension. As far as this feather merchant is concerned I enjoyed my voyage with this film

"The Dirty Dozen" was the main feature, but I'd already seen that. It's a fictional account of an ongoing sea battle between Robert Mitchum's USS Haynes and Curt Jurgens' German U-boat. It's directed by Dick Powell who does a pretty nice job of keeping the tension high. This is as much a thriller as a battle…

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Quite possibly the sleaziest, most violent film Bronson ever starred in, although the Death Wish series, 10 To Midnight and Kinjite: Forbidden Subjects are good competition. But there's something about this one that's unsettling - be it the torture scenes with "ze Doctor", the oppressed South American peasants walking around disfigured, the close-range shotgun blasts to the face and Bronson twisting a bad guys balls with his bare hands until the guy passes out. Bronson even finds time to hide out under a bed while a lesbian couple fornicate above him. It's sleazy. But the cruelty on screen only amplifies the incredible ending. It's hard to describe this film as "fun", but it has some power to it and remains one of Bronson's most memorable 80's actioners.

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: Still one of my all-time favorite films, a lumpy and weird labor of love that came out of a thoroughly amazing process of selective deception and an impulse to analyze the nature and power of storytelling. Lee Pace stars as a badly injured stuntman obsessed with a woman who doesn't love him; in his Los Angeles hospital (some time in a vague 1920s-ish period) he befriends a little girl with a broken collarbone and starts telling her an elaborate fantasy story in order to lure her into getting him the pills he needs to commit suicide. The fantasy story plays out onscreen as the little girl's demands and the stuntman's depression and self-hatred battle to shape it in different ways, and it's visually stunning on the one hand, and conceptually stunning on the other. Currently not streaming anywhere I'm aware of, so it takes some work to watch this, but you're not going to see anything else like it anywhere.

reviews.text: Graham Greene was one of those rare beasts that managed to jump from many formats (films, books, etc.) with such an ease and always keeping the same quality and level of excitement for each and one of his works. Films such as The Third Man and The Quiet American serve as few examples. This time around, Carol Reed adapts another of his film but this time there are no spies or Orson Welles running away from the law, but the endearing story between a kid and his father’s butler and how their strong bond will put into test when a murder is committed and his best friend is the prime example.

It starts off reasonably promisingly, dropping us into a well-renditioned iteration of Victorian London (albeit a strangely colour-graded one) in which we find our team of master criminals planning out a complex, multi-stage plot to steal a shipment of gold from a Crimea-bound train. reviews.text: The very definition of a 50/50 movie. On one hand, there’s sequences here that are among some of the creepiest and most disturbing of any Hollywood horror release of the past twenty years. It’s the fear of the unidentified other, the abstract terror on show in blurry camcorder footage. In the right movie, they’d be iconic. On the other hand, the messy combination of ‘documentary’ footage and stylised Mila Jovovich movie footage is just debilitating to the overall film. I feel like this thing could’ve gone full ‘fake documentary’ and been a terrifying cult classic 🤷‍♂️
