Respect that Bullit director Yates doesn't play any of this for tragic melodrama or explosive action despite how easy it would've been to do so, instead committing to a blunt, unadorned style that's equal parts mundane and melancholy because these are characters who (despite the friendly faces and desperate negotiations) feel it in their bones that there's no future. There is nothing for these gunrunners and bank robbers and hit men to do but just resign themselves to waiting…

What struck me most this time around is how masterfully Peter Yates stages the handful of suspense setpieces in this film-- very Rififi-esque in the way they develop quietly and matter-of-factly, with minimal sound cues. Seems to be that Yates' lack of big '70s auteur status is the only thing keeping this movie from being considered among the decade's best.

reviews.text: Every meeting in The Friends of Eddie Coyle is in a public setting. Sometimes they’re in a bar, sometimes they’re in a supermarket parking lot, and sometimes they’re in a park on the outskirts of town. Wherever these meetings take place, the behavioral protocol is standard. Trust no one. Size them up with a glance. Make it clear that you don’t give a shit about what the other person is offering. Take it or leave it, but be quick about it. Everyone’s suspect. If you think for a second that loyalty, ethics, and logic are part of the equation, it’s the penitentiary or a coffin for you.

Filing this away in the "O.C. and Stiggs" (1985) department for Altman, it's another oddball sourced medium that he chose to take on adapting for the screen that works in some capacities but also seems like a strange mesh at the same time. reviews.text: Robert Altman has always been a director who's films have interested me. With that said, I've only really enjoyed a couple of the films from his filmography that I've seen. As someone who almost always finishes what he starts, I'm ashamed to say that I've switched off two of his films, Nashville and Quintet, after they failed to engage me. Only M*A*S*H* and Gosford Park have truly been my thing, and although there are a couple more on his filmography that intrigue me, especially The Long Goodbye, his other films have been hugely disappointing given his reputation as a five-time Academy Award nominee.

It's a noir by the numbers. It's not as creative as The Long Goodbye.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Oddball pairing has Robert Altman working a John Grisham story, Altman-esque “eavesdropping” on its characters most of the way. Kenneth Branagh is a hotshot lawyer and divorcee who sleeps with cuckoo Embeth Davidtz one night and becomes obligated to protect her from her derelict father Robert Duvall (unhinged method acting). Some entrancing mossy Savannah, Georgia settings undone by a drab color palette. Farfetched complications start to frustrate the picture in the second half. Ending itself is enervating on the viewer, it’s just not enjoyable. But there are some scattered Altman pleasures, such as an offbeat courtroom scene and a later abduction scene as perceived outside of a motel that is goosebumpy. Robert Downey Jr., Tom Berenger, Famke Janssen and Daryl Hannah add some peculiarities but are not developed enough.

reviews.author: TheOwlBlind
reviews.text: Engaging, to a point. Altman’s attempt to pair his characteristic style of restless, observational cinema (where the camera picks out moments of interest from a kind of rolling tableau) with the more rigorous, conventional necessities of a John Grisham legal thriller, is not without virtue. The moral ambiguities that Altman introduces into the story, as well as the focus on the characters’ messy lives, creates tension, generating enough intrigue to carry us through the first half of the film. Sadly, it all gets a bit generic towards the end, unravelling into the safest, most predictable conclusion.

reviews.text: One perfect moment: When Michael and Kay discover Vito’s been shot, his immediate reaction is to race to a phone booth and call home to check on his father. Until this point in the movie, Michael insists he wants no part of his father’s business. But when he reads the newspaper headlines about the assassination attempt, something changes in his face. And then he goes to the phone booth and slams the door on Kay so she can’t overhear the conversation, echoing the way The Godfather conducted his business in his private study while the rest of the family remained oblivious at the wedding outside, and foreshadowing the final shot of the film.

reviews.text: The Jeep is one of the few giveaway clues that we are in the twentieth century. Roy and Trigger’s relationship harks back to days of centuries gone by. Roy makes his living from Trigger, but the relationship between horse and rider is deeper than that. Trigger is perhaps the only companion Roy has ever had. It’s evident in how they communicate with each other, in the gentle tremor in Roy’s voice as he calls to Trigger, and in the way Trigger responds to Roy’s touch and the sound of his voice. When Roy is with Trigger, they seem like one entity, synchronized in body and soul. That their performances admit of such elegant economy is, I think, in large part…

reviews.text: Makes so much more sense when you realize it doesn't have to make any sense: it's an anxiety-dream movie, and Howell waking up in the police station to a suddenly unlocked cell door and that roaming German Shepherd is pure, hushed, oneiric horror - closer to A Nightmare on Elm Street than Duel. Or maybe Nightmare 2 since the queer reading here rests pretty close to the surface, played up almost instantly when the road worker refers to Howell and Hauer as "sweethearts" and carried through all the way to the last scene, which seems all about one character exorcising something about himself (his sexuality? his fear? his mercy?) by killing off somebody else (the same thing that the Coens would do against a near-identical desert backdrop the next year in Raising Arizona). reviews.text: Worth watching for another glorious, and different, performance by Alec Guinness where he plays Gulley Jimson, an eccentric, dishevelled, curmudgeonly artist who has no qualms about lying and stealing to enable himself to continue painting, particularly on large, bare walls.Guinness wrote the (Oscar nominated) screenplay himself, adapting Irish writer Joyce Cary's novel, and he looks nothing like he does in any other picture. One of the themes of the story is getting old and dying and Guinness, 43 at the time of filming, convinces as the aging artist.But there are other delights in the film such as Scottish actress Renee Houston's performance as Gulley's ex-wife (and model for some of his best work) and the wonderful Technicolor images of London in the late fifties.Well worth searching out this little-known gem.

reviews.text: Alec Guinness gives a bravura performance in an unconventional role in this adaptation of Joyce Cary's novel, screenplay by -- Alec Guinness. Guinness the writer does magic with the script, wonderfully illuminating a fascinating and original character in a fellow named Gully Jimson, a painter with great dreams but no wherewithal. Guinness the actor creates a superb portrayal of Jimson, showcasing elements of the actor's talent not seen on screen before. His Jimson is conniving, ruminative, joyous, cynical, outrageous, misanthropic, reasonable, and unremittingly determined. His physicality is richly original, hunched, haggard, given to enthusiastic leaps on the occurrence of a new idea, a wholly unique persona made flesh. The story is both superb comedy and a rambunctious meditation on art…

reviews.text: All of Bong Joon-ho’s movies are about monsters, some more literally than others. In “Memories of Murder,” the monster is the boogeyman, ripped from the headlines and hiding in the darkness. In “Snowpiercer,” the monster is the abstract force of capitalism, rotting us from the inside out as we eat each other to survive and maintain some semblance of order at the end of the world. And in “The Host,” the wild 2006 genre mash-up that firmly established Bong as a creative force of nature and afforded him the cache to make “Mother” in 2009, the monster is… well, it’s an actual fucking monster, with slimy skin and a prehensile tail and a sweet tooth for small children.

The line “May the snake that did not touch me live forever” feels like the film’s unspoken thesis. Indifference becomes a survival strategy, and silence masquerades as neutrality. reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: I’ve always had a soft spot for those slick, fun adventure films from the ’80s. They don’t need to be held to the same standards I’d apply to more “serious” cinema, because that’s not the point. The real test is simple for me, does it entertain? If I’m tuned in, engaged, and having a good time, then the film has already done its job. Romancing the Stone nailed that balance, and while The Jewel of the Nile doesn’t quite capture the same lightning, it still carries the spirit of the first film.

reviews.text: An aspirational model for b-westerns: major fun and silliness and charm. I could listen to a movie's worth of these songs, and watch Slim Pickens attempt to dodge a zillion bulls, and I would still never be fatigued.

reviews.author: Jeff Williams
reviews.text: William Witney continues to reinvigorate the series not only with his fun action sequences, like the buckboard-splosion finale, and show-offy stunts, like Rex running across the top of two horses before mounting his own, but also by using all the actors' talents to their fullest. Slim Pickens clowns, sings and fights, Mary Ellen Kay emotes up a storm, sings and rides, and Rex aids and abets, commits manslaughter and conspiracy and - wait a minute - WHAT! Yes, he breaks a lot of laws in this one, but I guess if you're the good guy, it's OK. I like the continuing addition of the Republic Rhythm Riders who basically are there to follow Rex around and harmonize when needed (even when he's in jail). The only thing lacking was mega-evil characters like in Colorado Sundown. Roy Barcroft was sorely missed.

reviews.author: Jeremy Poulos
reviews.text: I'm just getting into Rex Allen westerns but I can already tell a couple of things. The threat of television made these B-Westerns get better. They are all around better, but especially in production value. That's a good thing. What used to be a B-Western is now on TV (The Lone Ranger) so they had to up their game a bit to compete.

reviews.author: JHall
reviews.text: As B-western productions were winding down in the early 1950’s, Republic was able to still crank out some decent Rex Allen westerns. THE LAST MUSKETEERS is another example of William Witney’s solid action formula with stuntman Joe Yrigoyen doubling Allen in some creative action sequences. And, the more I see Slim Pickens in these B’s, he may have been one of the top comedy sidekicks.Some stock footage from John Wayne’s IN OLD OKLAHOMA aka WAR OF THE WILDCATS turn up in the exciting climax.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "The Lavender Hill Mob" is a 1951 heist comedy directed by Charles Crichton. The film is a gem from Ealing Studios, representative of their golden years directly outside of the post-WWII era. In actuality the studio is still in use within these contemporary years, but the heighted romanticism of the studio in British film history is directly in this era in which "The Lavender Hill Mob" was one of the banner titles in representation. Other films such as "Kind Hearts and Coronets" (1949) and "The Ladykillers" (1955) are two others that equally stand out as such. Having seen those two films (and really enjoying both in high regard) "The Lavender Hill Mob" easily was on my radar to get in.…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: Tension coiled within shadows, beauty sharpened to a blade — a film that unravels like a wound hidden beneath the flesh of ideology, exposing the raw nerve of moral compromise. A fractured symphony of resistance and submission, where every silence hums with unease and every action stains the soul, this is Godard’s brutal message about war and humanity. It’s not the violence of battlefields that consumes us here, but the quiet, intimate violence of conviction colliding with doubt, love entangled with betrayal. A film as austere as it's devastating, it whispers truths too sharp to linger, leaving only the echo of its scars.

reviews.author: cuckoochanel
reviews.text: Le Petit Soldat, Jean-Luc Godard’s sophomore effort shot immediately following the instantly seminal Breathless, is supposedly a commentary on the Algerian War of Independence but unfortunately plays out as a lazy, shallow representation of decolonization, and the political convictions within the film are portrayed as flimsy indoctrinations on both sides. It had moments of action and suspense, but the plot was inconsistent and truly of little importance to Godard. The final act was arid, futile rambling and the closing action was presented as a clumsy anticlimax with rushed voiceover.

It does makes the sad desperation underneath far more pronounced. It, of course, adds Anna Karina and politics into Godard's world. She is a much more immediate presence and his relationship towards her follow suit. The movie relationship towards the Algerian war are ambivalent and in some ways it function like some later subjects would for Godard as a good starting point for his musings which are at this point far more…

reviews.text: Written and directed by men, and honestly, it shows, but it's a relatively good gothic film nonetheless. Incest as a gothic trope is one of those interesting Victorian things that has to do with a general fear of the sexuality of women, and the cloistered life that accompanies strict patriarchal notions of decorum and courting and propriety, women as property, and the self-imposed confines of the upper-class due to fear of outsiders; fear of "diluting" a lineage, and other such classist, racist, ableist notions. Sean being physically handicapped was a nice touch for several reasons, but especially because it nodded to this, Rachel's defiance of not only old curses, but her rejection of the wrongness that is such a worldview.…

reviews.text: Fantastic little gangster/conspiracy neo-noir about a violent, manic bulldog who fancies himself a "legitimate" businessman. Hoskins is incredible in all his barrel-chested, receding-hairline glory, screaming and snarling various cockney obscenities and gruesomely torturing people (those POV shots of dudes strung up like meat!! the squibs and explosions!!) while fatalistically wandering this ruthless London he rose from the gutter to help build in his own image. Mackenzie gives it a tough, workman quality; the style forms an almost perfect Venn diagram with the 70s grit/grime and 80s pulsing synth existentialism (the weird sometimes jazzy, sometimes electronic prog-rock score is so sick) and the 24-hour timeframe structure of it really helps crank up the minute stresses of the character decision-making, which distracts just long enough for you to not realize the doomed fate of this film's truly sublime ending was probably sealed about an hour back.

reviews.text: Boasting no less than five different directors, The Longest Day is an attempt to meticulously recreate the events surrounding D-Day and the Normandy landings. It was hugely ambitious in its scope and fairly expensive for the time ($10m budget); the result is technically remarkable, but lacking in substantive commentary beyond documenting the pivotal operation that precipitated the end of WW2. It has a huge cast of recognizable stars: Robert Mitchum, John Wayne, Henry Fonda, Richard Burton, as well as the then relatively unknown Sean Connery (he would make his debut as 007 in the same year). The commitment to realism extends to having a range of native speakers filling out French and German roles, rather than using American or British…

It presents the whole attack as a unified effort, and there's a great buildup with perspectives from English, French, and German sides. Obviously, with such an ambitious plot, there's a huge, ambitious cast here, and it's a very good cast, ranging from the likes of Robert Mitchum to Richard Burton, and features a whole heap of cameos, but I think Connery is a highlight here.

They are mostly a bunch of cretins--barnstorming through "Vietnam" on their bikes and acting like a bunch of louts. Gross. Maybe it's my fault for having the wrong expectations. reviews.author: Justine Smith
reviews.text: What an unusual film. Creeps up in unexpected ways. The dialogue really snaps against a backdrop of very physical work and images. Was surprised that it was the final act where Mitchum's romantic intentions come to the forefront that the film really clicked with me. Hayward is one of the actresses who can really match Mitchum's soft-faced, broad-shouldered brutalism with the same intensity. The backdrop of bucking beasts is such a twisted backbone of restrained passion. Love party images with the camera on the ground, bringing us intimately into the chaos of celebrating another escape from death. There is also magic to the way that Ray is able to make open spaces feel claustrophobic and closed rooms feel expansive. Dreams might be able to transform physical realities, but they can't protect you from a bull.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: There's great specificity to the rodeo world depicted in The Lusty Men. It is one in which honesty (about some things) is cherished, and all men know precisely what others are feeling, sharing their highs and their lows. The men (and women) in this world are unfailingly honest about their desires, dreams, and hunger, but it is only the women who are allowed to voice fear or regret. Often, the men are attached to women who voice their shared fears but, even when they are alone, the experiences of the men overlap so completely that they don't need to speak of their fear to ensure that their friends and rivals know just how they feel.

reviews.text: Superior western that I never knew existed. Thanks TCM! A train robbery, a rich woman running away from her husband accidentally mixed up in the robbery, a sheriff and the rich husband in pursuit. It has all the traditional elements of a western but it's the dramatic weight of the relationships on screen that sets it apart. A gifted cast with Bo Hopkins, Lee J. Cobb, Sarah Miles, Jack Warden, George Hamilton and Burt Reynolds in his prime. The fistfight between Burt and Warden has to be one of the best filmed western fights ever! You can tell there's no stunt doubles and they were really throwing down bouncing from wall to wall, through windows and doors in long tough takes! A fucking great western. The director also did another little seen excellent western called Man in the Wilderness. Check it out.

reviews.text: Failed attempt at a Western with a feminist slant, sabotaged by rewrites of Eleanor Perry’s original script, which adds an emphasis on violence, rape and jealousy, and is further weighed down by Sara Miles’s numb performance. To be fair on Miles, she was going through major personal issues on set, which ended in the apparent suicide of her manager and lover, David Whiting, during the shoot, which you can read about here: <a href=“http://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Whiting#Death”The production problems do not excuse Richard C. Sarafian’s attempt to reproduce his brother-in-law, Robert Altman’s lyricism, which John Williams’s score also tries to reinforce over an inordinately long movie. Despite some good work by Burt Reynolds in serious mode, there are times when the film seems little more than an old fashioned, female romantic fantasy.

reviews.text: Entirely possible I’m pulling a Theme That Wasn’t There from this (or even that I am seeing something that is extremely obvious to everybody else who knows!!) but, I think this is an ironic tragedy about a depressed queer man desperately aching for meaning. Whether that’s meaning through companionship or through success or through patronage of someone else’s talents (in exchange for companionship) and if so, that makes it the saddest and most tender film in the Coen canon as far as I’m concerned! Shocked to see this from a duo who is often criticized for being cruel and cold (though I can see people seeing this movie as both.) Thornton’s reserved performance is really good. And you know I love me some Tony Shalhoub! Not really close to my favorite of their works, but certainly under-discussed IMO!

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: THE underrated Coen brothers movie. Written off at the time as some kind of half-assed Miller's Crossing, this movie features the Coens at their most empathetic and contemplative. The film noir trappings aren't simply another slick genre goof. The Man Who Wasn't There is an examination of the alienating forces at work in post-war America that made film noir possible, and one man's struggle to define himself in the face of them. Considering the Coen's penchant for deliberately obscure endings, the graceful, elegiac finale of Man is even more impressive.

This might not be my favorite Coen brothers film in terms of sheer enjoyment, but it is by far the most impressed I've been by one of their collaborations. The contrast of the black and white images filled with shadows and billows of cigarette smoke is the only way they…

reviews.author: Nakul
reviews.text: I'm on my third watch of The Man Who Wasn't There and it gets better each time. A brilliant homage to film noir genre from the Coen brothers. It's one of their best movies, yet least known of their filmography. Just like classic noirs this is a moody and stylish exercise in existentialism with hints of Coens' own absurdity, quirk and surrealism. Also Billy Bob Thornton gives one of his greatest performances. The b&w cinematography is work of art, it's the one of the best looking noir movies and rightfully it's Roger Deakins' favorite Coen brothers movie he shot.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Maybe the Coens' most inscrutable movie, and as an author pastiche it isn't quite as uncanny as Miller's Crossing (maybe Billy Wilder was on to something when he said James M. Cain's prose doesn't work on film), but the overall effect is as haunting as anything else they've done. Billy Bob Thornton, who I'm beginning to think will go down in history as a wasted genius, is absolutely incredible here, in a performance courageous enough to be totally flat (Robert Bresson had to hire nonprofessional actors to get stuff like this, and Thornton does it better). And even when the camera is focused on obscure symbols and motifs, it's always graceful and thrilling to watch - I loved the slow pan up the side of a building as Thornton ascends inside on an elevator.

reviews.text: Huston was a jack of all trades, tackling many genres throughout his lustrous career. However, if one had to place him into a box, into one genre, there's no doubt "adventure" would be it, as even his much dramatic endeavors always have that sense of adventure and this film in no exception. From frame to frame, painfully hard to watch and sustain interest in. Say what you like about Laughlin’s acting as Billy Jack, he has charisma in those movies. Comparing his screen presence there with his performance (and wardrobe) here is an amazingly effective lesson in the importance of picking out the right hat.

reviews.text: While not part of the official “Billy Jack” canon (but still from the same production company), “The Master Gunfighter”has the same spirit as that series. There’s an irresistible campiness to the Billy Jack films that’s carried over to “The Master Gunfighter” and the film is better for it. There’s no way to take this material seriously, so it’s best to balance an attempted sense of gravity with a mix of camp. Beyond that, the film is beautifully photographed and the score by Schifrin is exceptional. You can’t take any of it at face value, but that’s part of the fun.

But I also felt almost no emotionally connection to the story and its characters, apart from mild dislike of some of them. Part of that is the result of Hellinger's clever, ironically detached voiceover — it intentionally reminds us of how routine everything that happens is, but the constant patter about how un-special these…

The plot focuses on a police investigation of the murder of a young girl inside her own apartment. The film begins with a voiceover and the style is somewhere between a news report and a drama. I've seen the voice over used in a handful of noir films and normally I don't like it; but here it gives the film a real pulpy kind of feel and it actually works quite well - the injections of humour here and there help also. The plot itself is well put together - the investigation is always interesting and the film is careful…

In this case, the precise minutia of an undercover detective aboard a train, assigned to protect a gangster's widow from hired goons who don't want to see her testify on the other end of the ride we're stuck on with them. It's a very solid script filled with punchy hard-boiled dialogue, a propulsive sense of movement, and twisty, overlapping characters all pretending to be someone they aren't as they violently collide into one another. But ultimately it's Fleischer's fluid formal control…

reviews.text: The Narrow Margin is a lean, mean 71 minutes long tension filled Noir Thriller that takes a simple premise, take the woman from A to B on a train, and makes the most of it. Strong performances, a tight script and effective cinematography that highlights the claustrophobia on the train setting perfectly. Charles McGraw is a really strong lead here. He brings authority, masculinity and integrity but also a certain vulnerability to the part. This really is how to make a great B-Film Noir. No big stars and sure a limited budget but great direction from Richard Fleischer, an exciting story and the Train setting used to its full potential make it a must-watch of the genre.

L'intento è stringere un'alleanza con uno Stato tecnologicamente avanzato per calmare le tensioni mediorientali. Le lobby petroliere, che hanno interessi enormi in quelle terre, incaricano un sicario di assassinare Khalil.Il petrolio insanguinato,la coscienza politica,le eminenze grigie occidentali:sono solo alcuni dei temi affrontati da Richard C. Sarafian, nell' occasione regista e sceneggiatore di un thriller con una buona dose di adrenalina,fra utopia, fantapolitica e realismo. "Il Prossimo Uomo"inventa in verità poco o nulla di quanto descrive:al centro i poteri oscuri,le delicatissime reti internazionali e riflessioni estremamente attuali. Il mio attore preferito di sempre Sean Connery,nel ruolo di un influente diplomatico arabo,ha ancora il DNA del suo celeberrimo James Bond.

reviews.text: At first, The Nickel Ride seems like it might be a worthy successor to slow burn grimy neo-noirs like The Friends of Eddie Coyle, but, in the end, the screenplay feels underwritten. We know early on that Cooper, played by Jason Miller, is losing his ability to deliver for the local crime boss. However, there’s so much “waiting for the other shoe to drop” in the middle of this film; most of the time, the tension is primarily derived from old school strong silent type Cooper having to hang out with the stupendously annoying young whipper snapper Turner (Bo Hopkins).

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: The Nickel Ride centres around Cooper (Jason Miller), an enterprising but luckless criminal stuck somewhere on the middle rungs of the Los Angeles underworld. Fresh from the commercial and critical success of William Friedkin's The Exorcist, it finds Miller delivering an excellently understated performance, from the slouched way he walks to his heavy-lidded eyes that fit the exhaustion of one who's been doing his business for too long. Based on a screenplay by Eric Roth (Forrest Gump) and directed by veteran journeyman director Robert Mulligan (To Kill A Mockingbird), Mulligan confers some charitable assistance to the rest of the cast, helping to orchestrate a good set of supporting characters. Shot primarily in and around seedy bars and deteriorating warehouses within…

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Simmering paranoia neo-noir starring a fresh-off-Exorcist Jason Miller. The Nickel Ride follows the just-business day-to-day of Miller’s “key-man”, managing warehouses for the mob’s stolen goods. But that small-time banality turns to nervous suspense as the underworld tides turn; the narrative vice palpably tightens in mood and in the increasing intensity of Miller’s performance.

reviews.text: I think I'm getting a handle on the general Robert Mulligan vibe now. This is the second film I've watched by him whose first act left me assuming that nothing much of interest was going to take place, only to grab hold of me by the collar sometime during the second act and drag me through the intensity of the rest of the film. Although in subject matter and tone, there's not a lot of similarity between this and The Other, they do both have that in common - as well as a final kick in the guts right at the end which is almost disorienting in its sudden savagery.

reviews.author: Zach Nabors
reviews.text: In many ways it is the lesser known Friends of Eddie Coyle. Full disclosure I am a sucker for the low level gangster picture. One of the key differences between this a Yates’ film is that Mulligan is the superior filmmaker. Also, Eddie Coyle is about timing, brute force and physicality, where The Nickel Ride is more about intimacy, the in between moments, lighting that affects the mood of the film, which is a mourning. What the two films have in common is a world that is/has evolved and is leaving the old guard behind. The Nickel Ride is ultimately more sad than Eddie Coyle, because it never slips into sentiment, only slow desperation. Brown and Mulligan’s editing is as…

reviews.text: A rare headlining big screen vehicle for Jason Miller, on the heels of his EXORCIST Oscar nomination, THE NICKEL RIDE is one of the great unsung and little-seen crime dramas of the 1970s. Belonging to that same school of gritty, blue collar, working-stiff mob sagas like THE FRIENDS OF EDDIE COYLE and later examples like DONNIE BRASCO and KILLING THEM SOFTLY, THE NICKEL RIDE benefits from effective location work in seedy bars, pool halls, barber shops, and run-down offices, as low-level mob flunky Cooper (Miller) manages a bunch of storage warehouses for the local syndicate. He's in the midst of closing a big deal for an entire block of warehouse space and is getting constant pressure from Carl (John Hillerman),…

reviews.text: Como indica ya el primer y sombrío plano de la película, The Nickel Ride (1974) es la crónica de los últimos días de un hombre solitario. La cámara de Mulligan nos muestra sucesivamente un reloj que marca, implacable, el paso de los segundos, el rostro de Cooper (Jason Miller), que se despierta sobresaltado, no sabremos nunca por qué, y se levanta: al salir de cuadro, descubrimos que una joven, Sarah (Linda Haynes), compartía con él la cama, pero sigue durmiendo, ajena a los preocupados movimientos de su amante, confirmando, en el fondo, nuestra primera sensación; Coop está solo, como lo están todos los protagonistas de Mulligan, salvo en los breves instantes en que logran compartir su soledad con otra persona…

The casting of Pierce Brosnan in the lead role was a wise decision, as he fits the role of the seasoned spy quite well. Alongside Brosnan is Olga Kurylenko, possibly the best actor or actress in the film, who delivered an exceptional performance as the sort of lynchpin to the whole narrative. Beyond the pair's good performances, the project unfortunately doesn't have a lot going for it. If one were to watch this as their first spy/action film, they may have another takeaway, but for any seasoned viewer, the constant tropes and clichés are quite difficult to look past. reviews.text: Roger Donaldson directs Pierce Brosnan in a perfectly watchable and enjoyable spy thriller. Brosnan is a veteran CIA agent who is seen at the beginning working with a new agent (Luke Bracey) and the assignment doesn't go as planned. Flash forward, years later, a retired Brosnan is called back to duty by his handler (Bill Smitrovich) and he finds that the agent that was once under him is now gunning for him. Multiple twists keep this film interesting. Brosnan is quite good even if the movie doesn't always do him justice. Audiences will be able to see at least one twist coming from a mile away and although the film is rote and predictable at times, it is never a bad film. The cast is more than capable and the direction is crisp especially in the action sequences. THE NOVEMBER MAN is the perfect definition of an o.k. film

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: A medium-scale thriller whose wire-tight beginning and end make up for a saggy middle, "The November Man" finds Pierce Brosnan's ex-CIA assassin working to settle old scores. The story engine crackles with double-crosses and geopolitical intrigue, and, while its twists and turns do not always feel fresh, the narrative packs sufficient punch. Roger Donaldson's direction ensures the film's audience stays engaged through even the most token stretches, and Brosnan glowers through the work with a haunted and investable presence. The experience is solid.

reviews.text: You know you're in for a damn good time when the credits 'Based on a novel by Richard Stark' appear onscreen. And John Flynn, the director of "Rolling Thunder" and "Out for Justice," is a perfect fit for this material: "The Outfit" is a taut and driving little film that feels like a retro 40's crime picture that just so happened to be made in 1973—there's very little that ties this to a specific period beyond the automobiles, and Southern California is portrayed as an open wasteland, its wide empty spaces dotted with rundown motels, its urban centers little more than empty structures meant to house backroom poker games and racketeering operations.

reviews.author: ♠ Ben ♠
reviews.text: Flynn's bare-bones crime outputs spiked with practical and realistic grit are often a safe bet, "The Outfit", though a worthy and effortless watch, feels particularly sustained by its unpolished quality and serves better as the restrained raw sketch for the highly superior "Rolling Thunder". Still, plenty of washed-out texture and period sleaze to satisfy the pulp craving.

reviews.text: A painful misfire of a WW2 adventure story that fails on all fronts and manages to turn some potentially suspenseful material into utter trash. Anthony Quinn does one of his patented grumpy but good-hearted peasant acts, this time as a Basque shepherd hired by French resistance to guide a very important scientist, sought by the Nazis, over the snowy Pyrenees. He’s not amused when he learns that the guy’s sickly wife and his adult son and daughter are along for the trek. They’re followed every step of the way…

reviews.text: It's easy to imagine a version of this story, with the same (incredible) visuals, laid out as a well-modulated adventure story with highs, lows, emotional catharsis, comic relief, and so on. But this is definitely not that movie - it's closer to von Trier than Spielberg, and it seems calculated to give the audience the bleakest possible view of the universe around them. It ultimately comes close to being more oppressive than satisfying, but the overall portrait of helpless innocence in a cruel world is a lot more resonant than the stuff you find in more "commercial" animated features.

reviews.text: I'm leaving the Bay Area in a few days and I absolutely cannot wait to get out of here, but here's the contradiction: I could happily watch a movie set in San Francisco every day of my life. It's a city meant for celluloid and director Peter Hyams—lighting his own film, as he was oft to do—totally gets it, orchestrating a series of kinetic setpieces that take advantage of their scenic backdrops, like the opening car chase over the city's massive hills or a later footchase through Chinatown. (The climax is set in a nondescript warehouse but feels right out of a Hong Kong heroic bloodshed flick.) Sean Connery is great in a role he could have easily phoned in, while Mark Harmon...well, let's just say I was wishing the producers had opted for Michael Douglas, Mel Gibson, Don Johnson, or...you get the idea.

reviews.text: It wasn't intentional at all, but this ended up being a perfect follow-up to "Ocean's Elven" as another 'cool guys come together to pull off an improbable job' film. "The Professionals" roars out of the gate with confidence, it's fast-paced editing introducing us to our central characters and setting them off on their mission in very short order. The pacing rarely lets up from there. This is one of the few Hollywood Westerns that truly reminds me of Sergio Leone's work; not so much for its shot compositions or epic close-ups, but simply for its massive sense of scale (this movie feels BIG) and the sheer amount of action it crams into 120 minutes.

reviews.text: Supernatural in nature but just barely a horror film in the traditional sense, this tale of murder, reincarnation, and the dark irony of fate is one that really sticks with you if you're open to its oddball wavelength. Margot Kidder delivers the best performance by far as a woman seen bashing her husband with an oar in the opening nightmare sequence, which sends Michael Sarrazin across the country trying to find out why he feels like his past life is impacting him so horribly. Spooky, perverse, and way more sexual than you'd expect, the film goes to some pretty uneasy places and deserves to be more widely seen. Exceptional work by composer Jerry Goldsmith, building on the creepy electronic ideas he'd used in the earlier, thematically similar The Mephisto Waltz and highlighted by a really haunting main title theme. mondo-digital.com/peterproud.html

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: There’s no way around it, The Sacrifice feels like a farewell. Not just to cinema, but to life itself. Tarkovsky, standing at the edge of his own mortality, crafts a film that aches with the weight of a man reflecting on everything he has given away for his art, for his faith, for some fleeting sense of transcendence. Watching it, I couldn’t shake the thought that this wasn’t just another film, it was Tarkovsky’s own prayer, his last confession.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Like John Huston's The Dead, Tarkovsky's final film addresses regret. Having spent his days crafting ideas, speaking his mind, and ultimately sacrificing his life for art, Tarkovsky bows out with a film that, among other things, demands to know why no one takes action. At the same time, it feels like an apologia of his leaving behind his family and pursuing his filmmaking in Italy and Sweden, and it is an expression of deep, profound faith. It staggers me to see so much put into a film, so ably made.

reviews.text: The way movies document history has always intrigued me. Not as historical records in and of themselves, but as things flavored heavily by what's going on at the time they're made and released. Whenever I hear of a film being selected for preservation, I hope that they're literally putting a non-degradable copy in a frozen seed vault somewhere in the Arctic, because historians of a future age will likely find more of value in cinema than our warped records of discourse.

Wise doesn’t hold back, leaning heavily into the grandeur of the work. as if to complete its maximalist aesthetic, the film runs a lengthy three and a half hours. but it’s worth the price of admission for the stunning cinematography alone, all shot on location in Taiwan and Hong Kong. Wise let legendary cinematographer Joseph MacDonald go all out, bringing this picture to life in breathtaking Panavision,…

reviews.text: The most Russell Mulcahy film Russell Mulcahy ever made. The role models are Burton’s Batman and Beatty’s Dick Tracy, but this is pulpier, sillier and a lot less worried in auteurial justification than either because Mulcahy isn’t slumming with material, he is it. The production design is first rate, the cast has tons of great surface acting (so many great overactors here: Lone, McKellen, Curry, Boyle, Baldwin), there’s plenty of nice detail and great gruesome imagery that pop up in the middle of the most innocuous scenarios. Also The Shadow has a well calibrated sense of scale that mostly eludes current big budget cinema that is always pleasing.

It's an understated performance, but his little mannerisms really add to depth to his character. The Skull is a real moody film, featuring a small number of well realised locations - not least Cushing's study, which is packed full of interesting bric-a-brac. Director Freddie Francis really makes the best of the simple concept. There's a real focus on the visuals, including…

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: As irresistible (and endlessly exploitable) as Dixon and Greelee’s genre hook is, what makes this so powerful is its dedication to the politics behind its revolution, weaving scene after scene of discourse on the sorts of issues that all activist groups face — assimilation vs separatism, respectability vs direct action, ‘what happens when we’re our own enemy?’ — between the expected wish fulfillment action. Ironically, the most thrilling of those action scenes is the one that feels the most verité — a Chicago riot that drops Herbie Hancock’s (great) paranoia-funk score in favor of the sounds of the people. Not too many films that still feel dangerous 45+ years on.

reviews.author: Silversaxophone
reviews.text: Overwrought but interesting mystery, weighed down by its lack of humour and unnecessary CinemaScope ratio. The cast is heavyweight and in good form, including a young Judi Dench in a small role. Steven Boyd is wound up tight and intense as a former psychiatric patient motivated by an existential crisis of faith in his treatment by a therapist who apparently committed suicide. Pamela Franklin is also excellent as the Therapist’s daughter who engages him to find her father’s killer. Its largely daytime settings shot in London give it an unusual tone, and Charles Crichton builds up the suspense well. Cinematographer, Douglas Slocombe, does his best finding space for the exterior widescreen shots, lending a bleak air to proceedings; and his exterior lighting bleeds effectively into noir territory at times. Clearly influenced by Psycho, without the gothic horror, the script looks forward to another girl in psycho-peril in Marnie, though it lacks Hitchcock’s tightness of construction.

reviews.text: To be fair to The Tommyknockers, the novel it's adapting is not exactly Stephen King's peak as an author, but this miniseries also doesn't cover itself in glory either. It has most of the many flaws of the source material and by visualizing the bizarre stuff that happens on the page, I think it actually makes the unlikeable characters and wonky plotting even more evident than in the book. The changes it makes are mostly to better adapt the novel's awkward structure for a TV miniseries along with some major alterations to the ending stretches, but none of it improves the story by much either as it's mostly still an incoherent mess. What I do like is how it expands the townpeople's roles in the story, but that's not enough to make The Tommyknockers much good as it's just a dull and overlong adaptation of a dull and overlong novel.

reviews.text: I've never been so glad not to be fluent in Ukrainian sign language. a fascinating reconfiguring of silent cinema modes, THE TRIBE does remarkable things with deep focus, however indebted to the Romanian New Wave those techniques might be. not entirely sure that the film had to be *that* brutal (at times it feels like an affect), but it certainly lubricates this bracingly unique portrait of sub-worlds and the price of escaping from them.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Impressively staged (each scene is a single unbroken take), and in case you hadn't, uh, heard, entirely in untranslated sign language. Too bad that's in service of a crushingly banal and generically bleak drama that utterly fails to explore the experience and stigma of being unable to hear or that condition's attendant problems of communication. Putting us in a similar headspace about the confusion over details that a deaf person might experience in the hearing world only works if there's some narrative or structural ambiguity, but there's none here (admittedly a testament to the clarity of the single takes and performances). Also the only female characters are sexual tokens. I'm only not calling this bullshit because of the formal rigor.

reviews.author: julianblair
reviews.text: I gave this three stars for sheer audacity by Roger Corman. This is one of a trio of particular ultra-cheap exploitations he made in the late 1950s. (Bucket of Blood and Little Shop of Horrors being the other two). Viewed as drive-in trash, they all had some devil-may-care wonderful weirdness woven into the horror, buxom ladies and rock-bottom budgets. It gives me pause though to imagine what unwary teens at the drive-ins, looking for simple monster thrills, actually thought about them.

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: About half of this film is the greatest movie you'll ever see: featuring the 50 foot woman herself Allison Hayes skulking around as an evil-doing witch in a low-cut gown, transforming into a black cat, summoning demonic line-dancers and making deals with Satan. Corman is smart to know what he's got there and films her entrance from the ankles up. A+. All of that is excellent. The other half of the movie is some z-grade hypnotist bullshit. Considering the film was shot in about a week and a half and for no money whatsoever that's alright.

Thy script also doth baffle thine audience and couldest, nay, shouldest have used more work. However! Thou hath chosen fine women for thine audience to lookest at. Allison Hayes most especially.

reviews.text: I enjoyed gruff mama Lillian Gish and horny virgin Doug McClure. Everything else about this is cacadoodoo, from the comically miscast Audrey Hepburn to the comically incongruous orchestral score.It takes nearly an hour of hoedowns and jibber-jabber to get to the plot, which involves Hepburn being of unknown parentage. John Huston seems lost in the wide open spaces, his camera is not intimate enough to convey much emotion. Lancaster and Hepburn have no chemistry at all which makes it hard to care about their awkward lurch into incest. The endless slaughter of Kiowa people makes it hard to take any meaning from the movie's nod to racism. By the end I was rooting for the Kiowa to kill them all. Way down on the list of Huston classics, maybe at the bottom.

reviews.author: Mario Melendez
reviews.text: For days I had been craving to watch a horror anthology and what better option than to see this film produced by Amicus and that after Tales from the Crypt came to this sort of sequel in 1973, which is also based on the stories of the EC Comics series. As in the previous film, here we meet five people who coincide in the elevator of an office building: the elevator takes them to the sub-basement, to a vault, where they all get locked in. As they wait for someone to come to help them, each of them recounts a dream that seems to haunt them night after night.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Another delightful anthology horror film from Amicus. The Vault of Horror is the follow up to Tales from the Crypt and runs very much along the same lines, with another five deserving victims retelling the stories of the evil things they did in life. This one really ramps up the comedy element - the film is clearly fully aware of how ludicrous it all is, and plays up to this brilliantly. The first story is rather simple but nicely sets the tone with its ghost town full of gourmet vampires. A glass full of blood is declared "quite a nice bouquet"! Terry-Thomas is perfectly cast as a neat freak in the subsequent story that sees the film reach its comedy…

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: More adaptations from the classic William Gaines comics, as five men are let out of an elevator in the sub-basement to tell tales of their own demise. First up, Daniel Massey tracks down his sister (Anna Massey) and attempts to murder her in a town filled with vampires. Then Terry-Thomas and Gynis Johns show us the inevitable end to the Marie Kondo method of tidying. The third story, featuring Curd Jürgens and Dawn Addams adapts one of my favorite stories from the old comic books, about the Indian Rope Trick, but sadly the movie version tones down the conclusion of the comics (here, we see bloodstains. In the comic, body parts are flying everywhere. God bless EC Comics!). The fourth…

reviews.text: Another solid horror anthology based off early horror comics. Honestly I enjoyed each segment of "Tales From the Crypt (1972)" a touch more than these segments, but that's not to say these were bad. There wasn't a single segment here that failed entertain. They were good, they just didn't seem to meet the high bar that the anthology from the previous year set. Also the original Crypt Keeper's crypt was a bit more of a fun tie-in than the hotel basement in my opinion. I'm actually looking forward to diving into the Tales from the Crypt TV series more after these.

reviews.text: The Vault of Horror aka Tales from the Crypt 2 from Amicus Productions is a 1973 sequel/ follow up to the hugely successful 1972 film Tales From The Crypt. Subotsky and Rosenberg hand the direction over to master craftsman, Roy Ward Baker, who tries his luck with another five chumps embarking on a supernatural lift that transports them to a octagonal room where they each share some recurring dream experience amongst the group. Unlike the preceding Tales from the Crypt, we get no Crypt Keeper guiding us this time, just the five shemps shooting the shit, as Britishy shemps do.

The short length of the movie obviously means that each short is actually really short (most run 15 minutes or less) and it is a service to the quality of the film that none of them are bad or boring. Instead, they are all pretty fun and even a little lighthearted with some dry comedy thrown in, while also having a few nicely gruesome moments in them to up the horror aspect. reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Starring Robert Vaughn as a one-time spy, dragged back into the game against his will, The Venetian Affair is transparently built to exploit Vaughn's fame as Napoleon Solo, though it's just a lucky coincidence that the film's title sounds like the name of a Man from U.N.C.L.E. episode — it was the name of the source novel, too. And there are certainly elements of Solo here, in the incapability of Vaughn's character (Bill Fenner) to keep his dick in his pants, as well as the occasional, familiar smirk. But Fenner is far darker and more tired than Solo ever was, and Vaughn is at his best when he embraces these things in small ways: his slightly pained expression at the…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: There is one perfect moment in The Venetian Affair; it comes when former CIA agent Bill Fenner (Robert Vaughn), pressed into working for the Agency again, realizes that the lonely secretary he thought he'd seduced the previous night was, in fact, a CIA operative. His mouth literally drops open, he slumps slightly, and he closes his eyes for a moment, a miserable almost-smile playing across his lips. Because, he thinks, of course she's CIA. Of course she is — only a fuckup like him would think he was picking up a woman, only to find out that she'd be literally assigned to fuck up.

The Venetian Affair was beautifully shot on location in Venice and bears a much darker tone than the campy TV series that made Vaughn famous. Vaughn plays Bill Fenner, an alcoholic journalist for an international wire service who is sent to Venice to report on a terrorist bombing at a peace conference. This is a serious spy thriller that starts out in a somber John Le Carré vein, but then enters into the farther-fetched paranoia territory of The Manchurian Candidate or The Parallax View. The plot is low on action but nonetheless high on suspense. It…

reviews.text: Let's talk nihilism. Philosophically I generally subscribe to the nihilist principle that life has no meaning. I'm also pessimistic and deeply cynical. However nihilism is not a justification for immorality. The Wild Bunch seems to miss this. It presents a world without hope or redemption, just harsh temporary survival leading to an inevitable death. Where the film missteps for me is that it replaces the nihilistic setup with a hedonistic tone, revelling in the violence to play things as a macho male fantasy. The Wild Bunch is openly sadistic in its prolonged violent sections. The storytelling is both misogynist and racist, without reason. There's also clear animal abuse, especially regarding horses. Although always unforgivable, such mistreatment doesn't always ruin art for me.…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: The Wild Bunch is an American western classic, and a must-see for any moviegoer. Its brutal, uncompromising nature puts it in the same echelon as classics such as The Godfather and Apocalypse Now. Directed by Sam Peckinpah, the film follows a gang of outlaws on their moral decline as local authorities pursue them. Peckinpah masterfully crafts his characters and story, carefully blending themes of mortality, loyalty and the effects of violence. The performances of William Holden, Ernest Borgnine and Robert Ryan capture the desperation of the outlaws' situation and the desperation of their loyalty to one another. This is complemented by a timeless score and stunning cinematography which vividly captures the desolation of the desert Southwest. The Wild Bunch is Peckinpah's finest achievement and has gone on to inspire generations of filmmakers, providing an invaluable insight into a time and place long forgotten. Essential viewing and a classic in every sense of the word.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A reminder that westerns were "revisionist" pretty much from the start. The frontier rendered as a hellscape of billowing sand, rain and snow, buffeting an increasingly unhinged Lillian Gish, who puts in her most expressionistic performance as a beleaguered woman swept around until she cannot think straight. This is the West as a literal howling void, a realm that exists as an unceasingly hostile force of nature outside what few shelters have been erected to protect settlers from a world so much bigger than they. The climax, of Gish being so violently buffeted that the film turns into an extended hallucination while maintaining Sjöstrom's paradoxical brutal realism, is among the scariest sequences of the silent era.

reviews.text: The Yakuza is a film I put off for a while due to not being wowed by its summary, but after a watch, it's a great film that mixes noir sensibilities with the Japanese code of honor to create something that feels fresh and fascinating. Its exploration of the Japanese underworld doesn't feel glamorizing but treats it as a structure bound by tradition, and it feels like a realistic depiction even if my knowledge of Japan is lacking. There are sprinkles of violence here, but most of it feels sudden and necessary and not entirely forced, but it's certainly more a slow-burn thriller than an action flick.

reviews.text: The best thing I can say about Roger Corman's racing film is that it looks great. The sweeping locations across 1960's Europe combined with that film grain look makes for a visually appealing movie. The use of real life racing footage is also nicely integrated. However, I didn't really buy any of the character drama. The film centers around a cocky race car driver and a writer out to smear him and nether of them are particularly likable. The racer goes on a big character journey and I wasn't sold on it at all. And while the racing scenes are cool to watch, it is pretty hard to tell which character is supposed to be in what car so you can't really follow the race.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: A bittersweet comedy about moving around while watching and fantasizing. The detective business is of course a thinly veiled metaphor for cinephilia and give it to Bogdanovich to make it at same time idealized and creepy. There's a wistful quality for the action, the way it is both takes place in fantasy New York and live on the strengths of its location shooting. It plays at same time as the closest an American film come to Demy and something like benign De Palma. One dreams of older great movies, but arrive into something else. The acting is terrific throughout (particularly Gazarra who is as good in his two PB movies as in his three Cassavetes ones). with Bogdanovich downplaying dialogue for a choreography of stolen glaces. It is all a big marvelous dream that everyone involved seems aware it is not build to last. Films end, after all.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A film whose various plot points are based in real life events that would become tragic, yet the film's effervescent energy pushes all of that out of mind until the melancholy of its final images let reality seep back in. Voyeurism as a series of coy glimpses, screwball filtered through a rough-'n-tumble New Wave prism, with the camera always darting after every turned head and reversing back as watchers and watched enter into a series of pas-de-deux that adds a sense of wistfulness to the mania. This movie moves fast, but measured enough that the collision and reconfiguring of romantic lines until each is sorted out into the ideal partner is not merely zany but a relief, stripped of much of the resistance of screwball partners who don't realize how alike they are. Instead, they are relieved to find a kindred soul, even if some stories end sadder than others. Bogdanovich's endearing pastiches here give way to something approaching grace.

reviews.author: brendanowicz
reviews.text: It should go without saying that in the annals of film history, and even of the auteur theory, there are ranked so many despicable and problematic personalities that Peter Bogdanovich's humdrum caddishness doesn't even merit an honorable mention, so it shouldn't be so very hard to admit that sometimes you had to hand it to him. Nobody wants to think of themselves as a Bogdanovich, though: a bad husband, a brown-noser, an incorrigible skirt-chaser whose grasping for the bygone era of Hollywood was evident in every frame he ever put to screen. But sometimes the critic just has to admit that he is that man, or that the seductive alchemy of screen romance simply has the power that it has, and a film like They All Laughed compels one to acknowledge that this is, at least within a certain tradition, exactly what movies are supposed to do. It's heaven.

reviews.text: A film as emotional and heartbreaking as it can be sensitive and touching, dealing with strong political themes that will upset you and horrify you to your core. We dive deep into loyalty and prejudice, and we see the ignorance of a child blindly following the misplaced and extremist nationalist ideologies of a former convict. It's a very interesting and, at times, horrific look at what the lack of a father figure can do to an uneducated young boy who seeks guidance... latching on to the first person who shows him that fatherly presence. This movie was absolutely brilliant in its raw and realistic execution. Certain scenes put my stomach in a blender. The camera work, lighting, and shot selections all added to the raw nature of this film. It's a ridiculously tough watch (especially as we moved to the back half of the film) and we drill into English racism and what fear can do to a young boy.

National treasure, and whether or not he'll ever truly climb the Hollywood chain, he'll always be remembered as one of the greats here. reviews.author: Lil Bo Deek
reviews.text: That the same bloke who made "Batman & Robin" also made "Tigerland" is pretty staggering. Gritty and restrained, "Tigerland" is a powerful look at the training process Vietnam grunts had to go through on American soil, depicting a military regime turned savage by a war that demanded it. Colin Farrell broke out on the back of his work here, and he's pretty fantastic, exuding charm and conflict as a cadet desperately trying to evade service. Schumacher's visuals almost pitched at the level of documentary, which compliments the drama with a full-bodied realism. It's rare to see a movie tackle these ideas and successfully extol a message on them within a 101 minute frame, but "Tigerland" does it rather wonderfully.

reviews.text: Near perfect. One of the best time-travel films I've seen, in part because of the juxtaposition of its intricate script & the simplicity of its setting. You would never guess that traveling only mere hours back in time would serve for such a compelling narrative, but "Timecrimes" pulls it off with brilliant pacing and a plot woven with intelligent twists, not ones that pander to its audience or insult their intelligence. Karra Elejalde [Hector] delivers a tremendously compelling lead performance[s], and is anchored by a keen supporting role from the film's director Nacho Vigalondo as a scientist in the wrong place at the wrong time[s]. For my money, I have trouble deciding which low-budget time-travel feature is better, "Timecrimes" or "Primer". And that is high praise in and of itself.

reviews.text: The concept of Tough Guys is kind of perfect. Burt Lancaster and Kirk Douglas play old gangsters who have been paroled in 1986 after serving thirty years in the penitentiary together for bank robberies. The classic Hollywood stars, each around 70, have to adjust to the ways the world has changed while they were locked up.

reviews.author: _pashabo
reviews.text: Harry and Archie --- friends released from prison into an unrecognizable world: aerobics, AI, obsessed youth, forgotten generation.The film works on the Rip Van Winkle principle --- fell asleep under a king, woke up in the middle of a revolution.It's a marathon of brilliant scenes: from the prison release and a pigeon shitting on a cop, to AI voices in cars and stores, to hilarious aging mobsters with equally ancient bodyguards. :DThe final scene is magnificent. Legends don't retire --- they exit like legends.This is the seventh and final film Lancaster and Douglas made together. Their on-screen chemistry is real because they walked decades together.A film about adaptation that hurts, about a world that moved on without asking permission, about choosing dignity over invisibility. But it never gets heavy --- stays light, sharp, funny. These two old pros know how to raise hell.Pure joy.

Trespass is removed from public conscience, nevertheless it should forever leave Nicolas Cage and Nicole Kidman secretly ashamed, and was a career-ending blight for director Joel Schumacher. It aspires to be a home invasion thriller that sets the bar above what’s been done before, but it’s bupkis –– the twists aren’t wallops, instead they are thuds to common sense. Worse, it manages to be one of the most unpleasant thrillers you could ever see. I don’t want to see the beautiful auburn-haired Kidman in a cocktail dress being slapped and whacked, hair-pulled and elbowed, and thrown to the ground. reviews.text: A weird take on the “bikers menacing squares in the desert” subgenre. Igo Kantor (who produced Kingdom of the Spiders, and worked with Ed Wood AND Russ Meyer) composed the oddball synth score for this. I could imagine going into my local record store and hearing the free jazz guy that works there listening to it. The main girls in trouble are all pretty good and play off of one another well. If your into this 70s babes in peril genre, then go for it, but I prefered the nastier Savage Abduction and The Love Thrill Murders, and if you’re into Crown International flicks, then go for it, but I prefer their comedy romps like Beach Girls and Pom Pom Girls. Trip With Teacher is just sort of stuck in the middle, I guess.

reviews.text: This feels like the comic book flipside to Coffy, cut from the same ragged cloth, but making that roughness go down easier with flashy costumes, coke-sprinkled funerals, and kitty kat comic relief. What really impresses me, though, is that even with all of the cartoonish dressings, this still has a moral center -- it's not glorifying the violence or the lifestyles that these rhinestone-studded eyepatch-wearing pimps live. Behind the dynamite clothes and the badass dialogue, these characters are all damaged humans doing what they have to in order to survive. The countless exploding squibs and gouts of paint blood splattered across the screen only serve as an exclamation point to all of this.

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: My favorite Blacksploitation film, easily. There’s a chill, low-stakes feel to TT thanks to Kaplan’s lighter touch with the harder material, the comradarie between Hayes and Alan Weeks (who nearly steals the movie every chance he gets) is almost enough to fuel the film and the style is way more confident and bold than an AIP film should be, especially with some of the camera angles and transitions between scenes. And that score…god DAMN. Just the right amount of Corman cameos (Dick Miller!) and low-budget flourishes to earn it the subgenre title and a hell of a good time. The editing by Michael Kahn (Spielberg’s long time cutter) is FANTASTIC; there’s one gunfire scene involving a dummy (IYKYK) that is truly shocking and visceral. Yaphett Koto gets one HELL of a climax. PS: “I’m Joe Dante”Badass Masterpiece.Happy 50th, Truck.

reviews.author: Magic Marzipan
reviews.text: One of the unspoken comforts of watching a film that originates from your own culture is that you already know the language and traditions that inform it. Even without explicitly studying the Western canon, we learn almost by osmosis about the myths and ethos and imagery of our cultural traditions. I never read the Bible, for example, but I grew up in the U.S. and was exposed mostly to American and English literature until college. In those literary traditions, the Bible echoes out everywhere. Literary curiosity in my mid-20s inspired me to read the book of Genesis, and I was not entirely surprised when it felt intensely familiar. It's one of the pillars of Western culture, after all.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: Apichatpong Weerasethakul is operating on a level unlike anyone else today: meshing interpersonal relationships with mortality and dreams in the most unique way you’ll ever see, an ever-expanding dissection of resurrection - what happens after death, and what happens to people around you once you're gone? Every time I go into one of his films, I find it so easy to let go, floating on a foundation of natural outdoor vibrations (noise-cancelling headphones watch always) and the idea of spiritual self-reflection, always leaving with so much to discuss and think further on - not films for everyone, of course, but I can’t help but love the philosophical tones and beautifully mythological imagery. This film being the one with truly everything going for it. feels odd to call a film centred around death like this beneficial for mental well-being (even given its optimism), but occasionally it's just what I need - as long as I'm in the right frame of mind.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: This is one of those films I've read about for years. I had some preconceptions about its tone, themes, and imagery, and many of them played out more or less as I expected. Part of that is a passing familiarity with Weerasethakul. On paper, he seems like a director I would wholeheartedly love, but in practice, there's always something to his style that holds me back. It's in mood of the film. Instead of allowing me the opportunity to drink in the quiet beauty, there's some violence, some sexual tension, some dangerous remove that keeps me from embracing it. Boonmee comes closer than either of his previous films that I've seen to breaking that barrier.

reviews.text: Undisputed won’t be one of the films Walter Hill is remembered for, but it’s still a very sturdy programmer, and along with Bullet to the Head, one of his better films since the turn of the century. While Snipes received top billing, Undisputed is really Ving Rhames’ flick, and the character actor puts in the work, turning in one of his signature performances, full of menace and brash bravado only one of the top boxers in the sport could muster. Snipes’ role is somewhat limited, and his character is nothing if not stoic, so don’t expect another Sidney Deane “swaggerific” performance from him. While the two leads are good together, the supporting cast is aces. Hill gets a scene stealing…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Undisputed" is a 2002 film directed by Walter Hill. The film follows a narrative of two boxers, each dominate in their different worlds that eventually collide. Wesley Snipes plays Monroe "Undisputed" Hutchen, a resident of Sweetwater Maximum Security Prison and the dominate rotating penitentiary boxing champion for the past decade. This title is threatened when Ving Rhames character of George "The Iceman" Chambers, the World Heavyweight Champion on the outside world, is sent to serve time in the same prison. Hutchen is the kind of person who is never hot-headed, only saving fights for the ring, but Chambers cannot stand to know that there is a potential opportunity (or threat) to his status within the same facility.

reviews.text: Wowwwww. I freely admit I might be overrating this, but only because it's so crazy/satisfying to see a sequel to Universal Soldier of all things and discover it to be a quasi-Lynchian surrealist nightmare, almost completely (if not completely) uninterested in fulfilling the crowd-pleasing requirements of the form. The emphasis isn't on adrenaline, despite the fact that it's pretty much packed with wall-to-wall violence, but instead on mind-bending abstraction, along with a meditation on memory that's worthy of Philip K. Dick. reviews.author: ButtNugget
reviews.text: Shane Carruth’s alluring Upstream Color is Invasion of the Body Snatchers for the art house crowd, with hogs replacing pods and identity crisis substituting for McCarthyism. That may be an awfully crude comparison but it’s the overall gist I got as I watched this beguiling, beautiful film. One thing’s for sure, the plot’s mind-control science fiction aspect plays only second fiddle to the transcendent yet universal overarching theme of emotional resonance in people in the vein of Henry David Thoreau’s literature. This is an ambitious, dense, slippery piece of experimental filmmaking with big ideas and Carruth conveys these enthralling notions through a masterwork in poetic editing, shot composition, and aural design.

reviews.text: Savage cinema. Pure relentless ugly and unflinching in its dedication to exploitation less savory aspects. The only escape is Carpenter’s formal control and the beauty of his scope compositions. In some ways, it is a rework of his early equal catholic tormented peek at pure evil Prince of Darkness with the elegant Langian/Tourneurian proposition stripped in name of some idea of American essentialism (western setting, Peckinpah violence, a very in your face contemporary attitude out of the sub Tarantino school). It is a big tell that not only this co-star the lesser of all Baldwins, but Carpenter’s Dracula wannabe is played by D-grade DTV star Thomas Ian Griffith. I’m pretty sure that outside of Harris’ Cop, no movie ever allowed James Woods to channel every vile instinct he cherishes as Vampires does. It is the anti-Bram Stoker’s Dracula. I saw this twice on Brazilian opening week.

But there's another way in which Viceroy's House is timely and much needed too - given the post-Brexit and hungry Heritage desire to depict Churchill as the great British hero it is refreshing to see Chadha's film reminds us that the man was far from saintly, dismissing India and its people as 'primitive' and using them in…

reviews.text: It has its flaws but seeing the story from an Indian perspective is a truly refreshing change. As an accurate historical document it probably wouldn't hold up, but it can join a whole battalion of films in that regard. A little too much white guilt in places. Mostly it feels utterly embarrassing to call yourself British when so clearly reminded of the past atrocities caused by your home land. There are personal reasons why this film resonates with me so much and I'm more than happy to selfishly overlook its issues.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: This gets a lot less interesting once the bad seeds sprout and the focus shifts to their goofy white hair and glowing eyes and their decidedly campy shenanigans like making mom stick her hands in boiling water. But the first 40 minutes or so are an eerie, occasionally even intimate look at an isolated community in crisis. In Carpenter's world Fordian collectivism crumbles in the face of uncontrollable fear, and he doesn't ignore the idea that the women, always a lynchpin of that collective, are traumatized by a literal alien invasion of their bodies. I continue to think this is one of Carpenter's weakest films but perhaps unsurprisingly it's proven to still be a grower.

The original book by John Wyndham and the initial film adaptation made sense in a culture steeped in anticommunist/anti-'youth movement' Baby Boom apocalyptics, wherein one culture is growing and harboring within itself a counterculture founded upon alien aesthetics, alien values, alien consciousness, which will overthrow and displace the host. This film could be perhaps be remade today, too, as an allegory of social media - as - hive mind. In 1995, however, what concerned parents was the fear that their kids would grow up as sociopathic murderers, 'superpredators', anesthetized by potent marijuana and crack cocaine and tv programs featuring…

reviews.text: Wake Island deserves credit for being one of Hollywood’s first major productions to tackle the U.S.’s entry into WWII. It focuses on Japan’s invasion of the titular military base in the Pacific Ocean. Battle began shortly after Pearl Harbor but didn’t end until two weeks later, thanks to the tenacity of the Marines stationed there. Reportedly, screenwriter W.R. Burnett began the story even before the battle’s outcome was known. The speed with which it was rushed into release shows in its lack of nuance, but its freshness struck a chord with audiences, critics, and other filmmakers. It was a big hit and earned a nomination for Best Picture. Subsequent WWII movies quickly eclipsed it in our collective memory, though. It’s…

This World War II film --- essentially a propaganda flick, given its release year of 1942 -- is concerned with the U.S. Marines' futile attempt to hold Wake Island, a speck in the Pacific Ocean, in the days following the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor late in 1941. The Americans got this speck back a month after the Japanese surrendered in 1945, but of course this movie couldn't know that. For the record, it's usually wise to wait until a real-life story ends before trying to dramatize that story. But this battle's…

reviews.author: Quintin
reviews.text: Wake Island depicts a battle that recently happened with American troops with notably impressive explosions for 1942 and… that’s about it. The movie can’t help but be propagandic with its depiction of the war since it’s obviously still going on at the time of release but it feels unnecessary. The movie is designed to emotionally manipulate the horrors of what is happening to their brothers across the world. It’s not a story, there’s nothing to spoil about the ending because it literally doesn’t have an ending. The movie cuts to narration that is saying the ending is still being written, outside the theatre our brave soldiers are fighting for freedom as we speak… which is powerful in the moment and understandably why the movie was nominated for Best Picture but it feels meaningless to anyone watching the film even five years later.

But because the film is made at the onset of the war, we can't actually sit with that defeat or the loss of men and are instead immediately hounded by propaganda messaging about how the troops will strike back at the Japanese with vengeance. I get it, thems was the times. It's still not very good. The first act is also corny and simplistic. The movie…

The sheer scale of this production will likely never be matched again—hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of extras in full costume, grand aerial battle sequence photography that would make Ridley Scott blush, slow Zooms on Rod Steiger's nail-chewing little gremlin grimace. If this is really the historical epic that killed historical epics, you can understand that its failure is not in execution per se, but in design; by elongating an entire 135-minute feature across a single battle (with a result known by every living human), there's an inherent absence of drama. But just seeing it mounted is special, like seeing an IBM Selectric typewriter or a '57 Chevy still in use. They used to make these and they sure did die hard.

The first half lacks pace and is overloaded with political maneuvering, making the wait for battle feel excessively slow. Although the war sequences have an impressive logistical achievement with thousands of extras and large-scale action, Bondarchuk’s direction feels empty, without a sense of urgency or real emotion.

He obliterates every rule of narrative storytelling, breaking the fourth wall, grinding the film to a halt to allow characters to spout Marxist rhetoric for minutes on end, almost daring the viewer to stop watching. Godard is telling the audience that every cheap thrill they yearn to experience at the movies is trite and meaningless and the very format of narrative cinema an enabler of exploitation. reviews.text: Hardly just an opportunistic snapshot of a celebrity's public implosion, Josh Kriegman and Elyse Steinberg's inside look at the spectacular failure of Anthony Weiner's 2013 mayoral campaign in New York is one of the best documentaries ever made about a political scandal. A passionate fighter for the middle class who nuked his career by accidentally tweeting a selfie of his bulge, the indefatigable Weiner is nothing less than a true American tragedy — but this hilarious and humbling portrait rightly sees him as so much more. At once a portrait of media sensationalism, a marriage under fire, and of a city that felt betrayed by its best hope, the movie is so unsparing that when they finally ask Weiner why he let them film him, the disgraced ex-congressman can only shrug.
